# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L318-L318


# Vulnerability details

In `RestakeManager`'s `CalculateTVLs` function, the TVLs for each operator delegator by individual token, total for each OD, and total for the protocol is calculated. In the second inner for loop, `CalculateTVLs` function also records withdraw queue's token values, however the indexing is wrong, instead of looking up each collateral token's value it always looks up the first token's value using every other token's balance of withdraw queue.
## Impact
High - leads to wrong TVL calculation.

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Change `collateralTokens[i]` to `collateralTokens[j]` on line 318.

# Vulnerability details

`RestakeManager`'s `deposit` function will take user deposits and if there is a buffer deficit use it to fill the withdraw buffer. The issue arises when the amount user wants to deposit is smaller than or equal to `bufferToFill`, as after buffer filling operations, `deposit` function tries to deposit an amount of 0 to `operatorDelegator`, leading to a revert.

## Impact
Users won't be able to deposit when the amount they want to deposit is smaller than buffer to fill.

## Tools Used

## Impact
Users front-running slashing and penalty updates will be stealing from other users.

Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ensure that the correct amount of penalties is distributed evenly among stakers.

raw_row.title: There would be undercollateralization or insolvency when L2 xezETH mints are greater than L1 ezETH locked

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L139-L201
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L245-L266
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L434-L442


# Vulnerability details

`xRenzoDeposit` on L2 chains would mint xezETH to users that deposits. After some amount has been accumulated, `sweep` would be called to transfer the `WETH` to L1. On L1, `xRenzoBridge` would deposit the ETH to restakeManager. The provided `ezETH` is locked and the `xezETH` is burnt. It is burnt so that it could be minted when users bridge their `xezETH` from L2 to L1 via connext bridge.

Simplified version of [xReceive](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L139-L201)
```
// Unwrap the WETH
uint256 ethAmount = IWeth(address(wETH)).withdraw(_amount);

// Deposit it into Renzo RestakeManager
uint256 ezETHAmount = restakeManager.depositETH{ value: ethAmount }();

// Approve the lockbox to spend the ezETH
ezETH.safeApprove(address(xezETHLockbox), ezETHAmount);

// Send to the lockbox to be wrapped into xezETH
uint256 xezETHAmount = xezETHLockbox.deposit(ezETHAmount);

// Burn it - it was already minted on the L2
IXERC20(address(xezETH)).burn(address(this), xezETHAmount);
```


However, there's nothing that ensures that the `ezETH` locked by `xRenzoBridge` on L1 is equal or greater than the `xezETH` minted on L2. This should have been a spec or invariant in the protocol.
```
ezETH locked >= xezETH totalSupply
```
If `ezETH` locked is less than `xezETH`, the protocol wouldn't be able to provide `ezETH` if every user withdraws.

In an ideal situation, `ezETH` locked would be less `xezETH` supply. This is mainly because exchange rate is expected to be increasing, and there's a lag between the exchangeRate used for mint on L2 vs the one used for deposit on L1. It might take several hours or days for exchangeRate to move from L1 to L2 and L2 ETH to move to L1 for deposits. A lot of things could change within that period including significant price movement.

This undercollateralization would be made worse with every deposit on every L2 chain.

## Impact
`xezETH` supply could be greater than the `ezETH` locked and that could lead to insolvency. There's not enough `ezETH` backing every `xezETH`

## Proof of Concept
* At hour 0, price of 1.0 is sent from L1
* At hour 4, the price arrives at L2
* At hour 23, the price is used to mint 100 xezETH at 1.0 price
* At hour 40, the tokens are sweeped and sent to L1
* At hour 44, the tokens are deposited to restakeManager at 1.01 price and therefore 99 ezETH is minted and locked
* user bridges 100 xezETH to L1
* user withdraws 99 xezETH for 99 ezETH in lockbox
* There's 1 xezETH that can not be redeemed

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ensure that ezETH locked is greater than or equal to xezETH minted.



## Assessed type

ERC20

Manual Review

Add balance of collateral token in deposit queue to the protocol TVL in `calculateTVLs` and revisit `depositTokenRewardsFromProtocol` cause TVL logic is different.

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L299-L307


# Vulnerability details

BRIDGE_ADMIN is not a trusted role according to the contest page. They are given access to recover ERC20 that are `accidentally` sent to the [xRenzoBridge](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L299-L307)

```solidity
/*
* @notice  Sweeps accidental ERC20 value sent to the contract
* @dev     Restricted to be called by the bridge admin only.
* @param   _token  address of the ERC20 token
* @param   _amount  amount of ERC20 token
* @param   _to  destination address
*/
function recoverERC20(address _token, uint256 _amount, address _to) external onlyBridgeAdmin {
    IERC20(_token).safeTransfer(_to, _amount);
}
```

If `xReceive` fails, the bridge WETH would be sent to the contract address. This is from [connext docs](https://docs.connext.network/developers/guides/handling-failures#reverts-on-receiver-contract).

> If the call on the receiver contract (also referred to as "target" contract) reverts, funds sent in with the call will end up on the receiver contract. To avoid situations where user funds get stuck on the receivers, developers should build any contract implementing IXReceive defensively.

It is possible for xReceive to revert such as `MaxTVLReached` on `restakeManager.depositETH`. This means that WETH could be on xRenzoBridge. This WETH is meant to be deposited into the protocol and not swept by an untrusted role. An untrusted role should not have access to the funds that belong to the protocol.


## Impact
An untrusted role has access to the protocol funds.

## Proof of Concept
* 5000 WETH is sent from L2
* `xReceive` fails on L1 because of `MaxTVLReached`
* The 5000 WETH is sent to xRenzoBridge nonetheless
* untrusted BRIDGE_ADMIN sweeps the 5000 WETH that belongs to the protocol

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Give BRIDGE_ADMIN access to only trusted individual. Or exclude WETH from being recovered and create another mechanism to rescue WETH that are transferred when xReceive fails.



## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L509-L516
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/pods/DelayedWithdrawalRouter.sol#L100-L105


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Admin never receives gas refunds as users abuse the fact that they may call `DelayedWithdrawalRouter::claimDelayedWithdrawals()`, not refunding the admin

## Proof of Concept

Withdrawals are [created](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L274) in `EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals()`. After the time delay, they may be claimed in the router via `DelayedWithdrawalRouter::claimDelayedWithdrawals()`, as it is not [permissioned](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/pods/DelayedWithdrawalRouter.sol#L100-L105). `OperatorDelegator::receive()` claims the gas refund to the admin whenever it [matches](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L509-L516) the `tx.origin`. However, if the tx is initiated by another user, no gas will be found in the mapping and the admin will not receive any refund.

Users are incentivized to do this because the gas refund discounts their tvl.

## Tools Used

Vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The gas refund should just go to the trusted admin instead of `tx.origin`.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L274
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L274


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Users rewards from native stake are in the `DelayedWithdrawalRouter` and wil lbe claimed later, leading to incorrect TVL and allowing users to easily frontrun tvl updates and profit.

## Proof of Concept

`RestakeManager::calculateTVLs()` does not take into account ETH in the `DelayedWithdrawalRouter`, which will happen every time a ETH withdrawal is executed in `OperatorDelegator::completeQueuedWithdrawal()`. In this function, the rewards from native staking will be [sent](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L274) to the `DelayedWithdrawalRouter`, where they will be kept until they are claimed and sent to the `OperatorDelegator`, where they are correctly accounted for. Thus, in the meantime users can buy ezETH cheaper than intended and sellers will take a loss.

## Tools Used

Vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Include the balance of the `DelayedWithdrawalRouter` in the calculation of the total TVL.


## Assessed type

Other

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L482-L485


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Claiming rewards from the `DelayedWithdrawalRouter` fail when the `msg.value` is smaller than the required gas refund, but the contract has enough ETH balance, so the admin will not receive the rewards.

## Proof of Concept

When claiming ETH rewards from the `DelayedWithdrawalRouter`, [here](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/pods/DelayedWithdrawalRouter.sol#L100-L105), they will be sent to the `OperatorDelegator`. In the `receive()` function, the gas refund is discounted from `msg.value`, but limited to `address(this).balance`. Thus, an overflow may occur, making the transaction revert. This will likely stop the admin from getting the gas refund.

## Tools Used

Vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Subtract the refund from the `msg.value`, not the balance of the contract.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L220-L224


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Malicious users profit from frontrunning and the shares/tvl ratio will be incorrect.

## Proof of Concept

`WithdrawQueue::withdraw()` pulls the ezETH from the withdrawer and calculates the corresponding tvl amount. Then, in `WithdrawQueue::claim()`, the shares are burned and the tokens are sent to the user. This means that a user may see a slashing event, frontrun it and withdraw, not taking the loss. Additionally, the ratio will be modified when the user claims the tokens, as it will burn the ezETH tokens and send the assets as calculated previously, not the current ratio, for the other users loss.

## Tools Used

Vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Calculate the ratio at the time of `claim()` and send the lowest amount of assets to the user. This is how LIDO handles it in the withdrawal queue, for example.


## Assessed type

Other

## Tools Used

Vscode

Include the token balances of `DepositQueue` in `RestakeManager::calculateTVLs()`, similar to what is done with the `WithdrawalQueue`.

## Tools Used

Vscode

Before depositing, check if the strategy is whitelisted for depositing. Withdrawals still work as the whitelist is only for depositing.

https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L300-L306
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L373-L378


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Protocol becomes insolvent as it becomes impossible to finalize withdrawals. It may be possible to finalize withdrawals if the withdrawal buffer is increased.

## Proof of Concept

`OperatorDelegator::completeQueuedWithdrawal()` finalizes withdrawals for strategy tokens and `ETH`. If the token balance of a given strategy exceeds the withdrawal buffer, it deposits to a strategy; however, the protocol may have reached the maximum strategies allowed in EigenLayer in the meantime. [Here](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L300-L306) is the check in EigenLayer for the maximum strategies. The flow that would cause this is:
1. Strategies are added until reaching 32, the limit.
2. All the funds are withdrawn from a strategy, [deleting](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L373-L378) it from the strategies on `OperatorDelegator::queueWithdrawals()`.
3. At the moment there are only 31 strategies from the `OperatorManager`, but some user deposits on another strategy, increasing the value to 32.
4. `OperatorDelegator::completeQueuedWithdrawal()` is called, the token balance is greater than the buffer and it deposits to the strategy. it will revert as it will try to add strategy 33 and revert. Withdrawals of all the tokens and ETH in the batch will be on hold due to this.


## Tools Used

Vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Check if the maximum strategy limit is reached before depositing.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L377-L384
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L419-L427


# Vulnerability details

The `chooseOperatorDelegatorForDeposit` and `chooseOperatorDelegatorForWithdraw` functions in `RestakeManager` incorrectly calculates the allocation threshold by dividing by `BASIS_POINTS` twice, which should only be divided once.

## Impact
This error could lead to the consistent selection of the first OperatorDelegator in the list, regardless of their actual TVL compared to their target allocation. This could result in an imbalance in the distribution of deposits and withdrawals across OperatorDelegators.

## Proof of Concept
The issue is located in the `chooseOperatorDelegatorForDeposit` and `chooseOperatorDelegatorForWithdraw` functions within the `RestakeManager` contract. The relevant code snippet is:

```solidity
    if (
        tvls[i] <
@-->    (operatorDelegatorAllocations[operatorDelegators[i]] * totalTVL) /
            BASIS_POINTS /
            BASIS_POINTS
    ) {
        return operatorDelegators[i];
    }
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L377C13-L384C14

```solidity
    if (
        operatorDelegatorTVLs[i] >
@-->    (operatorDelegatorAllocations[operatorDelegators[i]] * totalTVL) /
            BASIS_POINTS /
            BASIS_POINTS &&
        operatorDelegatorTokenTVLs[i][tokenIndex] >= ezETHValue
    ) {
        return operatorDelegators[i];
    }
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L419C13-L427C14

A numerical example is provided to illustrate the issue with the current logic:

- `BASIS_POINTS` is defined as 10000.
- Alice's OperatorDelegator has an allocation of 3000 basis points (30%).
- Bob's OperatorDelegator has an allocation of 7000 basis points (70%).
- The total TVL (`totalTVL`) is 1000 ETH.
- Alice's current TVL (`tvls[Alice]`) is 200 ETH.
- Bob's current TVL (`tvls[Bob]`) is 800 ETH.

The correct allocation threshold calculation for Alice should be:
- (3000 * 1000) / 10000 = 300 ETH

However, with the current logic, the calculation erroneously divides by `BASIS_POINTS` twice:
- (3000 * 1000) / 10000 / 10000 = 0.03 ETH

This incorrect calculation would always result in Alice's TVL being below the threshold, leading to her constant selection for new deposits and withdrawals, regardless of the actual TVLs.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Modify the calculation to divide by BASIS_POINTS only once to correctly convert the allocation basis points to a proportion. This ensures that the OperatorDelegator's TVL is compared against the correct allocation threshold.


## Assessed type

Math

    if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {

# Vulnerability details

## Description
The `recoverNative` function in the `xRenzoBridge` contract is not checking whether the `_amount` or `_to` is valid or not. This absence of validation may expose sweeping of `ETH` to potential vulnerabilities or unintended consequences, as it does not verify the legitimacy or correctness of the destination address before transferring native assets.
## Impact
As `transfer` function is used here which doesn't revert on zero address or amount. The main issue with using just transfer function is that it can fail silently without reverting. 

Without validation of the params, the contract may inadvertently transfer native assets to unintended or incorrect addresses, resulting in the loss of funds or misappropriation. Like if it sends ETH to zero address, or incorrect address. The funds can be lost forever. 

## Proof of Concept
See the following code:

```
 /**
     * @notice  Sweeps accidental ETH value sent to the contract
     * @dev     Restricted to be called by the bridge admin only.
     * @param   _amount  amount of native asset
     * @param   _to  destination address
     */
    function recoverNative(uint256 _amount, address _to) external onlyBridgeAdmin 
    {
        payable(_to).transfer(_amount);
    }
```

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L13

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L93
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L248


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`RenzoOracleL2` & `RenzoOracle` use the same heartbeat for all price feeds when checking if the data feed is fresh and also not verifying prices enough for staleness. 

The issue with this is that the `STETH/USD` oracle has a 3600s heartbeat, `STETH/ETH` oracle has 86400s heartbeat, `ETH/USD` has 3600s and vice versa. In short all feeds have different heartbeats which means that for each price feed, the `MAX_TIME_WINDOW` should be different. 

Consequently, even after verifying the freshness of a value, it could still be stale according to the specific oracle's update schedule, potentially leading to inaccurate price data.

Attackers could exploit the discrepancy in staleness assessments to manipulate the contract's behavior. By strategically timing transactions or oracle queries, attackers may exploit perceived data freshness to their advantage.

Either protocol or user will face loss of funds if oracle is considered fresh and price is accpeted at one price level while the real one is either dropped or pumped too much.

Even if we consider that all price feeds have the same heartbeat, still in `86400 + 60`, this 60 can also cause staleness. 

It also checking the price in `xRenzoDeposit:_deposit` function i.e 
```  
 if (block.timestamp > _lastPriceTimestamp + 1 days) {
            revert OraclePriceExpired();
  }
``` 

## Proof of Concept
Lets see the following scenario:

- The RenzoOracle contract is deployed and initialized with default parameters, including a fixed time window for staleness checks set to 86460 seconds (24 hours + 60 seconds).
- Chainlink oracles are configured with varying update intervals: Oracle A updates every 3600 seconds (1 hour), while Oracle B updates every 86400 seconds.
- User Alice queries the RenzoOracle contract for the latest price of a token using Oracle A.
- The contract retrieves the latest price data from Oracle A and timestamps the query.
- As per the contract's staleness check mechanism, the retrieved price data from Oracle A is considered fresh if its timestamp is within the fixed time window of 86460 seconds.
- However, since Oracle A updates every 3600 seconds, its data may become stale before the contract's fixed time window elapses.

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
User custom `MAX_TIME_WINDOW` for each price feed as this most of the price feeds have different heartbeats. 

The latestRoundData function also returns `roundId` and `answeredInRound`. You can check answeredInRound against the current roundId. If answeredInRound is less than roundId, the answer is being carried over. If answeredInRound is equal to roundId, then the answer is fresh.

Add the following extra lines for verification too:

```
 (roundID, int256 price, , timestamp, answeredInRound) = USDT.latestRoundData();
    require(price > 0, "ChainLink: Invalid Price");
    require(answeredInRound >= roundID, "ChainLink: Stale USDT price");
```






## Assessed type

Oracle

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L85
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L50


# Vulnerability details

## Description
Chainlink aggregators have a built in circuit breaker if the price of an asset goes outside of a predetermined price band. The result is that if an asset experiences a huge drop in value (i.e. LUNA crash) the price of the oracle will continue to return the minPrice instead of the actual price of the asset. This would allow user to continue borrowing with the asset but at the wrong price. This is exactly what happened to Venus on BSC when LUNA imploded.

## Vulnerability Details
ChainlinkAdapterOracle uses the ChainlinkFeedRegistry to obtain the price of the requested tokens.
```
function latestRoundData(
  address base,
  address quote
)
  external
  view
  override
  checkPairAccess()
  returns (
    uint80 roundId,
    int256 answer,
    uint256 startedAt,
    uint256 updatedAt,
    uint80 answeredInRound
  )
{
  uint16 currentPhaseId = s_currentPhaseId[base][quote];
  //@audit this pulls the Aggregator for the requested pair
  AggregatorV2V3Interface aggregator = _getFeed(base, quote);
  require(address(aggregator) != address(0), "Feed not found");
  (
    roundId,
    answer,
    startedAt,
    updatedAt,
    answeredInRound
  ) = aggregator.latestRoundData();
  return _addPhaseIds(roundId, answer, startedAt, updatedAt, answeredInRound, currentPhaseId);
}
```
ChainlinkFeedRegistry#latestRoundData pulls the associated aggregator and requests round data from it. ChainlinkAggregators have minPrice and maxPrice circuit breakers built into them. This means that if the price of the asset drops below the minPrice, the protocol will continue to value the token at minPrice instead of it's actual value. This will allow users to take out huge amounts of bad debt and bankrupt the protocol.

Example: TokenA has a minPrice of $1. The price of TokenA drops to $0.10. The aggregator still returns $1 allowing the user to borrow against TokenA as if it is $1 which is 10x it's actual value.

Note: Chainlink oracles are used a just one piece of the OracleAggregator system and it is assumed that using a combination of other oracles, a scenario like this can be avoided. However this is not the case because the other oracles also have their flaws that can still allow this to be exploited. As an example if the chainlink oracle is being used with a UniswapV3Oracle which uses a long TWAP then this will be exploitable when the TWAP is near the minPrice on the way down. In a scenario like that it wouldn't matter what the third oracle was because it would be bypassed with the two matching oracles prices. If secondary oracles like Band are used a malicious user could DDOS relayers to prevent update pricing. Once the price becomes stale the chainlink oracle would be the only oracle left and it's price would be used.

## Proof of Concept
- Present price of TokenA is $10
- TokenA has a minimum price set at $1 on chainlink
- The actual price of TokenA dips to $0.10
- The aggregator continues to report $1 as the price.

Consequently, users can interact with protocol using TokenA as though it were still valued at $1, which is a tenfold overestimate of its real market value.
## Impact
In the event that an asset crashes (i.e. LUNA) the protocol can be manipulated to give out loans at an inflated price

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Since there is going to be a whitelist of tokens to be added, the minPrice/maxPrice could be checked and a revert could be made when this is returned by chainlink or a fallback oracle that does not have circuit breakers could be implemented in that case


## Assessed type

Oracle

# Vulnerability details

## **Vulnerability Details:**

The Renzo protocol documentation mentions the **DEPOSIT_WITHDRAW_PAUSER** role as one of the trusted roles in the protocol with the ability to pause/unpause deposits and withdrawals.

- [Reference](https://code4rena.com/audits/2024-04-renzo#top:~:text=DEPOSIT_WITHDRAW_PAUSER)

This functionality is correctly implemented in the **[deposit](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L491)** function, which uses the **notPaused** modifier controlled by the **DEPOSIT_WITHDRAW_PAUSER** role. However, although the **PausableUpgradeable** contract is inherited by the **WithdrawQueue** contract and initialized, the **notPaused** modifier is not added to the **[withdraw](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206)** or **[claim](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279)** functions.

```solidity
    function withdraw(uint256 _amount, address _assetOut) external nonReentrant {
        ...
    }
```

```solidity
    function claim(uint256 withdrawRequestIndex) external nonReentrant {
        ...
    }
```

Consequently, neither the **withdraw** nor the **claim** functions will be able to be paused if needed. This could be problematic if the functionality needs to be paused due to the identification of a vulnerability or during a contract upgrade.

Additionally, the pausing ability is currently configured to another role contrary to the docs. However, this does not have any harmful impact.

## **Impact:**

- Severity: Medium.  The missing functionality could be costly if immediate pausing is required for security or upgrade purposes.
- Likelihood: Medium. While the need to pause these functions may not be frequent, it is essential for risk management and emergency situations.

## **Tools Used:**

- Manual analysis

## **Recommendation:**

To address this issue, add the **notPaused** modifier to the **withdraw** and **claim** functions in the **WithdrawQueue** contract to allow the protocol to pause these functions if needed.

```solidity
    function withdraw(uint256 _amount, address _assetOut) external nonReentrant notPaused {
	...
    }
```

```solidity
    function claim(uint256 withdrawRequestIndex) external nonReentrant notPaused {
        ...
    }
```

Access Control

A possible problem with the function is that it doesn’t let the user calling the function specify the amount being swept but will instead always sweep the full balance in the contract.

```solidity
    function sweep() public payable nonReentrant {
        // Verify the caller is whitelisted
        if (!allowedBridgeSweepers[msg.sender]) {
            revert UnauthorizedBridgeSweeper();
        }
        // Get the balance of nextWETH in the contract
        uint256 balance = collateralToken.balanceOf(address(this));
	...
        connext.xcall{value: msg.value}(
            bridgeDestinationDomain,
            bridgeTargetAddress,
            address(collateralToken),
            msg.sender,
            balance,
            0, // Asset is already nextWETH, so no slippage will be incurred
            bridgeCallData
        );
	...
    }
```

The reason this is problematic is because there are restrictions on the L1 side which will make the call fail if not met.

- When tokens are received by the **xRenzoBridge** contract on L1, the **xezETH** is burned since it was already minted to the user. However, the **XERC20** contract has a [daily burning limit](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20.sol#L328), so if the amount passes over that threshold, the bridged funds transaction will revert on the receiving contract's end.
- Another problem is that the **RestakeManager** contract has a TVL limit set when [depositing ETH](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L592) into Renzo. If the balance in the L2 side causes it to pass the threshold, the transaction will also revert.

Once a transaction fails in the receiving contract, it will have to be manually deposited, once possible by the team, as the full amount will still be deposited in the receiving contract but not to Renzo.

Note: If the Connext bridge transaction reverts on the receiving contract, the amount will still be deposited in the contract but not to Renzo.

This causes some more problems:

- Tokens would have been minted on the L2 side but not accounted for inside the protocol on the L1 side. This means that the value sitting idle could leave the L2 tokens undercollateralized.
- The protocol will be earning less rewards than it should, as the value will be sitting idle but shares have been minted for it, so all users will get less rewards.
- The team having to manually deposit tokens will mean this will not count towards the bridge's limits, and therefore the limit will be compromised as it can be bypassed for that duration until refilled.

## **Impact:**

- Severity: High. This can lead to losses for users and the protocol, as well as operational difficulties for the team.
- Likelihood: Medium. This issue will occur every time the conditions on the L1 side are not met.

## **Tools Used:**

- Manual analysis

## **Recommendation:**

Modify the **sweep** function to allow the user to specify the amount being swept, rather than sweeping the full balance in the contract. This will allow for more control over the bridging process and reduce the risk of exceeding limits on the L1 side. 

Additionally, consider implementing checks and limits on the L2 side to prevent the minting of amounts that could exceed daily burning limits or TVL thresholds.








## Assessed type

DoS

# Vulnerability details

## **Vulnerability Details:**

The **xRenzoDeposit** contract facilitates the minting of xezETH tokens on Layer 2 (L2) in exchange for ETH or WETH tokens.

Specifically, the internal **[_deposit](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L227)** function exchanges the deposit tokens for **nextWETH** and mints xezETH tokens to the user. Subsequently, the funds in the contract are aggregated and swept by an admin down to Layer 1.

Upon reaching the L1 contract, the collateral is unwrapped and deposited into Renzo. The ezETH from the deposit is then sent to the lockbox to be wrapped into xezETH, and the xezETH is burned, as it is already minted on L2.

```solidity
    function sweep() public payable nonReentrant {
	...
        // Get the balance of nextWETH in the contract
        uint256 balance = collateralToken.balanceOf(address(this));
	...
        // Approve it to the connext contract
        collateralToken.safeApprove(address(connext), balance);

        // Need to send some calldata so it triggers xReceive on the target
        bytes memory bridgeCallData = abi.encode(balance);

        connext.xcall{value: msg.value}(
            bridgeDestinationDomain,
            bridgeTargetAddress,
            address(collateralToken),
            msg.sender,
            balance,
            0, // Asset is already nextWETH, so no slippage will be incurred
            bridgeCallData
        );
	...
    }
```

Two potential problems exist:

1.  Deposits are not immediately swept, leading to a delay where funds sit in the L2 contract until the sweep function is called. This delay can result in differing exchange rates between the time shares are minted on L2 and the time funds are minted on L1, potentially leaving the L1 lockbox for xezETH undercollateralized.
2. The L2 price is updated every six hours. This infrequency could lead to differing exchange rates between L1 and L2, also resulting in fewer shares being minted on L1 than on L2.

## **Impact:**

- Severity: High. Minting fewer shares on the L1 could leave the L1 lockbox undercollateralized for the L2 shares.
- Likelihood: Medium. The likelihood will depend on the frequency of sweeping deposits and L2 price updates.

## **Tools Used:**

- Manual analysis

## **Recommendation:**

To reduce the discrepancy in price updates and deposits, increase the frequency of updates and deposits. A more permanent solution could involve minting and bridging for each deposit to the L1 and returning the minted shares' value on the L2, allowing users to mint the exact amount. However, this approach may incur higher fees.


## Assessed type

Context

However, a potential opportunity exists where a user can monitor the L1 mempool for the **sendPrice** function call, observe the new price, and sandwich it if profitable.

```solidity
    /**
     * @notice  Exposes the price via getRate()
     * @dev     This is required for a balancer pool to get the price of ezETH
     * @return  uint256  .
     */
    function getRate() external view override returns (uint256) {
        return lastPrice;
    }
```

Upon detecting a favourable price change, the user could mint xezETH on L2 before the price adjustment takes effect. Subsequently, when the price change is finalized, the user can sell the xezETH on a protocol that reads the price from the [**getRate**](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L456) function in the **xRenzoDeposit** contract, thus profiting from the price discrepancy.

## **Impact:**

- Severity: Medium. This will allow users to exploit price changes by minting xezETH at a favourable rate before the price update is reflected.
- Likelihood: High. Given the visibility of transactions in the mempool and the potential for arbitrage opportunities, it is likely that users will attempt to exploit this.

## **Tools Used:**

- Manual analysis

## **Recommendation:**

Since there are two fees associated with L2 deposits, this should help minimize this problem. Additionally, as ezETH is more on the stable side, it is less prone to significant price fluctuations. However, continuous monitoring and adjustment of the update frequency may be necessary to prevent potential exploitation.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The depegging of `stETH` from `ETH` creates a discrepancy between the actual value of `stETH ` and its expected parity with `ETH`. If an attacker `front-runs the oracle update`, they can mint `ezETH` at a stale price, obtaining an unfair advantage and potential profit. This action undermines the protocol's integrity and can lead to diminished user confidence and financial imbalances.

## Proof of Concept


Market Change: [stETH depegs](https://medium.com/huobi-research/steth-depegging-what-are-the-consequences-20b4b7327b0c). stETh down by 6% in terms of eth and the chailink deviation for `stEth/ETH` is `0.5%` which will trigger the price feed tom update but attacker frontrun the oracle and mint the at stale price for profit , reducing its value compared to ETH.

Oracle Update: Chainlink's deviation threshold for `stETH/ETH` is `0.5%`, triggering an impending price feed update.

Front-Running: The attacker observes the depegging event and anticipates the oracle update.

Minting at Stale Price: The attacker deposits `stETH` into the `RestakeManager::deposit` before the price feed updates.

Exploiting the Delay: The `RestakeManager` mints `ezETH` based on the outdated, more favorable price.

Oracle Update: The oracle adjusts the` stETH/ETH` price to reflect the current market value.

Profit Taking: The attacker sells the newly minted ezETH at the updated price, realizing a profit from the price difference.

[Similar Issue](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-11-kelp-findings/issues/443).

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Implement a time-weighted average price (TWAP) oracle to mitigate front-running.

Slippage Checks: Add slippage checks to compare the expected mint amount with a threshold.



## Assessed type

Oracle

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Stakers can exploit this timing gap to withdraw their staked tokens without incurring the losses that would normally result from [penalties](https://eth2book.info/capella/part2/incentives/penalties/) or [slashing events](https://eth2book.info/capella/part2/incentives/slashing/).

## Proof of Concept
A validator experiences penalties or is slashed, reducing their balance.

Before the TVL is updated via [EigenPod::verifyBalanceUpdates()](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L185) or [EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals()](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L232), a staker requests a withdraw all their `LRTTokens` using [withdraw](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206).

The staker then triggers the update of the TVL by calling one of the aforementioned functions.
When [withdraw](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206) is executed, the withdrawal is processed without accounting for the recent penalties or slashing, as the TVL drop is instantaneous upon the update.

for example:

Initial state:
2 validators 32 ETH each
10 users with equal LRT, 6.4 each.

1. Validator 1 is slashed for 16 ETH
2. User 1 front-runs `verifyBalanceUpdates()` with a call to tWithdrawal() and has sharesOwed = 6.4 since TVL is still 64 ETH.
3. `verifyBalanceUpdates()` is now called to update EigenLayer balance.
4. User 2 calls `withdraw()` and has sharesOwed = 4.8 since TVL has decreased to 48.

User 1 has stolen 1.4 ETH from the rest.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Locking Period: Implement a locking period after a slashing event is detected, during which no withdrawals can be processed. This allows the system to update the TVL accordingly.


## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L414

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Block reorgs can disrupt cross-chain transfers, leading to potential double-spending, loss of funds, or incorrect token supply.[Read here](https://abarbatei.xyz/blockchain-reorgs-for-managers-and-auditors)

## Proof of Concept

Multiple users, including Alice, have deposited WETH into the xRenzoDeposit contract on Chain A (L2), which has been swapped for a total of 1000 `nextWETH`.


Initial State:

Multiple users, including Alice, have deposited WETH into the `xRenzoDeposit` contract on Chain A (L2), which has been swapped for a total of 1000 nextWETH.

Bridging Process:

A sweep function is called, which triggers `connext.xcall` to bridge the entire balance of 1000 nextWETH to Chain B (L1).

Chain B Processing:

The `xRenzoBridge` contract on Chain B receives the `nextWETH`, unwraps it to WETH, and proceeds with restaking operations.

Blockchain Reorg: A reorg occurs on Chain A after the `xcall` is made but before the transaction is finalized. The deposit transaction that initiated the bridge is now reverted.

Resulting State: On Chain B, the `xRenzoBridge` contract has already unwrapped nextWETH to WETH and possibly completed restaking operations. However, due to the reorg on Chain A, the original WETH deposit no longer exists on L2.

There is now `WETH` on `Chain B` that is unbacked by an equivalent deposit on `Chain A`, leading to a discrepancy between the two chains. Essentially, Chain B has extra `WETH` that wasn't actually locked or bridged from Chain A due to the reorg. This creates an imbalance where more `WETH` exists on `L1` than is backed by L2 deposits, potentially affecting the integrity of the token peg and the restaking process.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Waiting for more confirmations: Chain B's contract could wait for a higher number of confirmations from Chain A before minting wrapped tokens, reducing the risk of acting on a transaction that might be dropped.

Reorg detection: Both chains implement mechanisms to detect reorgs and temporarily halt cross-chain operations until the network stabilizes.

State reconciliation: After detecting a reorg, Chain B's contract could verify the state of Chain A to ensure the lock transaction is still valid before minting wrapped tokens.

Fallback procedures: If a reorg invalidates a transfer, Chain B's contract could have a mechanism to burn the incorrectly minted wrapped tokens to correct the token supply.


## Assessed type

Other

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Users `withdrawing` after a slashing event may receive less than their entitled amount, bearing the cost of the slashing penalty, which should be distributed across all token holders.

## Proof of Concept

User initiates a []withdrawal via [withdraw()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206) function.

Slashing event occurs, reducing TVL.
[restakeManager.calculateTVLs()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L217) returns a reduced TVL.

User's redeemable amount is calculated based on the reduced TVL.
User receives less upon claiming, effectively paying the slashing penalty.

Example:

    Deposit such that we have 2 validators.

    Bob requests to withdraw 8 ezETH, expecting to receive an equivalent amount in ETH.

    Before Bob's withdrawal is processed, a slashing event occurs, reducing the total value locked (TVL) and creating an 8 ETH deficit.

    Bob's withdrawal is processed, but due to the deficit, the amount of ETH he receives is less than expected. If the deficit covers his entire withdrawal, he could receive 0 ETH.

    Carol requests to withdraw 31.99 ezETH after the slashing event.

    When Carol's withdrawal is processed, the deficit has already been covered by Bob's withdrawal, so she receives the full 31.99 ETH equivalent.

    As a result, Bob has absorbed the entire slashing penalty, while Carol's withdrawal is unaffected, leading to an inequitable outcome.

    Effectively, Carol's withdrawal has been subsidized by the slashing penalty that was fully absorbed by Bob, leading to an unfair distribution of losses.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Create a penalty distribution system to spread slashing costs proportionally among all token holders.


## Assessed type

Context

## Impact
Users may be unable to `deposit` funds if the TVL limit is reached, potentially leading to a loss of opportunity and trust in the protocol.

## Proof of Concept

Assume [maxDepositTVL](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L215) is currently set to `70,000 ETH`.

The current TVL is `69,990 ETH`.

A normal user attempts to deposit 10 ETH by calling `depositETH()`.

A malicious user observes the transaction in the mempool and decides to front-run.

The malicious user submits a transaction with a higher gas price to deposit 10 ETH, calling `depositETH()` as well.

The malicious user's transaction is mined first, increasing the TVL to 70,000 ETH.

The normal user's transaction is processed after but fails because `maxDepositTVL` has been reached.

```javascript
    function depositETH(uint256 _referralId) public payable nonReentrant notPaused {
        // Get the total TVL

        // Enforce TVL limit if set
        if (maxDepositTVL != 0 && totalTVL + msg.value > maxDepositTVL) {
            revert MaxTVLReached();
            //......
        }
    }
```

The normal user's deposit transaction is rejected, and they may lose the gas fee without their deposit being processed. Due to the `maxDepositTVL` check, the normal user is unable to deposit, resulting in the failure of the transaction

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement a fair ordering system like a first-come-first-serve queue to process deposits in the order they are received.

Dynamic Limits: Introduce dynamic maxDepositTVL limits that can adjust based on the number of pending transactions or a rolling time window.


## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Chainlink's price feeds are configured with predefined lower and upper price bounds; during market anomalies such as flash crashes, bridge failures, or asset depegging incidents, if an asset's market value drops beneath the feed's set floor price, the Chainlink feed will persist in reporting this floor price, even though it may not reflect the asset's true market price.

## Proof of Concept
If the RenzoOracle provides the price of [stETH/ETH](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L71) without implementing safeguards against incorrect price reporting from Chainlink during extreme market events:

The protocol could overvalue stETH when its market value diverges significantly from ETH, especially if stETH depegs.

Users could exploit this by depositing stETH and receiving more assets or benefits than the stETH is truly worth.

This could lead to a depletion of the protocol's reserves and affect its overall financial health.

[go to the Oracle Returns Incorrect Price During Flash Crashes section](https://medium.com/cyfrin/chainlink-oracle-defi-attacks-93b6cb6541bf#00ac).

[lookupTokenAmountFromValue also has the same issue](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L85C14-L85C40)

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement on-chain checks for `minAnswer` and `maxAnswer` on both `lookupTokenAmountFromValue` & `lookupTokenValue` functions.

# Lines of code

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Following the launch of LRT, which will enable the deposit of native ETH and wrapped staking tokens like stETH or wBETH, Renzo users will face additional economic risks that could result in capital loss. In the event of an anticipated price decline, such as due to a slashing event in an external liquid staking provider, external users can deposit their funds into Renzo prior to the price drop. They will receive LRT equivalent to the value before the price decline, as priceFeed updates the price only after the event occurs. Subsequently, they can withdraw their funds once the price has dropped, thereby sharing their loss with Renzo users.

## Proof of Concept
Users depositing their funds into Renzo are encouraged by the rewards of staking and re-staking through EigenLayer, but they also bear the risk of penalties and slashing of their deposited funds. However, in case of ezETh, the 3rd party users who are not associated in any way with Renzo ecosystem can take advantage of such LRT and make Rio users bear their losses.

Keeping in mind these things:

    Assets like stETH and wBETH typically appreciate over time. While occasional price drops may occur, they are often temporary in nature. 

    Factors contributing to such declines include slashing events, reduced demand, or a lack of trust in a particular asset. Notably, big withdrawals can be anticipated and slashing occurs gradually, allowing for a period of foresight into the asset's devaluation.

    Liquid staking providers such as LIDO mitigate the risk of "withdrawal before slashing" by implementing extended withdrawal processes, ensuring that users who request withdrawals are susceptible to potential slashing.

    Within the Renzo ecosystem, users can deposit asset1 to acquire LRT and subsequently request the withdrawal of asset2.

Consider the following scenario (values used for ease of calculation and to illustrate the attack, real values will be presented later in this description):

Renzo issues LRT (ezETH) that supports two assets (stETH, cbETh and native ETH).

    Attacker holds 100 stETH (1 stETH = 2 ETH, so worth 200 ETH).
    Attacker anticipates a price drop for stETH due to external events.

    Attacker deposits 100 stETH into the protocol, receiving 200 ezETH (as 1 stETH = 2 ezETH).

    TVL in the protocol increases from 200 ETH to 400 ETH (200 ETH + 200 ETH worth of stETH).

    stETH price drops by 50% (now 1 stETH = 1 ETH).
    TVL in the protocol decreases from 400 ETH to 300 ETH (200 ETH + 100 ETH worth of stETH).

    Attacker burns 150 ezETH to withdraw their 100 stETH (now worth 100 ETH).

    Attacker burns another 50 ezETH to withdraw 50 ETH.
    Attacker ends up with 100 stETH (worth 100 ETH) and 50 ETH.
    Attacker uses the 50 ETH to buy more stETH from another source, now holding 150 stETH.

    When stETH price recovers to 1 stETH = 2 ETH, the attacker has 150 stETH worth 300 ETH, while the protocol and its users bear the loss of 50 ETH.
   
However, the price drop is not expected to reach 50%. The actual figures could be as high as 10%.

Looking specifically at `stETH` as an example of an asset considered for addition, we can observe the following:
[stETH down by 7%](https://medium.com/huobi-research/steth-depegging-what-are-the-consequences-20b4b7327b0c)

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

1. Holding periods or cooldowns to delay withdrawals after deposits.

2. users could be allowed to withdraw only the type of assets they deposit


## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L327-L329


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Due to wrong `underlying token amount` return from each `OperatorDelegator.getTokenBalanceFromStrategy()`, `calculated TVL` will be less than actual locked value, which is a crucial part of the protocol.

For Detailed info refer `Description` part

## Descripion
So The bug exists like following
For TVL calculation in `RestakeManager.sol` `calculateTVLs()` called, its works as following 
- loop over all operatorDelegators
     - for each operatorDelegator it loop over all available collateral tokens and 
       call
```solidity
                uint256 operatorBalance = operatorDelegators[i].getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(
                    collateralTokens[j]
                );
```      
The implementation for `getTokenBalanceFromStrategy()` as follows where it `intended` to returns `underlying token amount from the amount of shares + queued withdrawal shares`

```solidity
    /// @dev Gets the underlying token amount from the amount of shares + queued withdrawal shares
    function getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(IERC20 token) external view returns (uint256) {
        return
            queuedShares[address(this)] == 0
                ? tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) 
                : tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) +
                    tokenStrategyMapping[token].sharesToUnderlyingView( 
                        queuedShares[address(token)] 
                    );
    }
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L327-L335

Here main point to give attetion is `queued withdrawal shares` i.e `queuedShares[address(token)]`

So basically `queuedShares` is `mapping of token shares in withdraw queue of EigenLayer`
```solidity
 mapping(address => uint256) public queuedShares;
```
This mapping for a token changes in 2 places `queueWithdrawals()` & `completeQueuedWithdrawal()`

So basically `queuedShares` mapping tracking the tokens present in withdrawal Queue

But when `getTokenBalanceFromStrategy()` called for `operatorDelegator` it has following ternary operator
```solidity
            queuedShares[address(this)] == 0
                ? tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) 
                : tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) +
                    tokenStrategyMapping[token].sharesToUnderlyingView( 
                        queuedShares[address(token)] 
```
So here `queuedShares[address(this)] == 0` always going to be `TRUE`
cause value stored for `address(this)` in `queuedShares` is `default i.e 0` as i mentioned `queuedShares` only tracks `collateralTokens`. So here always first condition will run(i.e never going to consider `queuedShares` for that token).

So in end result underlying amount returned by `getTokenBalanceFromStrategy()`  is wrong(less) when there is `queued withdrawal shares` present for the token in `queuedShares` mapping.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
In ternary operation check it should be `queuedShares[address(token)] == 0` as follows

`queuedShares mapping check` should present for `token` not for `address(this)`

```solidity
    function getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(IERC20 token) external view returns (uint256) {
        return
-           queuedShares[address(this)] == 0
+           queuedShares[address(token)] == 0
                ? tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) 
                : tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) +
                    tokenStrategyMapping[token].sharesToUnderlyingView( 
                        queuedShares[address(token)] 
                    );
    }
```

This bug also confirmed by sponcer on Discord private thread






## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L317


# Vulnerability details

## Summary

The `calculateTVL` function is very important function in the system used to calculate the total value Locked in the protocol denominated in ETH. As part of this it also needs to calculate the value of tokens in ETH present in the `WithdrawQueue` contract. The value of the tokens in ETH is gotten through the `RenzoOracle` contract in the `lookupTokenValue` function.

The inputs given to this function is wrong and results in the wrong calculation of the TVL.



## Impact

This results in the wrong calculation of the `operatorDelegatorTokenTVLs`, `operatorDelegatorTVLs` and the `totalTVL`.

As `calculateTVL` is used across the protocol to determine the [amount to mint](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L566) and [amount to redeem](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L223) ezETH tokens and depositing and withdrawing from Eigen Layer. 

## Proof of Concept

The `lookupTokenValue` function in the `RenzoOracle` takes the ERC20 interface of the token and the amount of tokens as input, while returning the value of that amount of the token in ETH. This happens in [line 317](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L317) in the `RestakeManager` contract.

```solidity

totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
                        collateralTokens[i], //Token in index i is given
                        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue) // but balance is of token in index j
);
```
As you can see from the code snippet above, the token in index i is given as the token but the balance of token in index j is given as the amount to calculate the price in ETH.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

```diff
- collateralTokens[i],
+ collateralTokens[j],
```





## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L327


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
The `OperatorDelegator::getTokenBalanceFromStrategy` function is used to calculate the amount of tokens deposited by the OperatorDelegator in the Strategy. The calculation of the `OperatorDelegator::getTokenBalanceFromStrategy` function is wrong.


## Impact
The `OperatorDelegator::getTokenBalanceFromStrategy` function is used in the `RestakeManager::calculateTVL` function which in turn is used to the total value of assets in the protocol. This return values of calculateTVL is used to determine the [amount to mint](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L566) and [amount to redeem](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L223) ezETH tokens and depositing and withdrawing from Eigen Layer.

The wrong calculation of the token Balance in strategies will result in the TVL being less than the actual TVL. The effects of this are
- Minting will result in minting more ezETH than it should have.
- Redeeming will result in redeeming less amount of token than it should have
- More TVL in the protocol than the max TVL Limit.

## Proof of Concept

Once a withdrawal from the Strategy is initiated the shares of the amounts withdrawn is stored in the state variable `OperatorDelegator::queuedShares`. This keeps track of the total shares which are waiting to be withdrawn.

Hence while calculating the token balance deposited in a Strategy, we have to add the tokens values of the shares waiting to be withdrawn as well (i.e token amounts corresponding to `queuedShares`). But in [line 329](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L329C13-L329C25) a logic error has been made which results in the queuedShares of the token never being considered for the balance calculation.

```solidity
queuedShares[address(this)] == 0 // Here since address(this) is not a token, it will never have shares
                ? tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this))
                : tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) +
                    tokenStrategyMapping[token].sharesToUnderlyingView(
                        queuedShares[address(token)]
                    );
```
From the above code snippet we can see that since address(this) is not a token, it will never have any shares and the condition will always remain true. Which will only make it only take into account the `userUnderlyingView` of the address and the queuedShares is never taken into consideration.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

```diff
- queuedShares[address(this)] == 0
+ queuedShares[address(token)] == 0
```


## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L123
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L355
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L163
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L352
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L605


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
[Inflation Attacks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3IMw7xbxJgY) usually happen in Vault like systems. A vault is any contract where funds are deposited and managed by the contract. This also has a receipt token to keep track of the deposited funds and manage it etc. There is usually an exchange rate between the deposited token and the receipt token. And this exchange rate might vary with time and other metrics. With respect to Renzo, the deposited token can be ETH, stETH etc. And the receipt token is the ezETH.

Renzo calculates it TVL by directly using the [`address(depositQueue).balance`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L352) and [`address(withdrawalQueue).balance`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L355). This makes it vulnerable to inflation attacks.

## Impact

Inflation attacks can cause loss of funds for early depositors and in case of Renzo can DOS any deposit less than a certain amount. And even deposits higher than that amount will loose funds due to this 

## Proof of Concept
The issue lies in the [`RenzoOracle::calculateMintAmount`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L123) function.

```solidity
function calculateMintAmount(
        uint256 _currentValueInProtocol,
        uint256 _newValueAdded,
        uint256 _existingEzETHSupply
    ) external pure returns (uint256) {
        // For first mint, just return the new value added.
        // Checking both current value and existing supply to guard against gaming the initial mint
        if (_currentValueInProtocol == 0 || _existingEzETHSupply == 0) {
            return _newValueAdded; // value is priced in base units, so divide by scale factor
        }

        // Calculate the percentage of value after the deposit
        uint256 inflationPercentaage = (SCALE_FACTOR * _newValueAdded) /
            (_currentValueInProtocol + _newValueAdded);

        // Calculate the new supply
        uint256 newEzETHSupply = (_existingEzETHSupply * SCALE_FACTOR) /
            (SCALE_FACTOR - inflationPercentaage);

        // Subtract the old supply from the new supply to get the amount to mint
        uint256 mintAmount = newEzETHSupply - _existingEzETHSupply;

        // Sanity check
        if (mintAmount == 0) revert InvalidTokenAmount();

        return mintAmount;
    }
```

This function is responsible to calculate the amount to ezETH tokens to be minted to a depositor, depending on the current Value locked in the protocol, the value of the newly deposited tokens and the existing ezETH supply.

Lets go through an scenario to better understand how the attack might happen.

Lets assume Renzo has just launched and has no TVL. Alice wants to deposit 1 ETH into Renzo and she broadcasts a transaction for the same. Now Bob(the attacker) sees Alices transaction and frontrun the transaction by doing a couple of thing.

1. Bob deposits 1 wei into Renzo. Gets 1 wei of ezETH minted. 
2. Bob directly sends 1.05 ETH to the `DepositQueue` contract. Its `recieve` function splits that 1.05 ETH into protocol fees and sends the rest to the WithdrawQueue contract.
3. Now Alice's transaction is executed, and it reverts cause of check in [line 146](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L146). Moreover, anyone who sends less than

Lets go into more details and how the states change in each step.

#### Bob deposits 1 wei into Renzo. Gets 1 wei of ezETH minted
The state at the beginning of this step is
```solidity
currentValueInProtocol = 0
ezETHSupply = 0
```
Since this is the first every deposit into Renzo, there is no TVL and no ezETHSupply.

As Bob deposits 1 wei, since TVL and ezETHSupply is zero according to [line 131](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L131), 1 wei of ezETH is minted to Bob.
After this step the state is.
```solidity
currentValueInProtocol = 1 wei
ezETHSupply = 1 wei
```

#### Bob directly sends 1.05 ETH to the `DepositQueue` contract.
Now Bob directly sends 1.05 ETH to the `DepositQueue` contract. The `DepositQueue` contract's [`receive`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L163) function is executed. There the fee is calculated and is sent to the fee address. In this scenarios lets assume the fee is 5%. So approximately 0.05 ETH (more like 0.047ETH but lets round it off for calculation) is sent to the fee address. And the remaining 1 ETH is send to the WithdrawQueue as it doesn't have any Buffer as of yet(other than the 1 wei of ETH Bob deposited).

Now the state of the Protocol is
```solidity
currentValueInProtocol = 1 ETH + 1 wei
ezETHSupply = 1 wei
```
#### Alice's transaction is executed, and it reverts
Now Alice's transaction will revert cause the amount of ezETH to be minted for her will become 0.

Lets see go line by in the `RenzoOracle::calculateMintAmount` function.
```solidity
function calculateMintAmount(
        uint256 _currentValueInProtocol,
        uint256 _newValueAdded,
        uint256 _existingEzETHSupply
    ) external pure returns (uint256) {
```

- The _currentValueInProtocol is the currentValueInProtocol which is currently 1 ETH + 1 wei.
- The _newValueAdded is the amount of ETH Alice is depositing which is 1 ETH
- The _existingEzETHSupply is the current ezETH supply which is 1 wei

In the next line,
```solidity
if (_currentValueInProtocol == 0 || _existingEzETHSupply == 0) {
            return _newValueAdded; // value is priced in base units, so divide by scale factor
        }
```
Neither `_currentValueInProtocol` or `_existingEzETHSupply` is zero. Hence it doesn't revert.

In the next lines,
```solidity
uint256 inflationPercentaage = (SCALE_FACTOR * _newValueAdded) /
            (_currentValueInProtocol + _newValueAdded);
``` 
The `inflationPercentaage` is 499999999999999999 wei as the SCALE_FACTOR= 1e18, and 1 ETH is 1e18 wei.

In the next line,
```solidity
uint256 newEzETHSupply = (_existingEzETHSupply * SCALE_FACTOR) /
            (SCALE_FACTOR - inflationPercentaage);
```
The newEzETHSupply will becomes rounded off to 1. 

In the next lines we can see where it reverts

```solidity
uint256 mintAmount = newEzETHSupply - _existingEzETHSupply;

// Sanity check
if (mintAmount == 0) revert InvalidTokenAmount();

```
Since the _existingEzETHSupply is 1 and newEzETHSupply is also 1. The mintAmount is 0 and it reverts.

Hence any deposit of less than 2 ETH will result in a Denial of Service. Even then if its 2 ETH or more, the ezETH tokens minted will be 1 wei and now the state of the protocol will be
```solidity
currentValueInProtocol = 3 ETH + 1 wei
ezETHSupply = 2 wei
```  
Now Bob will be able to redeem his 1 wei of ezETH token and get make 1.5 ETH. Basically stealing 0.5 ETH from Alice.

## Tools Used
Manual Review, Foundry
## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Keep Track of token balance in a state variable.


## Assessed type

ERC4626

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L318


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`calculateTVLs` function contains an error than can lead to incorrect calculations of TVL, leading to overvaluation or undervaluation of user position. 

Here are the lines of code in question: 

 https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L318

instead of 
```
if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
                    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
                        collateralTokens[i], 
                        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
                    );
                }
```

the formula should be
```
if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
                    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
                        collateralTokens[j], 
                        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
                    );
                }
```

i is the index of 'operatorDelegators' list, while j is the index of 'collateralTokens' list

i is used in outer loop and j in inner loop, with 'withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded' set to true after first outer loop, skipping this block in subsequent outer loops. 

This lead to all `totalWithdrawalQueueValue` TVL being calculated with `renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue` argument set to `collateralTokens[0]`, using first token of `collateralTokens` list for lookup, but values/amount of all other tokens, leading to incorrect totalWithdrawalQueueValue and subsequently TVL calculations. 

## Proof of Concept
Assume there are two tokens accepted in Renzo, e.g. stETH, wBETH, with stETH being 'collateralTokens[0]' and wBETH 'collateralTokens[1]'
Assume 100 units of value is in both, 50% in stETH and wBETH. 


If stETH depegs by 20%, the true TVL in queue would be 0.5*0.8+0.5 = 0.9. 
Per current code, it would be 0.5*0.8+0.5*0.8 = 0.8, leading to unfair decrease in user share prices. 

If instead wBETH depegs by 20%, the TVL would stay at 100, which would lead to unfair increase in user share prices and loss to protocol. 

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Correct the lookup index as described above. 





## Assessed type

Math

title: calculateTVLs does not correctly loop through all collateral tokens
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L274-L358
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L202-L263


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The  `calculateTVLs()` function in RestakeManager incorrectly calculates the TVL due to incorrect mixing of indexes in a nested loop. As a result, the amount to redeem calculated in the  `WithdrawQueue:: withdraw` function will not be correct.  


In the `calculateTVLs()`function, there is a nested loop with `i` for operatorDelegator and `j` for collateralToken. In the loop that counts the balance of the collateral tokens, the ERC20 token is index with `i` while the balance is indexed with `j`. This means that instead of looping through all the collateral tokens, the balance of each collateral token is counted as the balance of `i` collateral token.

Since the different collateral tokens are not equal in value and the different operatorDelegators will have different balances for each respective collateral token, the TVL calculated will be completely wrong. 

## Proof of Concept

Assume: 
4 operator delegators and 3 collateral tokens
odLength = [0,1,2,3]
tokenLength = [token1,token2,token3]

In the below function we first have a for loop that cycles through the operators with the `i` as index.
In this loop we find a nested loop which tries to add the value of all the collateral tokens to the tvl. It uses `j` as index. 

Yet in this second loop both indexes are mixed. Which twists the calculations.

When `i = 0`, it tries to loop through the 3 collateral tokens to add the value to the TVL. 

first loop: `j = 0` : `collateralTokens[0], collateralTokens[0].balanceOf()`
2nd loop: `j = 1` :  `collateralTokens[0], collateralTokens[1].balanceOf()`
3rd loop: `j = 2`  :  `collateralTokens[0], collateralTokens[2].balanceOf()`

So for the 1st operator, we get 0 for the 2nd & 3rd collateral token, while vastly overestimating the balance of the 1st collateral token.
So for the 2nd operator, we get 0 for the 1st & 3rd collateral token, while vastly overestimating the balance of the 2nd collateral token. 
So for the 3rd operator, we get 0 for the 1st & 2nd collateral token, while vastly overestimating the balance of the 3rd collateral token.   

In `RestakeManager :: calculateTVLs()`
```solidity
                if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) { 
                    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
@>                    collateralTokens[i], 
                        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
                    );
                }
``` 

Since the different collateral tokens are not equal in value and the different operatorDelegators will have different balances for each respective collateral token, the TVL calculated will be completely wrong. 

The **impact** is a definite loss of protocol users and/or the protocol, since the function is used to calculate the amount to redeem in the withdraw(). 


## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

```diff
                if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) { 
                    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
-                        collateralTokens[i], 
+                        collateralTokens[j], 
                        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
                    );
                }
``` 


## Assessed type

Loop

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L244-L259
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L274-L358
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L202-L263


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `removeCollateralToken` function breaks the `calculateTVLs` function since collateralTokens.length is used in the calculateTVLs function to determine the balance of the collateral tokens. If the removed collateral token is not the last token in the collateralTokens array before removal, the TVL calculation will use the removed collateral balance while not counting active collateral balance. 

As a result, the TVL calculation will be wrong and the amount protocol users will be able to withdraw will be completely incorrect. 

## Proof of Concept

Assume: 
collateralTokens = [token1,token2,token3,token4]
collateralTokens.length = 4
OperatorDelegator Alice with balances for each token. [100,10,27,66]

Admin calls `removeCollateralToken` for token3.  
collateralTokens = [token1,token2,token4]
collateralTokens.length = 3
OperatorDelegator Alice still have the same balances. [100,10,27,66]

The `calculateTVLs` function is used to to calculate the TVL based on collateralTokens.length.
TVL = 0
collateralTokens.length = 3
Loop 1: TVL+= 100
Loop 2: TVL+= 10
Loop 3: TVL+= 27

TVL = 137 
The balance of the removed collateral token3 is counted as valid TVL while the active token4 collateral token is not counted. 

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Before a collateral token is removed, all operatorDelegators must be required to completely empty their balance of said token. Only then should the function be called. This would require substantial additional logic to correctly implement this. 




## Assessed type

Loop

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L50-L57
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L245
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L293


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Due to a check that the scaled price of ezETH can not be less than 1 ether (1e18), if ezETH is ever worth more than ETH (which has occured in the past) the getMintRate() function call will always revert and users will be unable to call deposit or depositETH in the xRenzoDeposit contract.

## Proof of Concept
If ezETH price recovers and stabilizes around the 1 ETH price as it has in the past and a user attempts to make a deposit when the current ezETH/ETH price = 1.0008. i.e. 
1. Bob wishes to deposit 1 ETH using xRenzoDeposit#depositETH. 
2. _deposit will then attempt to fetch the price of ezETH by calling getMintRate()
```solidity
(uint256 _lastPrice, uint256 _lastPriceTimestamp) = getMintRate();
```
3. getMintRate will then include a call to oracle.getMintRate().
```solidity
(uint256 oraclePrice, uint256 oracleTimestamp) = oracle.getMintRate();
```
4. oracle.getMintRate() is called which will fetch the price of ezETH denominated in ETH.
```solidity
(, int256 price, , uint256 timestamp, ) = oracle.latestRoundData();
```
5. Which will return 0.999 or 9.99e17
6. Which will fail the check:
```solidity
if (_scaledPrice < 1 ether) revert InvalidOraclePrice();
```
7. As a result the deposit will fail.

## Tools Used
Manual Review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Instead of using a check of < 1 ether consider adding an allowable amount of slippage so that if the ezETH price recovers and stabilizes to the ETH price like it has in the past users are still able to deposit.


## Assessed type

Oracle
