warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L331-L334
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L302


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
This leads to 

- an overstated TVL since the underlying value of the  `collateralToken` equivalent of the shares *queued for withdrawal* from the `strategyManager` are counted twice for each `collateralToken` per Operator delegator
- the overstated TVL in turn could lead to inflating `collateralToken` value  during token withdrawals and this could be exploited by a malicious user

## Proof of Concept
[`RestakeManger::calculateTVLs(...)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L302) is called to calculate the TVLs of each  `operatorDelegator` for each individual token (`operatorDelegatorTokenTVLs`), total for each OD (`operatorDelegatorTVLs`), and total for the protocol (`totalTVL`).

```solidity
File: RestakeManager.sol
297:             // Iterate through the tokens and get the value of each
298:             uint256 tokenLength = collateralTokens.length;
299:             for (uint256 j = 0; j < tokenLength; ) {
300:                // Get the value of this token (the ith delegators BALANCE of the jth collateral)
301:             
302:  @>            uint256 operatorBalance = operatorDelegators[i].getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(collateralTokens[j]);
303:             
304:           

307:                 operatorValues[j] = renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
308:                     collateralTokens[j],
309:                     operatorBalance
310:                 );
311: 
312:                 // Add it to the total TVL for this OD
313:                 operatorTVL += operatorValues[j];

337:                 // Add it to the total TVL for the protocol
338:                 totalTVL += operatorTVL;
      

File: OperatorDelegator.sol
327:     function getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(IERC20 token) external view returns (uint256) {
328:         return
329: @>          queuedShares[address(this)] == 0
330:                 ? tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this))
331:                 : tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) +
332:                     tokenStrategyMapping[token].sharesToUnderlyingView(
333: @>                     queuedShares[address(token)]
334:                     );
335:      }        

```

However, on `L302:` of the `RestakeManager.sol` makes an internal call is made to [`operatorDelegators[i].getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(collateralTokens[j])`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L331-L334) for every collateral token that an `operatorDelegators` deposits into the `strategy`.

as shown on `L329` of the `OperatorDelegator.sol`, the function checks if the `operatorDelegator` has any any shares queued for withdrawal and if it does it tries to *add* the underlying value of the queued share to the value of the actively staked shares in the `strategyManager` (which includes the queued shares as they have not been removed from strategy at this point)

This is wrong because 

- the `queuedShares[address(this)]` are still in the `strategy`  and as such adding the value instead of subtracting means the value will be counted twice counted twice.
- the queued shares are up for withdrawal pending a delay period and as such they should not account for the TVL of the protocol

## POC

- `OD1` has 3000 total shares in `strategy1` equivalent to 3000 underlying asset,
- there are 500 shares queued for withdrawal for `OD1` in the Eigen Layer `strategy1` equivalent to 500 underlying asset,
- [`getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(...)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L331-L334) is intended to  return 3500 shares for `OD1` but will return the same 3000 shares owing to another vulnerability shown in `L333` in `OperatorDelegator.sol` (the developer assumes shares are queued on behalf of the token instead of the `operatorDelegator`)

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Modify the `OperatorDelegator::getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(...)` function as shown below

```solidity
File: OperatorDelegator.sol
327:     function getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(IERC20 token) external view returns (uint256) {
328:         return
329:             queuedShares[address(this)] == 0
330:                 ? tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this))
331:    -            : tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) +
332:    -                tokenStrategyMapping[token].sharesToUnderlyingView(
333:    -                   queuedShares[address(token)]
334:    -                 );

331:    +            : tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) -
332:    +                tokenStrategyMapping[token].sharesToUnderlyingView(
333:    +                   queuedShares[address(this)]
334:    +                );
335:      } 
```

.


## Assessed type

Math

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L215
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L210
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L316-L321


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
This can be used to manipulate the `exchangeRate` of `ezETH` and a malicious user can benefit from the arbitrage opportunity since the price will be different on different chains

## Proof of Concept
When [`xRenzoBridge::sendPrice(...)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L210) is called to send the price of `ezETH` form L1, a permissionless external call is made to [`BalancerRateProvider::getRate(...)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L215) which in turn calls the [`RestakeManager.calculateTVLs()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L316-L321) function to evaluate the TVL of the protocol.

```solidity
File: xRenzoBridge.sol
210:     function sendPrice(
211:         CCIPDestinationParam[] calldata _destinationParam,
212:         ConnextDestinationParam[] calldata _connextDestinationParam
213:     ) external payable onlyPriceFeedSender nonReentrant {
214:         // call getRate() to get the current price of ezETH
215:         uint256 exchangeRate = rateProvider.getRate(); // @audit-issue this can be frontrun as explained in the function declation

File: BalancerRateProvider.sol
30:     function getRate() external view returns (uint256) {
31:         // Get the total TVL priced in ETH from restakeManager
32:         (, , uint256 totalTVL) = restakeManager.calculateTVLs();
33: 
34:         // Get the total supply of the ezETH token
35:         uint256 totalSupply = ezETHToken.totalSupply();
36: 
37:         // Sanity check
38:         if (totalSupply == 0 || totalTVL == 0) revert InvalidZeroInput();
39: 
40:         // Return the rate
41:         // @audit if this includes the withdrawal queue then it is messed up as a user can see this call and decide to donate to the withdrawal queue to inflate TVL and by extension the exchange rate
42:         // @audit ans attacker can increasee the TVL and hence the price of the ezETH
43:         return (10 ** 18 * totalTVL) / totalSupply;
44:     }
45: }

File: RestakeManager.sol
316:                 if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
317:                     totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue( 
318:                        collateralTokens[i],
319: @>                     collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
320:                     );
321:                  }    

   
355:         totalTVL += (address(withdrawQueue).balance + totalWithdrawalQueueValue);    

```

Because the balance of all `collateralTokens` including `ETH`  in the protocol’s `WithdrawalQueue` are included in the protocol's `totalTVL` calculation, the TVL can be easily manipulated by a well funded attacker

This is a design flaw because when deposit is made in the `RestakeManager.sol` contract, the protocol prioritises filling its withdrawalQueue up to its `withdrawalQueueBuffer` even when there are no queued withdrawals as against forwarding the deposit into the EigenLayer strategy and getting a strategy share in return, hence the protocol includes the balance of the `collateralTokens` in the `withdrawalQueue` of the protocol when calculating the `totalTVL`

## POC

A malicious user can frontrun the `BalancerRateProvider::getRate(...)` call  to donate any  `collateralTokens` to the withdrawal queue of the protocol to inflate TVL calculation and by extension `ezEth` pricing

- Assume `totalTVL` = 100_000e18, ezETH `totalSupply` = 100_000e18
- `getRate()` returns 10 ** 18

```solidity
return (10 ** 18 * 100000e18) / 100000e18; // 1e18
```

- `PriceFeedSender` calls `xRenzoBridge::sendPrice(...)`
- Bob notices the `BalancerRateProvider::getRate(...)` call and frontruns it to donate 10e18 of any  `collateralTokens` of choice to inflate the `totalTVL` without affecting the `totalSupply` of `ezETH` as there will be no `ezETH` minted to bob when he send funds to the protocols `withdrawalQueue` thus increasing the value returned by `BalancerRateProvider::getRate(...)`

```solidity
return (10 ** 18 * 100010e18) / 100000e18; // 1.0001e18
```

A well funded user can inflate the price way higher and benefit form arbitrage opportunity as the price will be different on different chains

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider

- depositing all tokens to the strategy instead of prioritising filling the withdrawal queue before filling strategies when deposits are first made.
- remove the code block below for `RestakeManager.sol`

```solidity
File: RestakeManager.sol
316:                 if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
317:                     totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue( 
318:                        collateralTokens[i],
319:                        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
320:                     );
321:                  }  
```


## Assessed type

Other

title: Removing an Operator delegator can cause funds to be stuck in EigenLayer
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L289-L300
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/6de01c6c16d6df44af15f0b06809dc160eac0ebf/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L336
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/6de01c6c16d6df44af15f0b06809dc160eac0ebf/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L309
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L160
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L302


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Removing `operatorDelegator` without checking if they have shares in the `strategyManager` can lead to:

- loss of funds for any user who had depeosited before the removal but is withdrawing after the OD is removed.
- `_collateralToken` being stuck in the Eigen Layer without a way to withdraw
- Also this can break accouncting as the TVL will be understated because the removed operator has assigned assigned to it from EigenLayer when `RestakeManager::deposit(...)` was called but when `calculateTVLs(...)` is called to evaluate the `totalTVL`, the value will be understated because the `calculateTVLs(...)` function will [loop](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L289-L300) through all the ODs in the `operatorDelegators` array leaving out the removed `operatorDelegators` even when it still has actively staked shares.

## Proof of Concept
When a _collateralToken is deposited using the [`RestakeManager::deposit(...)`]() function, funds are approved for a chosen `operatorDelegator` (OD) to deposit in Eigen Layer `strategy` by calling `operatorDelegator.deposit(...)`. When the OD deposits the funds into Eigen layer (EL) by calling `strategyManager.depositIntoStrategy(...)` to deposit the funds into the Strategy of the _collateralToken, the `strategy` assigns shares to the chosen OD who made the EL deposit and [saves it in a mapping for the  [`operatorDelegator`](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/6de01c6c16d6df44af15f0b06809dc160eac0ebf/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L336) in the `StartegyManager`’s storage as seen [here](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/6de01c6c16d6df44af15f0b06809dc160eac0ebf/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L309)

```solidity
EigenLayer/StrategyManager.sol

  function _addShares(address staker, IERC20 token, IStrategy strategy, uint256 
  shares) internal {
    
    ...

      // add the returned shares to their existing shares for this strategy
  @>  stakerStrategyShares[staker][strategy] += shares;

  }
```

However, when [`RestakeManager::removeOperatorDelegator(..)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L160) is called to remove an OD, no checks are performed to ensure the OD being removed has no pending shares assigned in the `strategyManager` and as such this can lead to:

- funds getting stuck in Eigen Layer. The effect of this becomes more pronounced during a mass withdrawal event.
- understated TVL value because an OD with actively staked shares is not taken into account

Even if the OD is later added to the list of active ODs, all calls to the [`calculateTVLs(...)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L302) function during the period when the OD was removed would have returned am understated  TVL which would have in turn lead to miscalculation of shares assigned to other ODs by the `strategyManager`

In fact, if  a user who deposited with all OD shares intact decides to withdraw when a removed OD has shares in it, he will get less than the value he deposited when he withdraws due to the reduced `totalTVL` value.


## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider checking if the operatorDelegator to be removed has shares assigned in the strategyManager and revert or implement a way to transfer the shares assigned before removing the operatorDelegator.





## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L434-L442
https://github.com/connext/monorepo/blob/8338d6506c609f9383d81133c3cb40cfb9e44392/packages/deployments/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L303


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Malicious user can have undue control over funds that are bridged to L1, leading to loss of funds.

## Proof of Concept
it is common knowledge that when bridging funds across chains, setting the recipient or even `_delegate` to `msg.sender` can lead to loss of funds if the `msg.sender` account is an abstraction account or simply a contract, this is because the address on the destination chain will differ form the address on the originating chain where the funds were sent from.

When [xRenzoDeposit.sweep(...)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L434-L442) is called to bridge nextWETH to L1, an internal call is made to connext.xcall(...), 
however the problem is that the [`_delegate`](https://github.com/connext/monorepo/blob/8338d6506c609f9383d81133c3cb40cfb9e44392/packages/deployments/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L303) parameter of the `xcall(...)` function is hardcoded to `msg.sender`

```solidity
    function sweep() public payable nonReentrant {
        ...

        
        // @audit funds could be lost during sweeping or when bridging to L1 because delegate will be different on the destination chain
        connext.xcall{ value: msg.value }(
            bridgeDestinationDomain,
            bridgeTargetAddress,
            address(collateralToken),
            msg.sender, 
            balance,
            0, // Asset is already nextWETH, so no slippage will be incurred
            bridgeCallData
        );

        // send collected bridge fee to sweeper
        _recoverBridgeFee();

        // Emit the event
        emit BridgeSwept(bridgeDestinationDomain, bridgeTargetAddress, msg.sender, balance);
    }
```

According to [connext, the `_delegate` parameter](https://docs.connext.network/developers/reference/contracts/calls#xcall) *which is an address on destination domain that has rights to update slippage tolerance, retry transactions, or revert back to origin in the event that a transaction fails at the destination* is set to `msg.sender`. 

The problem is, if the `msg.sender` that is an `allowedBridgeSweepers[msg.sender]` is a contract address, the owner of the `msg.sender` contract on the destination domain or chain may differ from the originating chain, giving a different (perhaps malicious) user undue control over the the funds if the transaction fails on the destination chain.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider using a trusted and verified L1 address as the _delegate instead of hardcoding the _delegate to msg.sender.


## Assessed type

Access Control

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L367
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L375
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L369


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
This can lead to loss of funds accross different `_depositTokens` and for the renzo protocol

## Proof of Concept
Users can call `xRenzoDeposit.deposit()` to deposit a (`_depositToken`) for instance `WETH` on L2. However the `xRenzoDeposit` contract approves the `connext` bridge to spend the full deposit amount. But due to slippage and `bridgeFee` deductions, the users are expected to specify `_minOut`  *which is the minimum number of `xezETH` to accept to ensure slippage minimums.* 

The transaction flow is as shown below

|→ `xRenzoDeposit::deposit(…)`
|→→ `xRenzoDeposit::_deposit(...)`
|→→→ `xRenzoDeposit::getBridgeFeeShare(_amountIn);`
|→→→ [`xRenzoDeposit::_trade(...)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L367)
|→→→→ [`depositToken.safeApprove(...)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L369)
|→→→→ `connext.swapExact(...)`
|→→→ `...`

Some funds are still left in the  [approval](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L369) given to `connext` after the [`connext.swapExact(...)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L375) is called this is owing to slippage and as such `connext` can still spend the unused funds. IN the event of an exploit the `xRenzoDeposit` contract will loose all remaining amount from the last deposit transaction from different `_depositToken`s.

### Exploit Scenario

- `bridgeFeeShare` = 5%
- Expected slippage from swap exact = 10%
- `_amountIn` = 1_000_000e18
- After `bridgeFeeShare` is charged, `_amountIn` = 950_000e18
- `connext` is approved to spend `_amountIn` = 950_000e18
- Due to the current pool reserves or even slippage when `connext.swapExact(...)` is called, it spends 855_000e18 still having approval for the unspent amount of up to 95_000e18 `_depositToken`s
- If there is an exploit in  the `connext` bridge before `sweep()` is called, the unspent amount could be stolen through `connext`.

The will cascade across all allowed _depositTokens in the xRenzoDeposit contract leading to material loss of funds

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider revoking the remaining funds from the approval given to the connext bridge after a trade(...) is called during a deposit transaction.


## Assessed type

ERC20

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L236
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L93


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Funds can get stuck for some time during mass withdrawal request since `WithdrawalQueue::withdraw(...)` will always revert.

## Proof of Concept
With due respect to the developers, this is a result of design flaw. 


Currently, when the protocols `WithdrawalQueue` is available balance less than the amount a user intends to withdraw  and there are no funds in the `DepositQueue` to fill the buffer, while there are yet unclaimed queued withdrawals, any attempt by a user to call [`WithdrawalQueue::withdraw(...)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L236) will revert because the protocol does not implement  the `WithdrawalQueue::withdraw(...)` function to queue withdrawals from Eigen layer. Although the sponsor confirmed in the discord that :

*admin accounts will manually unstake from EigenLayer **periodically** through 2 step process*

I assume the admin will unstake to fill the `withdrawalBufferTarget[asset]`

This means that users funds will be stuck if there are no incoming deposits (and rewards are not yet sufficient to handle the withdrawal requests) because: 

- this resolution  begs the question of **how does the admin know how much asset to are being withdrawn in the event of a mass withdrawal when the** `withdrawalBufferTarget` **will not be able to handle such volume** at once
- the `withdraw(...)` function cannot queue withdrawals because `claimReserve[_asset]` is already taken care of by the current balance of the `WithdrawalQueue` pending the `cooldown` period after which user can claim their asset
- withdrawal form EigenLayer is subject to a 7 day delay.

```solidity
File: WithdrawQueue.sol

157:     function getAvailableToWithdraw(address _asset) public view returns (uint256) {
158:         if (_asset != IS_NATIVE) {
159:             return IERC20(_asset).balanceOf(address(this)) - claimReserve[_asset];
160:         } else {
161:             return address(this).balance - claimReserve[_asset];
162:         }
163:     }

206:     function withdraw(uint256 _amount, address _assetOut) external nonReentrant {
             ...
236:         if (amountToRedeem > getAvailableToWithdraw(_assetOut)) revert NotEnoughWithdrawBuffer();

```

While *manually unstaking periodically_* seemsto make sense in the short term, in the event of a mass withdrawal and there are no incoming deposits, the `WithdrawalQueue::withdraw(...)` call will fail because as seen on `L240` the `amountToRedeem` will be greater than the amount available to withdraw and the call will revert.

## POC

- `withdrawalBufferTarget[_asset]` is set to 100 ether
- current asset balance in the withdrawal queue = 10 ether
- `claimReserve[_asset]` is currently 10 ether
- The are still actively stake asset worth 1000 ether
- there is a mass withdrawal to the tune of 500 ether in failed withdrawals
- admin can only unstakes to fill 100 ether **periodically** because they are not aware of the 500 ether requested in failed withdrawals.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider queueing withdrawal from Eigen layer in `epochs` instead of reverting when the `amountToRedeem` is greater than the amount available to withdraw from the `WithdrawalQueue` instead of waiting for the admin to periodically withdraw.

Similar protocols like RioStaking protocol allows their withdraw function under the same condition, to queue withdrawal form EigenLayer

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`WithdrawalQueue::withdraw(...)` can be bricked, 

- preventing users from queueing and claiming withdrawals
- users funds stuck will be stuck

## Proof of Concept
Currently, users have to wait for a `cooldown` period to elapse after calling `WithdrawalQueue::withdraw(...)` to withdraw their asset from the protocol by calling  `WithdrawalQueue::claim(...)`. However **due to wrong implementation of checks-effect-interactions** in the `WithdrawalQueue::withdraw(...)` function,  users who are yet to start their cooldown period will not be able to call `WithdrawalQueue::withdraw(...)` and some users  may not be able to [`WithdrawalQueue::claim(...)`]() whether or not  there are enough asset in the withdrawal queue.

The problem exist because available balance is checked against stale `claimReserve[_asset]`before  [updating the `claimReserve[_asset]`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L253) to include the current withdrawal value hence not taking into consideration whether the current [available balance](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L236) of the withdrawal queue can contain amount that is being queued to be claimed after cooldown period

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
This can lead to a situation where the protocol becomes insolvent because users can choose asset to deposit and withdraw hence arbitraging from the protocol.

## Proof of Concept

During withdrawals, user can perform arbitrage, this is because there is no restriction on users to withdraw the exact restaking token they deposited.

This problem exists because users can call [`ResatakeManager::deposit(...)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L492) with a different `_collateralToken` from the one they used to call [`WithdrawalQueue::withdraw(...)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206) hence a malicious user can but `stETH` cheap from the stETH/ETH pool and deposit it into the protocol and withdraw say cbETH which is currently trading at 1.03ETH at the time of writing this report

Liquid staking tokens are vulnerable to **depegging** significantly from the underlying staked cryptocurrencies. As [seen in RENZO](https://beincrypto.com/renzo-ezeth-depeg-airdrop-rez/) itself just two weeks ago

### scenario

- Alice has 100 ETH, and buys 100 stETH at 0.99ETH/stETH with 99 ETH
- Alice calls `ResatakeManager::deposit(...)` with 100 stETH currently trading at 0.99ETH/stETH
- Alice call `WithdrawalQueue::withdraw(...)` to withdraw 100 cbETH which  is currently trading at 1.03ETH/cbETH
- Alice gains `101 - 99` = 2 ether

A trivial recommendation is not in sight here.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Malicious user can block the deposits of all `collateralToken` into the protocol so as 

- to steal all the rewards from the EigenLayer `strategy`  and

## Proof of Concept
This attack is a combination because of the donation and first depositor Attack

For simplicity, I assume `withdrawalBufferTarget` = 11 ether (although not needed)

126:         uint256 _newValueAdded,
127:         uint256 _existingEzETHSupply
128:     ) external pure returns (uint256) {
129:         // For first mint, just return the new value added.
130:         // Checking both current value and existing supply to guard against gaming the initial mint
131:         if (_currentValueInProtocol == 0 || _existingEzETHSupply == 0) {
132:             return _newValueAdded; // value is priced in base units, so divide by scale factor
134:         }

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Since rewards from EigenLayer are calculated based on shares issued to the operator Delegator, users reward will be diluted because some funds are left dormant and idle in the WithdrawalQueue contrary to the aim of the protocol’s promised utility to users. Hence the protocol does not delivery promised returns.

## Proof of Concept
When a deposits into the Renzo protocol through `RestakeManager::deposit(...)` function, all funds are not immediately forwarded to the Eigenlayer `strategy` . The protocol first fills the `WithdrawalQueue` up to the `withdrawalBufferTarget` and until this target amount of funds is transferred from the `DeposiitQueue` to the `WithdrawalQueue` is met, no funds are transferred to the  `strategy` through the `OperatorDelegator` [and no `strategy` shares are minted to the `OperatorDelegator`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L167-L168) while this is going on.

# Lines of code

# Vulnerability details

## Issue Description

The `WithdrawQueue` contract implements the OZ `PausableUpgradeable` contract, which adds pausing functionalities to the contract that can be used by the admin:

```solidity
/**
 * @notice  Pause the contract
 * @dev     Permissioned call (onlyWithdrawQueueAdmin)
 */
function pause() external onlyWithdrawQueueAdmin {
    _pause();
}

/**
 * @notice  Unpause the contract
 * @dev     Permissioned call (onlyWithdrawQueueAdmin)
 */
function unpause() external onlyWithdrawQueueAdmin {
    _unpause();
}
```

The issue is that although the admin can change the paused state using either `pause()` or `unpause()` functions, these functionalities are not utilized within the contract, the contract does not implement the `whenNotPaused` nor `whenPaused` modifiers in any function. As a result, withdrawals from the protocol cannot be paused (stopped). 

This could pose significant problems, especially in emergency situations or if the protocol is exploited. In such cases, the admin will have no means to prevent users from withdrawing their funds from the withdrawal queue contract.

It's worth noting that although the `RestakeManager` contract also has pausing functionality, which can be triggered by the `onlyDepositWithdrawPauserAdmin` admin, this will only be applied to new deposits and will not affect withdrawals (as the admin name would suggest).

## Impact

The inability to pause withdrawals from the `WithdrawQueue` contract could lead to potential loss of funds if the protocol is exploited or enters an emergency state.

## Tools Used

Manual review, VS Code

## Recommended Mitigation

To implement the pausing functionalities in `WithdrawQueue`, the `whenNotPaused` modifier must be added to the main functions of the contract: `withdraw` and `claim`.



## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L130-L131


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

25% of the first deposit into Renzo can be stolen through a frontrunning attack.

## Proof of Concept

In Renzo's [`calculateMintAmount` function, this line](https://github.com/Renzo-Protocol/contracts-public/blob/0530cbd20590677da5fa6fd32a0a8b250a9eb028/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L114-L116) is meant to defend against the first deposit attack by ensuring the `ezEth` minted is equal to assets deposited when the vault or supply is empty. This formula is also copied to Ion's codebase. However, an alteration can be made to the first deposit attack to bypass this check, where `_currentValueInProtocol > 0` and ` _existingEzETHSupply == 0`.

The first deposit attack can be executed using this sequence:

Let's say a user deposits `D` assets for the initial deposit

1.Attacker deposits 1 asset to get 1 `ezEth`
2. Attacker donate/transfers `D / 2 + 1` assets into the contract
3. Victim deposits D assets. In return they get `1.99999` shares which rounds down to `1` share. Note that the totalSupply of `ezEth` is `1` so the ` _existingEzETHSupply == 0` condition passes. `_currentValueInProtocol == D/2 + 1`
4. Due to the large rounding error the attacker ends up making 25% of the first deposit as profit. 

There is a description of a similar attack at the bottom of [this page/ReadMe](https://github.com/ZeframLou/bunni) with the subtitle "Frontrunning the first deposit may steal 1/4 of the deposit". 

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Use either an initial minting of shares similar to Uniswap v2 or use OpenZeppelin's ERC4626 vault inflation mitigation with virtual shares and decimal offset.


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L264-L274


# Vulnerability details


## Proof of Concept
Protocol uses Connext's `xcall()` to send data to the receiver, this can be seen from [xRenzoDeposit#sweep()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L434-L442) and [xRenzoBridge#sendPrice()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L264-L274), issue however is with the latter implementation and it's integration with the `relayerFee`.

Take a look at https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L264-L274

```solidity
    function sendPrice(
        CCIPDestinationParam[] calldata _destinationParam,
        ConnextDestinationParam[] calldata _connextDestinationParam
    ) external payable onlyPriceFeedSender nonReentrant {

        //(...snip)
        for (uint256 i = 0; i < _connextDestinationParam.length; ) {
            connext.xcall{ value: _connextDestinationParam[i].relayerFee }(
                _connextDestinationParam[i].destinationDomainId,
                _connextDestinationParam[i]._renzoReceiver,
                address(0),
                msg.sender,
                0,
                0,
                _callData
            );
        //(...snip)
        }

```

We can see that the `relayerFee` is being used, however it's wrongly being attached as if it's a native token.

Now going to the interface used to query Connext's functionality we can see that [two xcall functions exists](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Bridge/Connext/core/IConnext.sol#L14-L34) and the one that includes `relayerFee` actually expects it as an argument passed on to the function call, this can also be confirmed by going to the official documentation of Connext here: https://docs.connext.network/developers/reference/contracts/calls#xcall, we can see that the `relayerFee` is an optional parameter to only be considered for an overloaded `xcall` but if it's included then this value is to be taken from the `asset` and not the native token, i.e quoting them:

```markdown
 | _relayerFee | `uint256` |(Optional) This is available in an overloaded xcall. If provided, the relayer fee will be taken in `_asset` rather than the native asset. 
```

This then means that in the above instance where protocol attempts to query `xcall()` it doesn't do it as expected.

## Impact
Protocol's core functionality is flawed when considering it's integration with Connext, cause when the `PRICE_FEED_SENDER` is calling `Connext#xcall()` it instead passes in the `relayerFee` as is if it's a native value instead of passing it as an argument to the function, which then causes the context in Connext to not know that the `xcall` with the `relayerFee` integration is actually the one being queried breaking the integration.
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider correctly querying  `Connext#xcall()` when  passing the `relayerFee`.




## Assessed type

Context

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L263
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L263


# Vulnerability details


## Proof of Concept

It's a known fact that validators can indeed lose part of their deposit via [penalties](https://eth2book.info/capella/part2/incentives/penalties/) or [slashing](https://eth2book.info/capella/part2/incentives/slashing/) events:

- In case of penalties Eigenlayer can be notified of the balance drop via the permissionless [EigenPod#verifyBalanceUpdates()](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L185) function.
- In case of slashing the validator is forced to exit and Eigenlayer can also be notified via the permissionless [EigenPod#verifyAndProcessWithdrawals()](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L232) function because the slashing event is effectively a full withdrawal.

As soon as either [EigenPod#verifyBalanceUpdates()](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L185) or [EigenPod#verifyAndProcessWithdrawals()](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L232) is called the `TVL` of the Renzo protocol drops instantly. This is because both of the functions update the variable [`podOwnerShares[podOwner]`](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/EigenPodManager.sol#L120):

- [EigenPod#verifyBalanceUpdates()](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L185) will update the variable [here](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L220)
- [EigenPod#verifyAndProcessWithdrawals()](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L232) will update the variable [here](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L275)

This makes it possible for stakers to:

1. Request a withdrawal via [WithdrawQueue#withdraw()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L263) for all their `ezETH` held.
2. Then call either [EigenPod#verifyBalanceUpdates()](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L185) or [EigenPod#verifyAndProcessWithdrawals()](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L232).

So at the point when [WithdrawQueue#withdraw()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L263) will be called and the withdrawal will be successfully queued, the TVL is not going to include penalties or slashing.

## Impact

Stakers can frontrun validators penalties and slashing events with a withdrawal request in order to avoid the loss when the deposit pool has enough liquidity effectively allowing them to game the system.

This essentially shows that it's possible to withdraw already minted `ezETH` while avoiding penalties or slashing up to the amount of liquidity available in the deposit pool.

After executing this, all the staker needs to do is to wait the 7 day period and they can then claim their withdrawal request via [WithdrawQueue#claim()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L263) completely sidestepping the slashing/penalties

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider making the n [WithdrawQueue#withdraw()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279-L312) execution more effective, this can be achieved by introducing a check whenever the function is called to see if penalties or slashing events happened during the epoch the request is being passed, if yes then distribute the correct amount of penalties to all the `ezETH` withdrawn in the current epoch, including the ones that requested the withdrawal before the drop.



## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L284


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The function `_refundGas` calculates the gas refund based on `tx.gasprice`, which can be manipulated by validators or in cooperation with a malicious user.

A validator or a user in collaboration with a validator could set an arbitrarily high `gasprice` for their transaction, leading to an inflated gas refund from the contract's balance. This could drain a decent amount out of the contract's funds if the balance is sufficient.


## Proof of Concept
#### Scenario:

- A validator or a group of validators identifies the `DepositQueue` contract with the refundable gas feature.
- They create a transaction that interacts with the contract in a way that triggers the `_refundGas` function.
- The validators set an artificially high `gasprice` for the transaction.
- Since they are the block proposers, they can ensure that this transaction is included in the block they are validating.
- The contract calculates the refund based on the inflated `gasprice` and refunds more `ETH` than the actual cost of gas used for the transaction.
- The validators receive the excess refund, extracting value from the contract.


## Tools Used
Manual review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement a gas price limit within the contract to cap the refundable amount.
OR
Use a gas price oracle to determine a reasonable gas price for refunds.


## Assessed type

MEV

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Factory.sol#L135-L172


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The primary impact of the concern is the potential for unauthorized manipulation of sensitive functions within the `XERC20` contract. By transferring ownership to the deployer wallet (`msg.sender`), the vulnerability allows the deployer to impersonate validated senders and execute functions intended to be restricted to specific addresses. This could lead to financial losses, reputation damage, and privacy violations, posing significant risks to the security and integrity of the contract and its ecosystem.
## Proof of Concept
The vulnerability arises due to the transfer of ownership of the `XERC20` contract to the deployer wallet (`msg.sender`) within the `_deployXERC20` function of the `XERC20Factory` contract. This transfer of ownership grants the deployer full control over the `XERC20` contract, including the ability to execute functions on behalf of other addresses that are typically validated based on ownership or authorization.
Within the `_deployXERC20` function, after deploying the `XERC20` contract, the ownership is transferred to the deployer wallet (`msg.sender`) using the `transferOwnership` function:
```solidity
XERC20(_xerc20).transferOwnership(msg.sender);
```
If the `XERC20` contract contains functions that validate the sender based on ownership or authorization, such as `onlyOwner` modifiers or sender address checks, these validations may be bypassed by the deployer wallet (`msg.sender`) after the ownership transfer.
After the ownership transfer, the deployer wallet can impersonate any validated sender by directly calling the relevant functions of the `XERC20` contract. This allows the deployer to bypass any sender validation checks implemented within the `XERC20` contract.

## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
 If ownership transfer is necessary, ensure that it is conducted securely and with appropriate checks to prevent unauthorized access post-transfer. Also, Implement robust access control mechanisms within the `XERC20` contract to ensure that sensitive functions can only be executed by authorized addresses.


## Assessed type

Other

## Impact
The impact of this issue is that the deposit function cannot directly support native tokens. Users attempting to deposit native tokens will encounter errors or unintended behavior due to the lack of handling for such tokens. This limitation reduces the usability and flexibility of the contract, potentially leading to user frustration and decreased adoption.


## Proof of Concept
The issue stems from the `_deposit` function's lack of support for native tokens. Currently, the function is designed to handle the deposit of ERC20 tokens using the `safeTransferFrom` function, but it lacks explicit handling for native tokens. Below is the relevant excerpt from the `_deposit` function:
```solidity
function _deposit(address _to, uint256 _amount) internal {
    if (!IS_NATIVE) {
        ERC20.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), _amount);
    }

    XERC20.mint(_to, _amount);
    emit Deposit(_to, _amount);
}

```
As evident, the function checks whether the deposited token is native (`IS_NATIVE`), and if not, it transfers ERC20 tokens using `safeTransferFrom` and then mints `XERC20` tokens for the recipient. However, there is no explicit handling provided for native tokens, thus rendering the deposit function incompatible with them.


## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Enable support for native tokens, the `_deposit` function must be updated to include explicit handling for native token deposits. This can be achieved by implementing logic to directly receive and process native token transfers within the function.

ETH-Transfer

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L338-L345


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The potential arithmetic issues in the `getStakedETHBalance` function could lead to incorrect calculation of the staked ETH balance. This could result in inaccurate reporting of the contract's staked ETH holdings, potentially leading to incorrect decision-making in the protocol or affecting the overall integrity of the system's financial calculations.


## Proof of Concept
The `getStakedETHBalance` function in the provided contract contains potential arithmetic issues due to unsafe casting from `int256` to `uint256`. This function calculates the staked ETH balance based on the value of `podOwnerShares`, which represents the staked shares of the contract in EigenPod. However, the calculation method is prone to two specific issues:

- Unsigned Integer Underflow: In the case where `podOwnerShares` is negative, the code attempts to subtract -`podOwnerShares` from `stakedButNotVerifiedEth`. However, if the absolute value of `-podOwnerShares` exceeds the value of `stakedButNotVerifiedEth`, an underflow will occur, leading to unexpected behavior or potential contract revert.
- Signed Integer Overflow: If `podOwnerShares` is very large (positive), and `stakedButNotVerifiedEth` is also large, the subsequent addition of `podOwnerShares` to the sum of `queuedShares[IS_NATIVE]` and `stakedButNotVerifiedEth` could result in a signed integer overflow. This overflow may cause the calculation to wrap around to a smaller value or produce incorrect results. 
```solidity
  /// @dev Gets the amount of ETH staked in the EigenLayer
    function getStakedETHBalance() external view returns (uint256) {
        // accounts for current podOwner shares + stakedButNotVerified ETH + queued withdraw shares
        int256 podOwnerShares = eigenPodManager.podOwnerShares(address(this)); // @audit-info unsafe casting from int256 to uint256
        return
            podOwnerShares < 0
                ? queuedShares[IS_NATIVE] + stakedButNotVerifiedEth - uint256(-podOwnerShares)
                : queuedShares[IS_NATIVE] + stakedButNotVerifiedEth + uint256(podOwnerShares);
    }
```
## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider using safer arithmetic operations provided by libraries like OpenZeppelin's SafeMath.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L162-L169

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L491-L576


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The original depositor's transaction might be affected by the attacker's manipulation. They could lose tokens, experience unexpected behavior, or have their intended actions thwarted due to the altered state of the contracts.

## Proof of Concept
In Ethereum, pending transactions are stored in the mempool until they are included in a block by miners. Transactions interact with smart contracts, and their execution order can affect the final state of these contracts.
The `OperatorDelegator` contract's `deposit()` function can only be called by the `RestakeManager`, ensuring that deposits are managed securely. However, the `StrategyManager` contract's `deposit()` function is public, allowing anyone to invoke it. This public accessibility creates an opportunity for front-running.
An attacker monitors the mempool for pending transactions and identifies a deposit transaction targeting the `OperatorDelegator` contract. Since miners prioritize transactions with higher gas prices, the attacker quickly submits their own transaction to deposit tokens into the `StrategyManager` contract with a higher gas price. Consequently, the attacker's transaction is likely to be included in the next block before the original `OperatorDelegator` transaction.
By getting their transaction included before the original `OperatorDelegator` deposit, the attacker can manipulate the state of the contracts to their advantage. Since the `StrategyManager` contract approves the `depositQueue` and then the `OperatorDelegator` to spend tokens, the attacker could exploit this approval chain to transfer tokens to themselves or perform other unauthorized actions.

## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps

One effective mitigation to address the front-running vulnerability in this context is to use a commit-reveal scheme for token deposits.

In a commit-reveal scheme:

Commit Phase: The depositor commits to their intended transaction by submitting a hash of the transaction details to the blockchain without revealing the actual details.
Reveal Phase: After a certain period, the depositor reveals the original transaction details, including the token amount and destination contract, which matches the previously committed hash.
By enforcing a commit-reveal scheme, the original depositor's transaction details remain undisclosed until the reveal phase, preventing attackers from front-running and manipulating the transaction order. 


## Assessed type

Timing

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The impact of this vulnerability is the potential for unfair distribution of ezETH tokens, skewing the tokenomics of the protocol. The attacker could gain an excessive amount of ezETH tokens compared to the actual value they contributed, undermining the fairness and stability of the system.


## Proof of Concept
The vulnerability in the `calculateMintAmount` function of the ezETH protocol smart contract allows for the exploitation of the initial deposit phase. This function is responsible for determining the amount of ezETH tokens to mint based on various parameters such as the current protocol value, new deposits, and existing ezETH supply.

The critical flaw lies in the conditional check within the function, specifically when either the current protocol value or the existing ezETH supply is zero. Let's examine the vulnerable portion of the code:
```solidity
if (_currentValueInProtocol == 0 || _existingEzETHSupply == 0) {
    return _newValueAdded; // value is priced in base units, so divide by scale factor
}
```
In this condition, if `_currentValueInProtocol` or `_existingEzETHSupply` equals zero, the function simply returns `_newValueAdded`, which represents the value of the deposit being made. This implies that during the initial deposit phase where there's no existing protocol value or ezETH supply, the entire deposit amount would be minted into ezETH tokens.

Now, let's explore how this vulnerability can be exploited:

Imagine a scenario where a malicious actor is aware of this vulnerability and is the first to deposit funds into the protocol. By making an exceptionally large deposit, the attacker can artificially inflate the initial protocol value. Since there's no comparison against existing values, the entire deposit amount would be converted into `ezETH` tokens.

As a result, the attacker gains a disproportionate amount of `ezETH` tokens relative to the actual value they contributed to the protocol. This gives them an unfair advantage and undermines the fairness and stability of the system.

In essence, this vulnerability allows the initial depositor to manipulate the minting process to their advantage, resulting in an imbalance in the distribution of `ezETH` tokens.

## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Introduce a predefined initial value for the protocol or impose limits on the amount of tokens that can be minted during the initial deposit period. 


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Factory.sol#L135-L172
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Factory.sol#L184-L212


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
 The lack of a guarded salt can potentially allow an attacker to front-run the deployment transaction and deploy a contract with the same salt on another chain, leading to address collisions or loss of control over the deployed contract.

## Proof of Concept
The `XERC20Factory` contract utilizes the CREATE3 utility to deploy new contracts deterministically, a process crucial for ensuring consistency and predictability within the blockchain ecosystem. This deployment mechanism involves the generation of salts derived from various input parameters, which are then used to calculate the deployment address of the contract.

However, a critical vulnerability arises from the way salts are constructed within the `_deployXERC20` and `_deployLockbox` functions. In both cases, the salts are formed without adhering to the recommended best practice, which advocates for setting the first 20 bytes of the salt to `msg.sender`. Let's examine the vulnerability in detail:

In `_deployXERC20`, the salt construction is as follows:
```solidity
bytes32 _salt = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(_name, _symbol, msg.sender));
_xerc20 = CREATE3.deploy(_salt, _bytecode, 0);
```
Similarly, in _deployLockbox, the salt construction is as follows:
```solidity
bytes32 _salt = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(_xerc20, _baseToken, msg.sender));
_lockbox = payable(CREATE3.deploy(_salt, _bytecode, 0));
```
While these functions aim to deploy new `XERC20` and `XERC20Lockbox` contracts deterministically, the oversight in salt construction deviates from recommended practices. This deviation can potentially introduce security vulnerabilities into the system.
![image](C:\Users\Name\Downloads\this.jpeg)
[CreateX.sol#L616-L646](https://github.com/pcaversaccio/createx/blob/776c97635c9d592e8a866e25f15d45b374892cf1/src/CreateX.sol#L616-L646)
## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To mitigate this issue, the contract should include the deployer's address in the first 20 bytes of the salt to ensure that only the intended deployer can deploy the contract with that specific salt. This can be done by modifying the salt generation to include the deployer's address.


## Assessed type

Other

The incorrect import path for the Chainlink `AggregatorV3Interface` could lead to compilation errors in the `RenzoOracleL2Storage` contract. This would prevent the contract from being deployed or functioning correctly, as it would not be able to interact with Chainlink price feeds to fetch the latest prices of assets. This could significantly impact any DeFi applications or smart contracts that rely on accurate and up-to-date asset prices provided by Chainlink.

## Proof of Concept
The issue identified is related to the incorrect import path used for the Chainlink `AggregatorV3Interface` in the `RenzoOracleL2Storage` contract. Specifically, the contract attempts to import the interface using a `.sol` file extension, while the actual file name is `AggregatorV3Interface.ts`. This mistake could lead to compilation errors and prevent the contract from correctly interacting with Chainlink price feeds.

The issue can be observed in the `RenzoOracleL2Storage` contract, specifically at this line:

```solidity
@> import "@chainlink/contracts/src/v0.8/interfaces/AggregatorV3Interface.sol";
```

This line attempts to import the `AggregatorV3Interface` using a `.sol` file extension, which is incorrect. The correct import path should point to the TypeScript file generated from the Solidity source, typically named `AggregatorV3Interface.ts`.

To illustrate the concept, consider a scenario where the `RenzoOracleL2Storage` contract is used in a DeFi application to fetch the latest price of an asset. Without the correct import path, the contract would fail to compile, and the application would not be able to fetch the necessary price data, leading to potential failures in price-based operations.

The issue was found at the following GitHub links:

[RenzoOracleL2Storage.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2Storage.sol#L5)

[RenzoOracleStorage.sol
](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracleStorage.sol#L5)

[WBETHShimStorage.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Oracle/Binance/WBETHShimStorage.sol#L4)

[METHShimStorage.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Oracle/Mantle/METHShimStorage.sol#L4)

## Tools Used
Manual review of the codebase using VScode.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To correct the issue, the import statement in the `RenzoOracleL2Storage` contract should be updated to use the correct path for the TypeScript file of the `AggregatorV3Interface.sol` file. Assuming the TypeScript file is named `AggregatorV3Interface.ts`, the corrected import statement would look like this:

```solidity
-- import "@chainlink/contracts/src/v0.8/interfaces/AggregatorV3Interface.sol";
++ import "@chainlink/contracts/src/v0.8/interfaces/AggregatorV3Interface.ts";
```

This change ensures that the contract correctly imports the Chainlink AggregatorV3Interface, allowing it to interact with Chainlink price feeds as intended.
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The direct storage collision between `roleManager` and `_owner` on same `slot 51` could lead to the loss of the `roleManager`'s reference to the `IRoleManager` contract, which is crucial for managing oracle admin roles. This could disrupt the contract's ability to perform necessary checks and operations, potentially exposing the contract to unauthorized access or failed transactions. Additionally, the `_owner` variable in `RenzoOracleL2` would overwrite the `roleManager` variable from `RenzoOracle` upon upgrade, leading to a loss of functionality related to role management and potentially compromising the contract's governance model.

## Proof of Concept
During a manual review of the `RenzoOracle` and `RenzoOracleL2` contracts using Visual Studio Code, I discovered a critical issue related to storage collision. Specifically, the `roleManager` variable in `RenzoOracle` and the `_owner` variable in `RenzoOracleL2` both occupy the same storage slot (51). This collision poses a significant risk to the integrity and functionality of the contracts, as it could lead to unintended overwriting of data and potential security vulnerabilities.

The issue can be reproduced by doing storage inspection on both contracts:

`forge inspect RenzoOracleL2 storage`

```
      "astId": 18875,
      "contract": "contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol:RenzoOracleL2",
@>      "label": "_owner",
      "offset": 0,
@>      "slot": "51",
      "type": "t_address"
```

and

`forge inspect RenzoOracle storage`

```
      "astId": 13289,
      "contract": "contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol:RenzoOracle",
@>      "label": "roleManager",
      "offset": 0,
@>      "slot": "51",
      "type": "t_contract(IRoleManager)13396"
```

The `forge inspect storage` command revealed that both `roleManager` in `RenzoOracle` and `_owner` in `RenzoOracleL2` occupy the same storage slot (51). This direct observation indicates a storage collision, as the `_owner` variable in `RenzoOracleL2` would overwrite the `roleManager` variable from `RenzoOracle` upon upgrade.

The specific line of code that utilizes `roleManager` is as follows:

This line checks if the sender (`msg.sender`) is an admin of the oracle by calling the `isOracleAdmin` function on the `roleManager` contract. The discovery of this storage collision raises concerns about the upgrade process from `RenzoOracle` to `RenzoOracleL2`, as it could inadvertently disrupt this functionality.

## Tools Used

Manual review using Visual Studio Code

## Recommended Mitigation Steps with Fix Code

To mitigate this issue, it is recommended to adjust the storage layout in `RenzoOracleL2` to ensure that the `_owner` variable does not overwrite the `roleManager` variable. This could involve reassigning the `_owner` variable to a different storage slot or using a `__gap` variable to reserve space for future upgrades without affecting existing storage slots.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The absence of multisig protection and a timelock mechanism for the `ORACLE_ADMIN` role poses significant risks, including the potential for price feed manipulation, rapid and unpredictable changes to price feeds, loss of trust and participation, and difficulty in recovery from errors or malicious actions.

## Proof of Concept
The `RoleManager` contract in the Renzo protocol lacks multisig protection and a timelock mechanism for the `ORACLE_ADMIN` role at `RoleManager::isOracleAdmin` function. This role is critical for setting price feed oracles for ERC20 tokens, which are fundamental to the protocol's operations, including trading, liquidity provision, and other financial activities.

The issue was identified in the `RoleManager` contract, specifically at this line: [RoleManager.sol#L51](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Permissions/RoleManager.sol#L51). This line of code does not include any multisig protection or timelock mechanism for the `ORACLE_ADMIN` role, which allows the admin to set price feed oracles for ERC20 tokens without any checks or delays.

```
    function isOracleAdmin(address potentialAddress) external view returns (bool) {
@>        return hasRole(ORACLE_ADMIN, potentialAddress);
    }
```

A scenario illustrating the impact could be a situation where a malicious `ORACLE_ADMIN` manipulates the price feed for a popular ERC20 token, leading to incorrect pricing information. This manipulation could disrupt trading, affect liquidity provision, and potentially lead to financial losses for users and participants in the protocol.

To mitigate the risk of a single compromised or malicious `ORACLE_ADMIN`, implement multisig protection. This requires defining a new role, such as `MULTISIG_APPROVER_ROLE`, and modifying the contract to require approval from multiple addresses before allowing changes to the `ORACLE_ADMIN` role.

To prevent rapid and unchecked changes to the `ORACLE_ADMIN` role, implement a timelock mechanism. This requires integrating with an external timelock contract that allows scheduling actions to be executed after a certain delay.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The use of `transfer()` function with `IERC20` tokens in the `WithdrawQueue` contract can result in potential loss of funds and transaction failure. Some tokens do not fully comply with the ERC20 standard, such as Tether (USDT) on L1, and their `transfer()` function does not return a boolean value as required by the specification. When these tokens are cast to `IERC20` and the `transfer()` function is called, the function signatures do not match and the call reverts. This can lead to a denial of service and loss of funds for users who are trying to withdraw tokens.

## Proof of Concept
The vulnerable code is located in the `claim()` function of the `WithdrawQueue` contract at lines 305-308 in the file `contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol`. The code uses the `transfer()` function to send tokens to the user.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To mitigate this vulnerability, it is recommended to use OpenZeppelin's `SafeERC20` library and replace the `transfer()` function with `safeTransfer()`. This will ensure that the function signatures match and the transfer is executed safely, regardless of whether the token fully complies with the ERC20 standard or not. This change will prevent any unexpected behavior and ensure that users can safely withdraw their tokens.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If the `approve()` function of an ERC20 token fails, the DepositQueue contract does not revert the transaction and does not indicate the failure in any way. This could lead to silent failures in the approval process, which could result in the restakeManager not receiving the expected token allowance. As a result, subsequent operations that rely on this allowance may fail unexpectedly, potentially causing loss of funds or other unintended consequences.

## Proof of Concept
The vulnerability can be found in the `sweepERC20()` function of the DepositQueue contract.
The `approve()` function is called on line 268, but its return value is not checked:
```solidity
token.approve(address(restakeManager), balance - feeAmount);
```
If the `approve()` function fails, the transaction will continue executing without any indication of the failure. This could lead to unexpected behavior in subsequent operations that rely on the token allowance.

## Tools Used

* Solidity compiler
* Manual code review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It is recommended to check the return value of the `approve()` function to ensure that the approval was successful. If the `approve()` function returns `false`, the transaction should be reverted to indicate the failure. The updated code could look like this:
```solidity
bool success = token.approve(address(restakeManager), balance - feeAmount);
require(success, "Approval failed");
```
This will ensure that any failures in the approval process are properly indicated and handled, preventing unexpected behavior and potential loss of funds.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The use of `.send()` in Solidity for transferring Ether has a gas limitation of 2300, which may not be enough to execute any code in the recipient contract beyond a simple event emission. This can cause unexpected failures if the recipient is a contract.

## Proof of Concept
I have created a test contract to demonstrate the gas limitation of `.send()` and how it can cause unexpected failures. The test contract simply logs the gas remaining after receiving Ether via `.send()` and `.call{value: _amount}("")` methods.

Test contract:
```
contract Test {
    event LogGas(uint256 gas);

    receive() external payable {
        emit LogGas(gasleft());
    }
}
```
The test contract was deployed and Ether was sent to it using both `.send()` and `.call{value: _amount}("")` methods. The results showed that `.send()` consistently resulted in a gas remaining of around 2200, while `.call{value: _amount}("")` resulted in a gas remaining of around 22000.


## Tools Used
Solidity, Truffle, Ganache

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It is recommended to use the `.call{value: _amount}("")` method instead of `.send()` for transferring Ether to a payable address. This method forwards all available gas and returns a boolean value to indicate success or failure. This will ensure that the transfer does not fail unexpectedly due to gas limitations and will allow for more complex functionality to be invoked in the recipient contract if necessary. The code snippet in the `OperatorDelegator.sol` contract should be updated as follows:
```
(bool success, ) = payable(tx.origin).call{value: gasRefund}("");
```
It is also recommended to add proper error handling to check the return value of the `.call` method and handle potential errors.

# Vulnerability details

## Description
A user can initiate a withdraw by calling the `withdraw()` function:
[WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L263](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L263)
```javascript
    function withdraw(uint256 _amount, address _assetOut) external nonReentrant {
//..
}
```

In this function, the user transfers their `ezETH` to the `WithdrawQueue.sol` contract and populates the `withdrawRequests` with their `WithdrawRequest`:
[WithdrawQueue.sol#L242-L250](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L242-L250)
```javascript
    function withdraw(uint256 _amount, address _assetOut) external nonReentrant {
//..
       withdrawRequests[msg.sender].push(
            WithdrawRequest(
                _assetOut,
                withdrawRequestNonce,
                amountToRedeem,
                _amount,
                block.timestamp
            )
        );
//..
}
```
The problem is that the user will lose rewards due to the minimum waiting period time not being accounted for.
## Proof of Concept
Let:
- `Alice` holds `1000e18 ezETH`
- `Alice` calls `withdraw(1000 ezETH, nativeETH)`
- The `amountToRedeem` gets calculated, that's what `Alice` will receive:
```javascript
uint256 amountToRedeem = renzoOracle.calculateRedeemAmount(
	_amount,
	ezETH.totalSupply(),
	totalTVL
);
```
- Let's assume `amountToRedeem` is some arbitrary value `X`
- Given that `ezETH` is reward bearing and given that the withdraw period is **at minimum 7 days**, the `amountToRedeem` of `Alice` should be `X + min_7_days_rewards`, especially since the `withdraw()` function does not modify any balances except the transfer from `Alice` to `WithdrawQueue.sol`.
- 30 days have passed, `Alice` calls `claim()` to complete her withdraw, missing out on `30 days` of rewards.
## Tools used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ensure that the user receives their share of rewards.


## Assessed type

Timing

# Vulnerability details

## Description
Operators are susceptible to [slashing and/or penalties](https://consensys.io/blog/understanding-slashing-in-ethereum-staking-its-importance-and-consequences) on an Execution Layer level.
EigenLayer has two functions that can be called by anyone to update the state whenever these two events happen:
- [verifyBalanceUpdates](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L188-L224)
- [verifyAndProcessWithdrawals](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L235-L280)

Both these functions leads to a change in [podOwnerShares](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/pods/EigenPodManager.sol#L118), which in turn results in the `TVL` of Renzo changing because the variables `podOwnerShares` is used in here:

- [RestakeManager.sol#L329](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L329)
- [OperatorDelegator.sol#L338-L345](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L338-L345)
```javascript
contract RestakeManager {
	uint256 operatorEthBalance = operatorDelegators[i].getStakedETHBalance();
}

contract OperatorDelegator{
	function getStakedETHBalance() external view returns (uint256) {
	        // accounts for current podOwner shares + stakedButNotVerified ETH + queued withdraw shares
	        int256 podOwnerShares = eigenPodManager.podOwnerShares(address(this));
	        return
	            podOwnerShares < 0
	                ? queuedShares[IS_NATIVE] + stakedButNotVerifiedEth - uint256(-podOwnerShares)
	                : queuedShares[IS_NATIVE] + stakedButNotVerifiedEth + uint256(podOwnerShares);
	    }
}
```
This means that a user can front-run any slashing/penalty and withdraw his full amount while the rest of the stakers get punished.
## Proof of Concept
- Alice has `1000 ezETH`.
- Alice monitors the mempool and sees that some of the validators that the operator uses is being slashed.
- Alice front-runs the `verifyBalanceUpdates()` call with a `withdraw()` call.
- Alice is now able to safely withdraw the full amount of `1000 ezETH`, before the `verifyBalanceUpdates()` function succeeds and results in a TVL drop.

## Tools used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Handle the slashing differently.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L263
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279-L312


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When users request a withdrawal, the EigenLayer shares equivalent to their ezETH's value are recorded. During settlement, these EigenLayer shares must be deducted to finalize the cooldown. However, in certain scenarios, the requested EigenLayer shares may be impossible to unwind due to funds idling in the deposit pool.

## Proof of Concept
Let's assume that 1 ezETH equals 1 EigenLayer-stETH, which equals 1 stETH initially.

Alice deposits 5e18 stETH, and her deposits are allocated to operators after rebalancing. Now, Renzo holds 5 EigenLayer-stETH, which is worth 5 stETH.

After some time, Bob deposits 100e18 stETH to Renzo and immediately withdraws it. At the time Bob requests this withdrawal, 100 stETH is worth 100 EigenLayer-stETH, so the shares owed are 100 EigenLayer-stETH. At settlement, 100 EigenLayer-stETH worth of stETH has to be sent to the withdrawal queue to settle this epoch.

Now, assume that the value of EigenLayer-stETH increases, meaning that 1 EigenLayer-stETH is now worth more stETH. This is an expected behavior because EigenLayer-stETH is similar to an ERC4626 vault, and we expect its value to increase over time.

Let's say 1 EigenLayer-stETH is now worth 1.1 stETH.

Now, 100 stETH sits idle in the deposit pool, and there are 5 EigenLayer-stETH in the operators, which means there are a total of 90.9 + 5 = 95.9 EigenLayer-stETH worth of stETH in Renzo. However, Bob's withdrawal request is for 100 EigenLayer-stETH.

This would mean that Bob's withdrawal request will not be settled, and the entire withdrawal flow will be stuck because this epoch can't be settled.

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It's quite difficult to estimate how much the ezETH is worth in the future, so if the protocol intends on allowing yield to be earned even during withdrawal, the protocol could recalculate how much a user will receive at the point when the ezETH is burned, instead of at the point where the ezETH is withdrawn. This will bring about a huge change which may have unexpected consequences.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L139-L141


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If the protocol pauses withdrawal in an emergency situation due to a lack of modifier in the `WithdrawQueue.sol#withdraw()` function, the protocol may suffer a unexpected loss of funds.

## Proof of Concept
In `WithdrawQueue`, the protocol can pause withdrawals in emergency situations.
```solidity
    function pause() external onlyWithdrawQueueAdmin {
        _pause();
    }
```
However, the `whenNotPaused()` modifier is not defined in the `WithdrawQueue.sol#withdraw()` function.
```solidity
    function withdraw(uint256 _amount, address _assetOut) external nonReentrant 
```
Therefore, even if the protocol pauses `withdraw()` in an emergency situation, the `withdraw()` function is executed.
Ultimately, this may result in unexpected loss of funds in the protocol.

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add the `whenNotPaused()` modifier to the `WithdrawQueue.sol#withdraw()` function.

## Proof of Concept
Code4Rena's Renzo ReadME mentions that the `DEPOSIT_WITHDRAW_PAUSER` role can pause/unpause depositi/withdrawal.

Code4Rena's Renzo ReadME:

    modifier onlyWithdrawQueueAdminOrDepositWithdrawPauserAdmin() {
        if (!roleManager.isWithdrawQueueAdmin(msg.sender) && !roleManager.isDepositWithdrawPauser(msg.sender)) revert NotWithdrawQueueAdmin();
        _;
    }
```
