# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L274
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L315-L321


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Detail
Within `RestakeManager.calculateTVL()`, it intends to calculate the value held by the `WithdrawalQueue` for each token.

The issue is that it passes `collateralTokens[i]` rather than `collateralTokens[j]` for the first parameter of `RenzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(IERC20 token, uint256 balance)`

```solidity
if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
        collateralTokens[i], //@audit this should be 'j'
        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
    );
}
```
Since this block of code will only execute in the first iteration of the outer loop, `i` would be `0`. So the value of all collateral tokens will be calculated using a price corresponding to `collateralTokens[0]`. 

## Impact
This leads to an incorrect TVL calculation within `RestakeManager.calculateTVL()`, leading to incorrect pricing of `ezETH`.

## Proof of Concept
**[RestakeManager.calculateTVL()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L274)**


**[The incorrect block of code](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L315-L321)**


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use `collateralTokens[j]` to ensure that the correct prices are used to calculate the total value stored in the withdrawalQueue.

```diff
if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
-       collateralTokens[i],
+       collateralTokens[j],
        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
    );
}
```


## Assessed type

Error

raw_row.title: Key invariant violation due to incorrectly decrementing `stakedButNotVerifiedETH`, without considering validators getting slashed

title: Key invariant violation due to incorrectly decrementing `stakedButNotVerifiedETH`, without considering validators getting slashed
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L385


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Detail
When `OperatorDelegator.stakeETH()` is called by `RestakeManager`, the storage variable `stakedButNotVerifiedETH` is incremented:
```solidity
stakedButNotVerifiedEth += msg.value; 
```

Then later when admin calls `OperatorDelegator.verifyWithdrawalCredentials()`, the variable is decremented:
```solidity
uint64 validatorCurrentBalanceGwei = BeaconChainProofs.getEffectiveBalanceGwei(
    validatorFields[i]
);
stakedButNotVerifiedEth -= (validatorCurrentBalanceGwei * GWEI_TO_WEI); 
```

As seen above, it is decremented by the effective balance of the validator. 

However, the code does not consider the fact that since the funds have been staked in the beacon chain contract (this occurs in the same tx as `OperatorDelegator.stakeETH()`), they can be slashed.

However since the validator could have been slashed, the effective balance of the validator may not be 32 (it can be less than that).

Hence, `stakedButNotVerifiedEth` will not be reduced to 0 even though after calling `verifyWithdrawalCredentials()` there would be `0` unverified ETH that has been staked.

Since the value of `stakedButNotVerifiedEth` is now inflated, the value returned by `OperatorDelegator.getStakedETHBalance()` will be inflated. This will inflate the total TVL calculated within `RestakeManager.calculateTVLs()`. This will inflate the value of ezETH more than what it should be.

## Impact
Users can withdraw collateral tokens at a higher rate than they should be allowed to, due to the inflation of ezETH's value. This breaks the main invariant stated in the README: 

> ezETH should be minted or redeemed based on current supply and TVL

## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenario:
1. Admin calls `DepositQueue.stakeEthFromQueue()`, this ends up calling `OperatorDelegator.stakeETH{value: 32 ether}()`
    - this increments `stakedButNotVerifiedEth` by 32 ether
    - within this transaction, the 32 ether is deposited into the beacon chain deposit contract for ethereum staking
2. The validator misbehaves and gets slashed, so it's effective balance drops to 20 ether. (lost 12 ether)
3. The admin calls `OperatorDelegator.verifyWithdrawalCredentials()`, and this decrements `stakedButNotVerifiedEth` by 20 ether.
4. As a result, `stakedButNotVerifiedEth` = 12 ether (even though it should be 0)

Now, `totalTVL` is calculated to be 12 ether more than what it should be, causing the value of ezETH to be inflated. This allows people to redeem more collateral tokens than what is deserved, leading to loss for the protocol. 

**Code referenced**:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L385

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider also subtracting `stakedButNotVerifiedETH` by the slashed value if the validator has been slashed.


## Assessed type

Error

raw_row.title: All staked funds are un-redeemable when operator calls `DelegationManager.undelegate()`

title: All staked funds are un-redeemable when operator calls `DelegationManager.undelegate()`
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L232
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L281


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Detail
The expected withdrawal flow in the `OperatorDelegator` is:
1. Admin calls `OperatorDelegator.queueWithdrawals()`
2. Admin/anyone calls `OperatorDelegator.verifyAndProcessWithdrawals()`
3. Admin calls `OperatorDelegator.completeQueuedWithdrawal()`

Step 1 increases `queuedShares[strategy]` for each strategy by the withdrawal amount, and Step 3 decreases the value by the same amount. 

The issue is that the protocol has not accounted for the following scenario:

For any reason, the operator can call `DelegationManager.undelegate(staker)` where `staker` is the `OperatorDelegator` contract.
This is normal functionality of EigenLayer's `DelegationManager` contract.
(Here are the [docs for the `undelegate()` function](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/docs/core/DelegationManager.md#undelegate))

This function calls `_removeSharesAndQueueWithdrawal()` for each strategy, to queue a withdrawal for all the staker's strategies.

Now these funds can only be obtained by admin calling `OperatorDelegator.completeQueuedWithdrawal()`, so the funds are supposed to be retrievable.

**The key issue:**
However since these withdrawals were not queued via `queueWithdrawals()`, the `queuedShares[strategyAddress]` mapping was not incremented as expected. This means that the following line in `completeQueuedWithdrawal()` will revert due to underflow:

[OperatorDelegator.sol#L280-281](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L281)
```solidity
// deduct queued shares for tracking TVL
queuedShares[address(tokens[i])] -= withdrawal.shares[i];
```

This means that `completeQueuedWithdrawal()` will be un-callable, so the operator can (knowingly or unknowingly) grief the ENTIRE value of all the delegated shares by simply calling `undelegate()`.

## Impact

### Primary Impact:
When an operator calls `undelegate(staker)` where the `staker` is an `OperatorDelegator`, it permanently locks the ALL the staked  funds of that specific `OperatorDelegator`, they will be irretrievable due to underflow in `OperatorDelegator.completeQueudWithdrawal()`.

Note that the impact of this issue is not the same as a malicious operator simply misbehaving and getting the validators slashed.
This is because unlike in this vulnerability, getting slashed would equally affect ALL the stakers in the EigenPod/Strategy, not just one. 

### Secondary Impact:
A secondary impact is that since the `podOwnerShares` of the `OperatorDelegator` has been drastically decreased without increasing `queuedShares[strategy]` (which is what is expected to happen when the admin calls `OperatorDelegator.queueWithdrawals`), the values returned by `getStakedETHBalance` and `getTokenBalanceFromStrategy` will be severely lower. This leads to lower TVL calculations. ezETH holders who observe this in the mempool can front-run it to withdraw their ezETH at a much better rate, stealing value from the protocol. 

## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenario:

Initial state: queuedShares[ETH] = 0, `podOwnerShares[OD]` = 32 ether

1. Operator calls `DelegationManager.undelegate(staker)`
    - staker is the `OperatorDelegator` address
    - this queues the 32 ether to be withdrawn
2. Renzo admin calls `OperatorDelegator.completeQueuedWithdrawal()` as this is the only way to obtain the withdrawn funds.
    - This call will always revert since it tries to subtract 32 ether from `queuedShares[ETH]` which will revert due to underflow.
    - Hence, all the withdrawn funds (32 ether) are stuck forever

The above example is only for ether, but the same issue arises for all the different strategies that the `OperatorDelegator` has shares in.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add an extra boolean flag within `completeQueuedWithdrawals` so that if true, skips the decrementing of `queuedShares[address(tokens[i])]` when withdrawing funds after `DelegationManager.undelegate()` was called.

This will prevent it from reverting.

Example:
```diff
+   if (!skipUpdateQueuedShares) {
         // deduct queued shares for tracking TVL
         queuedShares[address(tokens[i])] -= withdrawal.shares[i];
+    }
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/ef2ea4a7459884f381057aa9bbcd29c7148cfb63/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L188-L224
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/ef2ea4a7459884f381057aa9bbcd29c7148cfb63/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L235-L280
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L263


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Detail
A malicious ezEth holder can sandwich eigenlayer's updates to a validator's penalty or slashing event in order to avoid the loss. 

Validators can lose some or all of their deposit via penalties or slashing events

* In case of penalties Eigenlayer can be notified of the balance drop via the permissionless function `EigenPod::verifyBalanceUpdates()`.
* In case of slashing the validator is forced to exit and Eigenlayer can be notified via the permissionless function `EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals()`

As soon as either `EigenPod::verifyBalanceUpdates()` or `EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals()` is called, the total TVL of the protocol drops instantly. This is because both of the functions reduce the `podOwnerShares[podOwner]` which is used in the TVL calculations.

A malicious ezEth holder can take advantage (in a single tx) of this by the following steps:

1. Identify a slashing or penalty event taking place
3. Request a withdrawal via `WithdrawQueue::withdraw()` at an inflated stale TVL to redeem all their ezETH holdings to ETH 
4. Call the permissionless function `EigenPod::verifyBalanceUpdates()` or `EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals()`, to instantly drop the TVL
5. Deposit the same amount of ETH back into the protocol, at the new reduced TVL, so they will be minted more ezETH than they initially redeemed. 


## Impact
The attacker has avoided the loss due to validator penalties/slashing which will be paid by all other ezETH holders

The sandwich attack will end up with the attacker extracting value from all other ezETH holders.

The attack vector also involves redeeming ETH at an inflated stale TVL. This breaks the following main invariant defined by the protocol:

>ezETH should be minted or redeemed based on current supply and TVL.

## Proof of Concept
Refer to vulnerability detail

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
One solution would be for the Renzo protocol to monitor validator slashing/penalty events and call `EigenPod::verifyBalanceUpdates()` or `EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals()` immediately to decrease the likelihood of the attack.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Rewards/RewardHandler.sol#L52-L54
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Rewards/RewardHandler.sol#L58-L60
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Rewards/RewardHandler.sol#L62-L70


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Detail
The protocol's accrued rewards are sent to the `RewardHandler` contract.

This will end up calling the `RewardHandler::receive()` function which in turn calls `_forwardETH()`, which forwards the ETH to the DepositQueue.

This will instantly increase the total TVL of the protocol, since the balance of the deposit queue is included in [`RestakeManager::calculateTVL()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L352)

An attacker can take advantage of this to partially steal the ETH rewards using the following steps:

1. Attacker identifies an incoming rewards Tx that will increase the protocol's TVL
2. Attacker frontruns the rewards Tx by minting ezETH at the current TVL level
3. Rewards Tx goes through and increases the TVL of the protocol
4. Attacker backruns the rewards Tx by redeeming all their minted ezETH at the higher exchange rate (since TVL increased), obtaining ether (or LSTs) at a confirmed profit

Consensus layer rewards will be credited to the `RewardHandler` contract without a transaction, so the `NativeEthRestakeAdmin` will have to manually call `forwardRewards()` to send the ETH to the DepositQueue. This call by the `NativeEthRestakeAdmin` will increase the protocol's TVL, therefore it is also vulnerable to the previously described sandwich attack.

## Impact
A portion of the ETH rewards can be stolen from honest users with 0 risk. The attacker makes profit while reducing the yield of honest stakers.

This significantly reduces the incentive for honest users to stake their funds for continuous periods since any non-participant can simply front-run the forwarding of rewards from `RewardHandler` to `DepositQueue` and steal rewards.

## Proof of Concept
Refer to Vulnerability Detail

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
This does not have a simple solution. It will require a redesign of the reward distribution.


## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Detail
When `EigenPod.verifyAndProcessWithdrawals` is called, the funds are sent to the `DelayedWithdrawalRouter` and attributed to the `OperatorDelegator`. This can be seen in the below two code snippets:


``` solidity
function verifyAndProcessWithdrawals(
    ...
    ...
    _sendETH_AsDelayedWithdrawal(podOwner, withdrawalSummary.amountToSendGwei * GWEI_TO_WEI);
    ...
```


``` solidity
function _sendETH_AsDelayedWithdrawal(address recipient, uint256 amountWei) internal {
        delayedWithdrawalRouter.createDelayedWithdrawal{value: amountWei}(podOwner, recipient);
    }
```
When calling `_sendETH_AsDelayedWithdrawal()`, the `recipient` is set to `podOwner` which is the `OperatorDelegator` contract.


Now to redeem the funds (to the recipient), any user can call the following permissionless function in EigenLayer `DelayedWithdrawalRouter::claimDelayedWithdrawals`

<Details>
<summary>claimDelayedWithdrawals</summary>

``` solidity
/**
     * @notice Called in order to withdraw delayed withdrawals made to the `recipient` that have passed the `withdrawalDelayBlocks` period.
     * @param recipient The address to claim delayedWithdrawals for.
     * @param maxNumberOfDelayedWithdrawalsToClaim Used to limit the maximum number of delayedWithdrawals to loop through claiming.
     * @dev
     *      WARNING: Note that the caller of this function cannot control where the funds are sent, but they can control when the
     *              funds are sent once the withdrawal becomes claimable.
     */
    function claimDelayedWithdrawals(
        address recipient,
        uint256 maxNumberOfDelayedWithdrawalsToClaim
    ) external nonReentrant onlyWhenNotPaused(PAUSED_DELAYED_WITHDRAWAL_CLAIMS) {
        _claimDelayedWithdrawals(recipient, maxNumberOfDelayedWithdrawalsToClaim);
    }
```

</Details>


This will end up sending ETH to the set `recipient` through the internal function `_claimDelayedWithdrawals`

<Details>
<summary>_claimDelayedWithdrawals</summary>

``` solidity
function _claimDelayedWithdrawals(address recipient, uint256 maxNumberOfDelayedWithdrawalsToClaim) internal {
        ...
        ...
        // actually send the ETH
        if (amountToSend != 0) {
            AddressUpgradeable.sendValue(payable(recipient), amountToSend);
        }
        emit DelayedWithdrawalsClaimed(recipient, amountToSend, delayedWithdrawalsCompletedBefore + i);
    }      
```
    
</Details>


Since the recipient was set as the `OperatorDelegator`, it will trigger the `OperatorDelegator::receive()` function that ends up sending the ETH to the DepositQueue, which will increase the TVL of the protocol.

Therefore whenever the `DelayedWithdrawalRouter.createDelayedWithdrawal()` function is called  with the `OperatorDelegator` as the recipient, an attacker can take advantage of this with a sandwich attack. It includes the following steps:

1. Attacker mints ezETH at the current TVL level
2. Attacker calls `DelayedWithdrawalRouter.claimDelayedWithdrawals()` which will end up increasing the TVL of the protocol
3. Attacker backruns the call to `claimDelayedWithdrawals` by redeeming all their minted ezETH at the higher exchange rate (since TVL increased), obtaining ether (or LSTs) at a confirmed profit

## Impact
A portion of the ETH rewards can be stolen from honest users with 0 risk. The attacker makes profit while reducing the yield of honest stakers.

This significantly reduces the incentive for honest users to stake their funds for continuous periods since any non-participant can simply front-run the forwarding of rewards from `RewardHandler` to `DepositQueue` and steal rewards.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L168-L191
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L414-L449
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L139-L201
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Lockbox.sol#L103-L105
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Lockbox.sol#L125-L136https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Lockbox.sol#L125-L136


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Detail
Users on an L2 can interact with the renzo protocol on mainnet by calling `xRenzoDeposit::depositETH()`

This will end up minting the user xezETH on the L2 and converting the deposited ETH to nextWETH.

Then later an admin (allowedBridgeSweepers) will call `xRenzoDeposit::sweep()`, this function will take the balance of nextWETH in the contract and bridge it down to the L1, The L1 contract will unwrap, deposit in Renzo, and lock up the ezETH in the lockbox on L1.

The problem is that inbetween the user's call to `depositETH()` and the admin's call to `sweep()`, the price of ezETH can change, this price change will result in a different amount of ezETH being minted to back the xezETH on the L2. 

Having different amounts of xezETH compared to the ezETH backing it is dangerous as the lockbox always converts xezETH to ezETH in a 1:1 ratio.

The following are the worst case scenarios, they ignore fees for simplicity sake. 

**Scenario 1:** Price of ezETH goes up in between the calls.
Initially 1 ezETH = 1ETH

1. Alice calls `xRenzoDeposit::depositETH()` depositing 5 ETH and is minted 5 xezETH
2. Bob calls `xRenzoDeposit::depositETH()` depositing 5 ETH and is minted 5 xezETH
3. The price of ezETH grows to 1 ezETH = 2 ETH
4. Admin calls `sweep()`, this will result in `xRenzoBridge` depositing the 10 ETH into the protocol and minting 5 ezETH, the 5 ezETH will be deposited into the xezETHLockbox
5. Now Alice will be able to burn her 5 xezETH for 5 ezETH because the lockbox always converts xezETH to ezETH in a 1:1 ratio
6. Now Bob is stuck with a useless xezETH and will not be able to redeem it for anything

**Scenario 2:** Price of ezETH goes down in between the calls.
Initially 1 ezETH = 2ETH

1. Alice calls `xRenzoDeposit::depositETH()` depositing 10 ETH and is minted 5 xezETH
2. The price of ezETH drops to 1 ezETH = 1 ETH
3. Admin calls `sweep()`, this will result in `xRenzoBridge` depositing the 10 ETH into the protocol and minting 10 ezETH, the 10 ezETH will be deposited into the xezETHLockbox
4. Now Alice will be able to burn her 5 xezETH for 5 ezETH 
5. Now 5 ezETH is stuck in the lockbox and cannot be redeemed 

**Scenario 3:** Price of ezETH goes up in between the calls.
Initially 1 ezETH = 1ETH

1. Alice calls `xRenzoDeposit::depositETH()` depositing 5 ETH and is minted 5 xezETH
2. The price of ezETH grows to 1 ezETH = 2 ETH
3. Admin calls `sweep()`, this will result in `xRenzoBridge` depositing the 5 ETH into the protocol and minting 2.5 ezETH, the 2.5 ezETH will be deposited into the xezETHLockbox
4. Now Alice will only be able to burn 2.5 of her 5 xezETH for 2.5 ezETH
5. The only way she can redeem the remaining 2.5 xezETH is if she waits for another user to deposit from an L2 then steal their ezETH in the lockbox, effectively passing her problem to them.

These scenarios do involve significant price changes BUT even smaller changes in price will result in having different amounts of xezETH compared to the ezETH backing it and will cause significant loss of funds.


## Impact
depends on the scenario, Refer to vulnerability detail

## Proof of Concept
Refer to vulnerability detail

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
will require a redesign of the current L2 deposit and sweep system. 

Is it necessary for an admin to call `sweep()`, one solution would be to implement the `sweep()` function directly after the logic for `deposit`.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L274-L358


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

All functions relying on `RestakeManager::calculateTVLs()` are broken resulting in multiple side-effects in the protocol, one of them being :
- users are able/unable to deposit collateral in the protocol while they shouldn't/should

## Proof of concept

The `RestakeManager::calculateTVLs()` calculates the TVL (as ETH) of all the collateral tokens held by the `operatorDelegators` and also includes the funds pending in the `withdrawQueue` contract.

To do so, the function is looping through all the `operatorDelegators` using the `i` variable and for each of them, is looping through all the `collateralTokens` using the `j` variable.

It is during the very first iteration of the `i` loop that the `withdrawQueue` funds is calculated using an oracle

[https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L316-L321](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L316-L321)

```js
// record token value of withdraw queue
if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
        collateralTokens[i],
        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
    );
}
```

The `withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded` variable is set to `true` right before incrementing `i` meaning the contract enters the previous section only on the first iteration, when `i == 0`

[https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L344-L348](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L344-L348)

```js
// Set withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded flag to true
withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded = true;

unchecked {
    ++i;
}
```

The oracle takes as parameters :
- a collateral token
- the balance of the collateral token an address holds (in this case, `withdrawQueue`)

Since `i` will always be equal to `0` when the contract calculates the `withdrawQueue` TVL, the oracle is going to return the price of the first collateral tokens BUT using another token's balance and this for every collateral tokens supported by the protocol.

## Tools used

Manual analysis

## Recommended mitigation steps

Change the `i` iterator to `j` like such :

```js
if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
        collateralTokens[j],
        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
    );
}
```



## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L369


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The contract xRenzoDeposit.sol does not re-set allowance before setting a new one in the function _trade().
 This can potentially make the contract vulnerable to an "Infinite Approval Attack". 

An infinite approval means setting the allowance to the maximum possible uint256 value. The issue with infinite approvals is that while they require less gas (and thus less fees for users), they can potentially be unsafe. If an attacker is able to manipulate the token contract or if the spender is malicious, they can potentially steal an unlimited amount of tokens from the user.

Here's a simple example of how an infinite approval attack might work:
1. The contract approves a transfer of `N` tokens to another (malicious) address or contract.
2. The malicious contract transfers `N` tokens from the contract.
3. The malicious contract then increments its allowance by `M`, effectively increasing its total allowance to `N + M`.
4. This process can be repeated indefinitely to drain funds from the contract.


## Proof of Concept


https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L369

In the code below, the contract approves the deposit asset to the connext contract but does not first reset the allowance:
```solidity
depositToken.safeApprove(address(connext), _amountIn);
```



## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To mitigate this potential risk, the contract should call the `approve` function to set the allowance to 0 before setting it to another value. Here is an example of how to safely approve tokens:

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The smart contract RenzoOracleL2.sol relies extensively on an external price oracle for proper functioning especially for mint rate computations. However, there is a potential vulnerability with how results from the price oracle are handled. 

While the smart contract correctly checks if the `timestamp` variable from `oracle.latestRoundData()` is stale and also whether the `_scaledPrice` is less than 1 ether, but fails to handle the cases where the latest round data function from the oracle might fail.

An oracle can essentially fail to provide data for various reasons like expired keys, a paused network, exceeding request thresholds, or any unforeseen malfunction at the oracle's end. These failures often result in the oracle returning an error code.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L51-L52

```solidity
(, int256 price, , uint256 timestamp, ) = oracle.latestRoundData();
if (timestamp < block.timestamp - MAX_TIME_WINDOW) revert OraclePriceExpired();
```
Here, the function `oracle.latestRoundData()` can potentially throw an error.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

It's recommended to handle potential errors that could arise from the external oracle service. Implement error handling by checking if the data returned from the oracle is valid before proceeding with further smart contract operations. This will improve overall contract reliability and ensure deterministic behaviour of your contract under all conditions. 


## Assessed type

Oracle

brief_summary: The function `getMintRate` reads the price from an oracle and scales it to a value with 18 decimal places. This operation to adjust the decimals involves a multiplication of the price with `10 ** (18 - oracle.decimals())`, which could cause numerical overflow if not properly safeguarded. An overflow occurs when an operation tries to create a number that is outside the maximum limit that can be held by the data type. In Solidity, a `uint256` has a maximum limit of 2^256 - 1, and any calculation that exceeds this value will result in an overflow and the value will loop around to zero.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L123-L149


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the method `calculateMintAmount`, fixed point arithmetic calculations are carried out to result into inflation, which is subsequently subtracted from a constant (SCALE_FACTOR). Fixed point arithmetic always rounds down the results of its calculations, a potential vulnerability that might be exploited in a downgrade attack. 

Here is how an attacker might exploit this: they'd make a deposit such that the inflation computation is not a whole number, hence causing rounding down to happen. That means that the attacker's subsequent deposit would cause a decrease in inflation, potentially allowing more tokens to be minted off this decreased value.


## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L123-L149

```solidity
    // Calculate the percentage of value after the deposit
    uint256 inflationPercentage = (SCALE_FACTOR * _newValueAdded) /
        (_currentValueInProtocol + _newValueAdded);

    // Calculate the new supply
    uint256 newEzETHSupply = (_existingEzETHSupply * SCALE_FACTOR) /
        (SCALE_FACTOR - inflationPercentage);
```

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To mitigate this risk, consider using a library for fixed point arithmetic that does not round down results or otherwise avoids the precision differences that could be exploited. 

Additionally, you could implement a check to ensure that the inflation is only decreased by a legitimate deposit, rather than by a small crafted one aimed at exploiting the round-down effect of fixed point operations.

Another good security measure would be to limit the smallest possible deposit or consider implementing slippage protection in order to prevent individuals from benefiting inappropriately from such calculated deposits. This would help control the scope of potential manipulation. 

Finally, you could also monitor unusual deposit patterns that may indicate that someone is attempting such manipulation, though this would be more reactive than preventative.



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L134-L144
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L491-L576


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A similar logic to the `_checkAndFillETHWithdrawBuffer` logic was not implemented for the ERC20 token deposit. This means that the `withdrawalBufferTarget` through the `fillERC20withdrawBuffer` can be exceeded.

This could have a big impact on the system as there is a possibility of a large imbalance between the value of the depositQueue contract which does the restaking on the restakingManager contract. There could be a dearth of value on deposits if a large number of ERC20 ETH derivatives were deposited through the `deposit` function in the `restakeManager` contract and it takes 7 days before a withdrawal is claimed.

While there is an implementation of bufferFill in the restakeManager contract, the original impact is not solved which is having some value of ETH for staking in the Operator Delegate through the reStakingManager, instead the ERC20 tokens are sent to the OD.

## Proof of Concept

- Deploy and initialize the `WithdrawQueue` with ETH and stETH withdrawalBufferTarget of 1 ETH.
- Deploy the `DepositQueue` contract
- call the `fillERC20withdrawBuffer` with 2 stETH or add the update the depositQueue in the restakeManager and call the deposit
- all stETH is transferred to the `WithdrawQueue` contract with no value left for restaking as the restakeManage

The implementation for erc20 withdraw buffer can be found here
```solidity
function fillERC20withdrawBuffer(
        address _asset,
        uint256 _amount
    ) external nonReentrant onlyRestakeManager {
        if (_amount == 0 || _asset == address(0)) revert InvalidZeroInput();
        // safeTransfer from restake manager to this address
        IERC20(_asset).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), _amount);
        // approve the token amount for withdraw queue
        IERC20(_asset).safeApprove(address(withdrawQueue), _amount);
        // call the withdraw queue to fill up the buffer
        withdrawQueue.fillERC20WithdrawBuffer(_asset, _amount);
    }
```

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

implement the similar swap system in the `WithdrawQueue` to send the needed deficit and the rest of the ERC20 value is converted to ETH for ETH restaking.
- send all ERC20 token to the depositQueue and then,
- implement similar `_checkAndFillETHWithdrawBuffer` but for ERC20 token
- execute `withdrawQueue.fillERC20WithdrawBuffer(_asset, deficit);`. `deficit` is `bufferToFill`
- get the equivalent value of eth for the remaining ERC20 token after `bufferToFill`
- swap ERC20 token e.g stETH for ETH
- `stakeEthFromQueue` or `stakeEthFromQueueMulti` can be called at any time by restakeadmin when the value is up to 32 ETH

The `address.send(...)` function is used to send `gasRefund` `ETH` to recipient on line 485 of `OperatorDelegator.sol`. function _refundGas() internal returns (uint256) {
```
        uint256 gasRefund = address(this).balance >= adminGasSpentInWei[tx.origin]
            ? adminGasSpentInWei[tx.origin]

@>        bool success = payable(tx.origin).send(gasRefund);//@audit finding

```

Another example is with the innovation of smart accounts. This will most likely cause a denial of service with smart contract accounts.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L175
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L598


# Vulnerability details

## How L2 Native Restaking in Renzo works
1. User initiates the process by depositing ETH/wETH into the [`xRenzoDeposit.sol`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol) contract particularly using the function [`xRenzoDeposit::deposit()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L204) or the function [`xRenzoDeposit::depositETH()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L168). If the user deposited ETH using the latter function, the ETH will then be wrapped into wETH.
2. `xRenzoDeposit::_deposit()` function will then be called, and it will do three things:
   1. Retrieve the bridge fee for the amount you deposited, using the function [`xRenzoDeposit::getBridgeFeeShare()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L277) and it'll subtract it from the `amountIn` (the amount you deposited).
   2. It'll then utilize Connext's swapping feature to swap the ETH or wETH you deposited to `nextWETH`.
   3. It'll then retrieve the price and last price timestamp of `ezETH` from the `RenzoOracleL2.sol` and calculate how much `xezETH` (XERC20) to mint you, and then it'll mint you that amount of `xezETH`.
   4. The resulted `nextWETH` from the swap will remain in the `xRenzoDeposit` contract for now.
3. Periodically, the [`xRenzoDeposit::sweep()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L414) function will be called by an admin. This function simply takes the balance of `nextWETH` in the contract and bridges it down to the L1.
4. After the bridging occurs and we're now in L1, the function [`xRenzoBridge::xReceive()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L139) will be triggered. It'll simply unwrap the received `nextWETH` to ETH and then deposit it into the `RestakeManager` using the function [`RestakeManager::depositETH()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L592)
5. The `xRenzoBridge` then [sends the minted ezETH tokens to the Lockbox contract to be wrapped](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L187).
6. `xRenzoBridge` will then burn the amount of `xezETH` tokens minted since they were already minted on L2.

## The vulnerability
The [Connext documentation](https://docs.connext.network/developers/guides/handling-failures#reverts-on-receiver-contract) discusses how a receiver contract should be created. It explicitly mentions that any contract implementing the `IXReceive` interface, should be built defensively and any revert-susceptible code should always be handled properly. From the [docs](https://docs.connext.network/developers/guides/handling-failures#reverts-on-receiver-contract):
> If the call on the receiver contract (also referred to as "target" contract) reverts, funds sent in with the call will end up on the receiver contract.
> 
> Ultimately, the goal should be to handle any revert-susceptible code and ensure that the logical owner of funds always maintains agency over them.

The [`xRenzoBridge::xReceive()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L139) function does not wrap the `restakeManager.depositETH{value:ethAmount}()` call in a try/catch block, which is dangerous given that the function [`RestakeManager::depositETH()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L592) can revert under certain circumstances.

[`xRenzoBridge::xReceive()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L139) :
```solidity
    function xReceive(
        bytes32 _transferId,
        uint256 _amount,
        address _asset,
        address _originSender,
        uint32 _origin,
        bytes memory
    ) external nonReentrant returns (bytes memory) {

        ...............

        // Get the amonut of ezETH before the deposit
        uint256 ezETHBalanceBeforeDeposit = ezETH.balanceOf(address(this));

        // Deposit it into Renzo RestakeManager
------> restakeManager.depositETH{ value: ethAmount }();

        // Get the amount of ezETH that was minted
        uint256 ezETHAmount = ezETH.balanceOf(address(this)) - ezETHBalanceBeforeDeposit;

        ................
```

[`RestakeManager::depositETH()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L592) : 
```solidity
    function depositETH(uint256 _referralId) public payable nonReentrant notPaused {
        // Get the total TVL
        (, , uint256 totalTVL) = calculateTVLs();

        // Enforce TVL limit if set
------> if (maxDepositTVL != 0 && totalTVL + msg.value > maxDepositTVL) {
            revert MaxTVLReached();
        }

        // Deposit the remaining ETH into the DepositQueue
        depositQueue.depositETHFromProtocol{ value: msg.value }();

        .............
```

Looking at [`RestakeManager::depositETH()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L592), it is evident that it can revert anytime `xRenzoBridge` tries to deposit an amount of ETH which would exceed the `maxDepositTVL` threshold.

## Impact
When that happens, there are several consequences:
1. The continued execution flow in `L1` will fail silently. The admin calling `sweep()` won't immediately notice that this has failed in L1.
2. The bridged `WETH` from L2 -> L1 will be stuck in the L1 `xRenzoBridge` contract. 
3. The minted `xezETH` on L2 will become insolvent, as a corresponding amount to be redeemed for `ezETH` will not be minted on L1.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Wrap the `restakeManager.depositETH{}()` call in a try/catch block and handle any potential reverts.



## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L244-L253


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The [`xRenzoDeposit`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol) contract on L2 allows users to exchange ETH for `xezETH` tokens at a price that is streamed from the L1 chain. However, this price feed may not always be in sync with the actual current price of `ezETH` on L1, leading to potential arbitrage opportunities.

## Proof of Concept
If the `ezETH` price on L1 increases, an attacker can exploit the outdated price on L2 by following these steps:

1. Bridge ETH to L2.
2. Deposit the ETH in the `xRenzoDeposit` contract to mint `xezETH` at the old, lower price.
3. Bridge the `xezETH` back to L1.
4. Redeem the `xezETH` for `ezETH`, and `ezETH` for ETH at the higher, current price on L1.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
While the cooldown period on withdrawals already removes the risk of immediate cascading arbitrage, the following steps may further mitigate the issue:
1. The safest mitigation would be to disallow instant minting of xezETH on L2. Instead, send the collateral to L1, have the bridge reply with the actual mint rate at which ezETH was minted and mint xezETH at the same rate.
3. Ensure that the price feed from L1 to L2 is updated frequently enough to minimize the potential for price discrepancies.


## Assessed type

MEV

title: Deposits will be bricked if `RenzoOracleL2` price is stale
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L293
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L52


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The [`xRenzoDeposit`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol) contract allows users to deposit ETH or WETH on L2 in exchange for `xezETH` tokens. The exchange rate between the deposited asset and `xezETH` is determined by calling the internal [`getMintRate()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L289) function. 

`getMintRate()` is supposed to return the latest price from either the oracle (by calling `oracle.getMintRate()`) or from the `lastPrice` state variable, which can be updated directly by a receiver contract or the owner via [`updatePrice()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L310) and [`updatePriceByOwner()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L320) respectively.

The intention is for `getMintRate()` to always return the most recent price, whether it comes from the oracle or the receiver/owner. However, `getMintRate()` does not gracefully handle the case where `oracle.getMintRate()` reverts, failing to return a value even if a fresh `lastPrice` is available to be used.

In `RenzoOracleL2`, [`getMintRate()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L50) fetches the latest round data from a custom Chainlink price feed, but reverts if the timestamp of this data is older than `MAX_TIME_WINDOW` (24 hours + 60 seconds):

```solidity
function getMintRate() public view returns (uint256, uint256) {
    (, int256 price, , uint256 timestamp, ) = oracle.latestRoundData();
    if (timestamp < block.timestamp - MAX_TIME_WINDOW) revert OraclePriceExpired();
    // ...
}
```

If `oracle.getMintRate()` reverts, `xRenzoDeposit.getMintRate()` will also revert, bubbling up the revert reason. This will prevent `getMintRate()` from falling back to the receiver or owner-provided `lastPrice`, and will cause the whole deposit transaction to revert.

The staleness check in `RenzoOracleL2.getMintRate()` is unnecessary, because `xRenzoDeposit._deposit()` already checks the returned timestamp and reverts if it is stale. The redundant check in the oracle will brick deposits whenever the oracle price is stale, even if there is a more recent price available from the receiver or owner.

## Proof of Concept
1. Oracle price on L2 becomes stale, i.e. its timestamp is older than 24 hours + 60 seconds
2. User attempts to call `depositETH()` or `deposit()` to deposit assets and mint `xezETH`
3. `_deposit()` is called internally, which calls `getMintRate()`
4. `getMintRate()` calls `oracle.getMintRate()`
5. `oracle.getMintRate()` reverts with `OraclePriceExpired`
6. The revert bubbles up and causes `xRenzoDeposit.getMintRate()` to revert
7. The user's deposit transaction fails
8. Any subsequent attempts to deposit by any user will also revert at step 6

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Remove the staleness check and revert from `RenzoOracleL2.getMintRate()`.

The staleness check is already performed in `xRenzoDeposit._deposit()`, so it is redundant and harmful to have it in `RenzoOracleL2.getMintRate()` as well. Removing it will allow `xRenzoDeposit.getMintRate()` to fall back gracefully to the receiver or owner price when the oracle is stale.





## Assessed type

Other

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L287


# Vulnerability details

To prevent users from immediately claiming their withdrawals, the [`WithdrawQueue`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol) enforces a cooldown period during which the funds cannot be claimed. This cooldown period is stored in the `coolDownPeriod` variable and can be modified by the admin via the [`updateCoolDownPeriod()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L129) function.

The issue is that when a user goes to claim their withdrawal by calling [`claim()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279), the current value of `coolDownPeriod` is used to check if enough time has elapsed since the withdrawal was initiated:

```solidity
if (block.timestamp - _withdrawRequest.createdAt < coolDownPeriod) revert EarlyClaim();
```

This means that if the cooldown period is increased after a user initiates a withdrawal, they will have to wait longer than expected to claim their funds. This is unfair as the terms of the withdrawal should be honored as they were when the user initiated it. Conversely, if the cooldown period is decreased, users can claim their withdrawals sooner than was originally enforced when they initiated the withdrawal. 

## Impact
Changes to the cooldown period will unexpectedly affect existing user withdrawals.

## Proof of Concept
1. User initiates a withdrawal via `withdraw()` when the `coolDownPeriod` is set to 7 days 
2. Admin calls `updateCoolDownPeriod()` to change the `coolDownPeriod` to 30 days
3. 7 days later, when the user tries to `claim()` their withdrawal, the transaction reverts with `EarlyClaim`
4. User has to wait a total of 30 days to claim their withdrawal, even though the original terms were 7 days

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Instead of storing the timestamp at which the request was created as `WithdrawRequest.createdAt`, store the timestamp at which it can be claimed by adding the current cooldown period to `block.timestamp` on creation and storing it as e.g. `unlockTime`.


## Assessed type

Other

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L244-L253
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L174-L178


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The [`xRenzoBridge`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol) contract on L1 is responsible for receiving ETH from the L2 chain, depositing it into the [`RestakeManager`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol) to mint `ezETH`, and then sending the minted `ezETH` to the `xezETHLockbox` to be wrapped into `xezETH`. However, the conversion rate from ETH to `ezETH` in this process is [determined](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L605-L609) by the `RestakeManager.depositETH()` function, which may not always match the rate at which `xezETH` was minted on L2.

When a user deposits ETH on L2 through the [`xRenzoDeposit`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol) contract, `xezETH` is minted immediately at a price retrieved from an L1 price feed. This price may be different from the actual conversion rate used when the deposited ETH is swept to L1 and converted to `ezETH` via `RestakeManager.depositETH()`.

If the `RestakeManager` mints `ezETH` at a lower rate than the rate used for minting `xezETH` on L2, the lockbox on L1 (i.e., the `xezETHLockbox` contract) will not hold enough `ezETH` to back all the circulating `xezETH` supply. This can lead to insolvency, as there might not be enough `ezETH` to redeem all the `xezETH` tokens.

## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenario:
1. The price feed on L2 indicates that 1 ETH is worth 1,000 `ezETH`.
2. Alice deposits 1 ETH into the `xRenzoDeposit` contract on L2 and receives 1,000 `xezETH`.
3. The deposited ETH is swept to L1 and received by the `xRenzoBridge` contract.
4. The `xRenzoBridge` contract deposits the ETH into the `RestakeManager`, which mints only 900 `ezETH` due to a different conversion rate.
5. The minted 900 `ezETH` is sent to the `xezETHLockbox`, leaving the lockbox undercollateralized, as it holds less `ezETH` than the amount of `xezETH` in circulation.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To mitigate this risk, consider the following:
1. The safest mitigation would be to disallow instant minting of `xezETH` on L2. Instead, when a user deposits ETH on L2, send the collateral to L1 first. Then, have the `xRenzoBridge` contract reply to L2 with the actual mint rate at which `ezETH` was minted, and mint `xezETH` on L2 at the same rate. This ensures that the `xezETH` supply is always backed by an equal amount of `ezETH` in the lockboxes.
2. Modify the `RestakeManager` contract to provide a separate function that can only be called by the `xRenzoBridge` contract. This function should mint `ezETH` for ETH at a predetermined rate that matches the rate used when minting `xezETH` on L2.
3. Implement a mechanism to periodically reconcile the `xezETH` supply on L2 with the `ezETH` balance in the lockboxes on L1. If a discrepancy is detected, adjust the `xezETH` supply or the `ezETH` balance to maintain a 1:1 backing.



## Assessed type

Other

title: Incorrect exchange rate provided to Balancer pools
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L451-L458


# Vulnerability details

The [`xRenzoDeposit`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol) contract, apart from being the entry point for deposits on L2s, also acts as a rate provider for Balancer pools on L2s, allowing them to determine the exchange rate between `xezWETH` and `WETH` tokens. Rate providers are crucial for Balancer pools to calculate token prices and determine yield protocol fees during joins and exits, as explained in the [Balancer documentation](https://docs.balancer.fi/reference/contracts/rate-providers.html).

However, the [`getRate()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L456) function in `xRenzoDeposit` does not provide the correct exchange rate. It simply returns the `lastPrice` state variable, which:
- may be stale if `updatePrice()` or `updatePriceByOwner()` have not been called recently
- may be older than the rate provided by `oracle.getMintRate()`
- can hence be different from the rate at which xezETH are minted in [`_deposit()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L227), which uses the newest of the oracle and internal `lastPrice` values, opening up arbitrage opportunities

## Impact
By providing an incorrect and potentially outdated exchange rate, `xRenzoDeposit` can cause Balancer pools to misprice `xezWETH` relative to `WETH`. This can lead to incorrect yield calculations and enable manipulation of pool joins and exits.

## Proof of Concept
1. `xRenzoDeposit` is set as the rate provider between `xezWETH` and `WETH` for a Balancer pool.
2. The price of `ezETH` relative to `ETH` changes on L1, but the receiver fails and `updatePrice()` is not called on `xRenzoDeposit`.
3. However, the oracle feed still provides accurate data
4. A user executes an operation on a WETH/xezETH Balancer pool, which calls `getRate()` on `xRenzoDeposit` to fetch the price
5. `getRate()` returns the stale price from the internal `lastPrice` variable
6. The Balancer pool uses this incorrect rate for its calculations, leading to mispricing of `xezWETH` and potential manipulation.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update the `getRate()` function to provide the same exchange rate used when minting `xezETH`. This can be achieved by calling `getMintRate()` instead of returning `lastPrice` directly:

```diff
- return lastPrice;
+ (uint256 rate, uint256 timestamp) = getMintRate();
+ require(block.timestamp <= timestamp + 1 days, "Price is stale");
+ return rate;
```

This ensures that the rate provided to Balancer pools is consistent with the actual minting rate and is not stale.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L274


# Vulnerability details

The [`OperatorDelegator`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol) contract allows an admin to queue withdrawals of multiple tokens from different strategies in the EigenLayer protocol via the [`queueWithdrawals()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L193) function. These queued withdrawals are later completed by the admin calling the [`completeQueuedWithdrawal()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L265) function.

However, the `completeQueuedWithdrawal()` function calls [`DelegationManager.completeQueuedWithdrawal()`](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/84ca899c715dbc577af1c8db5965188b061fe464/src/contracts/core/DelegationManager.sol#L305) with the `receiveAsTokens` parameter hardcoded to `true`. If any of the strategies included in the queued withdrawal fails or reverts, this will cause the entire withdrawal to revert. 

As mentioned in this [comment](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-eigenlayer-findings/issues/132#issuecomment-1575599410) and further confirmed [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-eigenlayer-findings/issues/132#issuecomment-1582291971), users can work around this by setting `receiveAsTokens` to `false`, allowing them to queue a new withdrawal excluding the failing strategy. However, the `OperatorDelegator` has no way to do this, as it can only call `completeQueuedWithdrawal()` with `receiveAsTokens == true`. 

This means a single failing strategy can block queued `OperatorDelegator` withdrawals indefinitely.

## Impact
Admin withdrawals from the `OperatorDelegator` can be blocked if any of the strategies included in their queued withdrawal fails or reverts when completing the withdrawal. The only way to recover is to upgrade the `OperatorDelegator` contract.

## Proof of Concept
1. Admin calls `OperatorDelegator.queueWithdrawals()`, including a withdrawal from `StrategyA` and `StrategyB`
2. Later, when trying to complete the withdrawal via `OperatorDelegator.completeQueuedWithdrawal()`, `StrategyB` is paused or fails
3. The call to `DelegationManager.completeQueuedWithdrawal()` with `receiveAsTokens == true` reverts due to the failure in `StrategyB`
4. The admin's entire withdrawal, including from `StrategyA`, is blocked
5. There is no way for `OperatorDelegator` to recover the withdrawal from `StrategyA`, short of upgrading the contract

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider adding a recovery function in `OperatorDelegator` that the admin can call in case a queued withdrawal fails. This function should call `DelegationManager.completeQueuedWithdrawal()` with `receiveAsTokens == false`, allowing the shares to be transferred to the withdrawing address, who can then queue a new withdrawal excluding the failing strategy.

It is important to ensure the shares are accredited to an address that is included in the TVL calculations, or to perform the emergency withdrawal and redeposit atomically in order to ensure no inaccuracies in TVL.



## Assessed type

Other

title: Pending withdrawals prevent safe removal of collateral assets
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L244
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L316-L321
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279


# Vulnerability details

The [`RestakeManager`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol) contract allows the admin to add and remove collateral tokens that are accepted for deposits into the protocol via the [`addCollateralToken()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L220) and [`removeCollateralToken()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L244) functions.

From the protocol team:
> \[In order to\] remove a collateral token we can withdraw full and increase the withdraw buffer to let users withdraw it.

However, since users cannot be forced to claim their withdrawals, it is always possible that a significant amount of the collateral token remains in the `WithdrawQueue` indefinitely in outstanding withdrawals.

In that case, calling `removeCollateralToken()` for that token would break accounting in the protocol. The `ezETH` total supply would still reflect the amounts that were burned to initiate those withdrawals, but the token balance in the `WithdrawQueue` would no longer be counted towards the TVL.

## Impact
The `RestakeManager` admin is unable to safely remove a collateral token. Removing the token anyway would inflate the `ezETH` mint and redeem rate compared to the actual backing collateral value.

## Proof of Concept
Assume `token1` has a balance of `Y` in the `WithdrawQueue` from pending user withdrawals. If `removeCollateralToken(token1)` is called:
1. `token1` is removed from the `collateralTokens` array 
2. `token1` balance of `Y` is still in `WithdrawQueue` but no longer counted in `totalTVL`
3. Mint rate for `ezETH` increases since `totalTVL` is lower but `ezETH` total supply is unchanged
4. Redeem rate for `ezETH` also increases since `ezETH` is now redeemable for a larger share of the remaining collateral

The mint and redeem rates for `ezETH` are now inflated compared to the true value of the collateral backing it, since `Y` worth of `token1` is not accounted for in `totalTVL` but is still effectively backing the `ezETH` that was burned to withdraw it.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider forcing pending withdrawals of a token to be claimed before that token can be removed as collateral. This could be done by only allowing `removeCollateralToken()` to be called if `claimReserve[token] == 0`. 

Alternatively, include the balance of the `WithdrawQueue` in the TVL calculation even for tokens that have been removed, as long as there are still pending withdrawals of that token. This would ensure mint and redeem rates remain correct.


## Assessed type

Other

raw_row.title: Attacker can sandwich protocol reward deposits to manipulate ezETH exchange rate

title: Attacker can sandwich protocol reward deposits to manipulate ezETH exchange rate
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L506-L523
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L163-L183


# Vulnerability details

The [`DepositQueue`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol) contract receives ETH rewards from various sources, such as execution layer rewards and MEV from native staking, likely via the [`OperatorDelegator`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol) contracts. These rewards are immediately sent to either the deposit queue or withdrawal queue by the [`receive()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L163) function, after deducting a protocol fee if configured.

The core issue lies in the fact that the ETH rewards sent to the deposit or withdrawal queue are counted towards the protocol's TVL. Consequently, when a reward is received, it instantaneously increases the exchange rate between ETH and ezETH.

An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by sandwiching the reward transaction. The attack would involve first minting ezETH for a given amount of ETH at the current exchange rate. Subsequently, after the reward is received and the exchange rate increases, they could immediately withdraw their ezETH for ETH at the higher rate, thereby profiting from the difference.

The root cause of this vulnerability stems from the fact that external rewards directly affect the ETH/ezETH exchange rate before being distributed to ezETH holders.

## Impact
An attacker can extract value from the protocol by sandwiching reward transactions. This would be at the expense of other ezETH holders, as the attacker mints ezETH at a lower rate and withdraws at a higher rate. 

The attacker's profit would be proportional to the amount of the reward relative to the TVL. The higher the reward as a percentage of TVL, the more value they could extract.

## Proof of Concept
Here is a step-by-step illustration of how an attacker could exploit this vulnerability:

1. Assume the ETH/ezETH exchange rate is 1:1 and the TVL is 1000 ETH. 
   
2. Attacker mints 100 ezETH by depositing 100 ETH at the 1:1 rate.
   1. The function `calculateMintAmount()` will be called with the following arguments:
      1. `_currentValueInProtocol` -> `1000e18`
      2. `_newValueAdded` -> `100e18`
      3. `_existingEzETHSupply` -> `1000e18`
      4. It will return `100 ETH (100e18)`, which will be the amount of `ezETH` that the attacker will be minted.
   
3. The totalTVL will be increased by `100 ETH`. So it'll be `1100 ETH` now.

4. The protocol receives a `100 ETH` reward from EigenLayer. This increases the TVL to `1200 ETH`.

5. The new ETH/ezETH exchange rate is 1.2:1.1. For 1 ezETH you can now withdraw ~1.09 ETH.

6. Attacker immediately withdraws their 100 ezETH and receives 109 ETH due to the higher rate.
   1. The function `calculateRedeemAmount()` will be called with the following arguments:
      1. `_ezETHBeingBurned` -> `100e18`
      2. `_existingEzETHSupply` -> `1100e18` (1000 + the 100 ezETH which are transferred to the withdrawal queue to be burnt)
      3. `_currentValueInProtocol` -> `1200e18` (Total TVL)
      4. It will return `109.09 ETH`. So the attacker will be walking away with `9.09` more ETH than he is supposed to.

7. Attacker profits 9.09 ETH from the sandwich attack, while the protocol's TVL is reduced by 9.09 ETH.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It would be advisable to accumulate external rewards in the `DepositQueue` contract and then distribute them pro-rata to ezETH holders over time. This approach would effectively decouple the rewards from the ETH/ezETH exchange rate, mitigating the risk of the identified vulnerability.





## Assessed type

MEV

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L303


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The [`WithdrawQueue`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L303) contract allows users to request withdrawals of their ezETH tokens in exchange for a selected asset, such as ETH or an ERC20 token. After a cooldown period, users can call the [`claim()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279) function to receive their withdrawn assets.

When the selected asset is ETH, the `claim()` function sends the ETH using the low-level `transfer()` function:

```solidity
payable(msg.sender).transfer(_withdrawRequest.amountToRedeem);
```

However, `transfer()` only forwards 2300 gas, which is not enough for the recipient to execute any non-trivial logic in a `receive()` or fallback function. For instance, it is not enough for Safes (such as [this one](https://etherscan.io/address/0xd1e6626310fd54eceb5b9a51da2ec329d6d4b68a) in use by the protocol) to receive funds, which require > 6k gas for the call to reach the implementation contract and emit an event:

![image](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/assets/153658521/6690e690-b759-4057-ba92-25514fa8f210)

In this case, the impact is higher than that reported by [4naly3er](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/4naly3er-report.md#m-4-call-should-be-used-instead-of-transfer-on-an-address-payable) because `claim()` requires the caller to be the same address that initiated the original withdrawal request via `withdraw()`.

If a user calls `withdraw()` from a contract account like a multisig or smart contract wallet that has a `receive()` function requiring >2300 gas, their subsequent `claim()` call will fail permanently. The withdrawn ETH will be locked in the `WithdrawQueue` contract forever, leading to loss of funds.

## Proof of Concept
1. Alice calls `withdraw()` from her multisig wallet contract to withdraw 10 ETH worth of ezETH. The multisig contract is the `msg.sender` and gets saved as the withdrawal requester.
4. After the cooldown period, Alice tries to call `claim()` from the multisig contract. However, the multisig has a `receive()` function that uses >2300 gas. 
5. When `claim()` executes `payable(msg.sender).transfer(_withdrawRequest.amountToRedeem)`, the multisig's `receive()` fails due to out of gas, and the transaction reverts.
6. The 10 ETH is now permanently locked in `WithdrawQueue`, with no way for Alice to claim it.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use `call()` instead of `transfer()` to send ETH in `claim()`:

```
(bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{value: _withdrawRequest.amountToRedeem}("");
require(success, "ETH transfer failed");
```

This forwards all available gas and allows contract recipients to execute arbitrary logic.


## Assessed type

ETH-Transfer

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L289
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L299
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L316-L321


# Vulnerability details

The [`RestakeManager.calculateTVLs()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L274) function serves to calculate the protocol's TVL, which is used together with the total ezETH supply to determine the mint and redeem rates. This function iterates through all `OperatorDelegator` contracts and sums up the value of their staked collateral tokens and ETH, and adds the balance of collateral tokens held in the `WithdrawQueue` contract.

This is implemented as an outer loop that iterates over the operator delegators, and an inner loop that iterates over the collateral tokens for each operator delegator.

However, there is an issue with how the TVL locked in the withdrawal queues is accounted for. The TVL in the queue is only counted if there is at least one operator delegator. If there are no operator delegators, either when the protocol is freshly deployed or if they are later removed e.g. in order to migrate to new ones, the queues will not be accounted for in the TVL calculation, leading to an incorrect value being reported.

This incorrect TVL value is then used in the [`depositETH()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L592) function to calculate the amount of ezETH to mint for a given ETH deposit. If the TVL is underreported due to the issue described above, users will be able to mint ezETH at an artificially inflated rate.

## Impact
If the protocol has no operator delegators, either when it is freshly deployed or if they are later removed, users will be able to mint ezETH at an artificially inflated rate when calling `depositETH()`. This is because the TVL used in the calculation will be underreported, not accounting for the value locked in the withdrawal queue.

## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenario:

1. The protocol is freshly deployed, and no operator delegators have been added yet.
2. All user deposits go to the withdrawal queue, so it holds a significant amount of value in various collateral tokens.
3. User calls `depositETH()` with an ETH amount, which calls  `calculateTVLs()`.
4. `calculateTVLs()` only reports the ETH value in the deposit and withdraw queues.
8. User receives more ezETH than they should, based on the actual total value locked in the protocol.

The same scenario could occur if the protocol previously had operator delegators, but they were later removed, leaving the queues holding value that is not accounted for in the TVL calculation.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To fix this issue, the order of the loops should be swapped. The outer loop should iterate over the collateral tokens, and the inner loop should iterate over the operator delegators. This way, the value locked in the queues can be accounted for outside the inner loop, regardless of whether there are any operator delegators or not.

```solidity
// Iterate through the collateral tokens
for (uint256 j = 0; j < collateralTokens.length; j++) {
    uint256 tokenBalance = collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue);
    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(collateralTokens[j], tokenBalance);

    // Iterate through the operator delegators
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < operatorDelegators.length; i++) {
        // ...
    }
}
```

Additionally, the `withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded` flag should be removed, as it is no longer needed with the swapped loop order.



## Assessed type

Loop

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L300
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L137
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L50-L53


# Vulnerability details

The [`OperatorDelegator`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol) contract allows an admin to queue withdrawals of tokens from EigenLayer strategies via the [`queueWithdrawals()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L193) function. These queued withdrawals are later completed via the [`completeQueuedWithdrawal()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L265) function. 

When completing a queued withdrawal, any tokens withdrawn over the `WithdrawQueue`'s buffer amount for that token are deposited back into the corresponding EigenLayer strategy via [`OperatorDelegator._deposit()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L162). However, before depositing back into the strategy, `completeQueuedWithdrawal()` tops up the `WithdrawQueue`'s buffer for the token if it is below the target amount.

This is done by approving the `DepositQueue` to spend the tokens and then calling [`DepositQueue.fillERC20withdrawBuffer()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L134). However, `fillERC20withdrawBuffer()` has the [`onlyRestakeManager`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L50-L53) modifier which only allows the `RestakeManager` contract to call it. 

Therefore, any queued withdrawal that contains a token with a buffer deficit in the `WithdrawQueue` will fail when the admin tries to complete it, unless the `withdrawQueueAdmin` first nullifies the deficit by adjusting the buffer target.

## Impact
Queued withdrawals containing tokens with a `WithdrawQueue` buffer deficit will fail when the admin attempts to complete them via `completeQueuedWithdrawal()`. 

More severely, this prevents collateral tokens from being withdrawn out of EigenLayer strategies into the `WithdrawQueue`. As a result, once collateral tokens are deposited into EigenLayer via an `OperatorDelegator`, they can never be removed. This is because any attempt to withdraw them will fail on trying to top up the `WithdrawQueue` buffer.

## Proof of Concept
1. Admin queues a withdrawal of token X via `OperatorDelegator.queueWithdrawals()`
2. Token X's balance in the `WithdrawQueue` falls below the buffer target amount
3. Admin calls `completeQueuedWithdrawal()` to complete the queued withdrawal of token X
4. `completeQueuedWithdrawal()` calculates an amount of token X to top up the `WithdrawQueue` buffer with
5. It approves the `DepositQueue` to spend token X and calls `fillERC20withdrawBuffer()`
6. `fillERC20withdrawBuffer()` reverts because it can only be called by the `RestakeManager`
7. The queued withdrawal fails and token X remains stuck in EigenLayer

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Remove the `onlyRestakeManager` modifier from `DepositQueue.fillERC20withdrawBuffer()`:

```diff
- function fillERC20withdrawBuffer(address token, uint256 amount) external onlyRestakeManager {  
+ function fillERC20withdrawBuffer(address token, uint256 amount) external {
```

This would allow both the `RestakeManager` and the different `OperatorDelegator` contracts to top up the `WithdrawQueue` buffer when needed. 

Any calls to `fillERC20withdrawBuffer()` can only add tokens to the `WithdrawQueue`, which benefits the protocol. There is no risk of funds being stolen or drained by allowing this function to be called by any address. Therefore, having no access control modifier on `fillERC20withdrawBuffer()` is safe and solves the issue.



## Assessed type

Access Control

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L269

# Vulnerability details

We note that both this and the OperatorDelegator's `receive()` functions are `nonReentrant`:

```Solidity
File: OperatorDelegator.sol
265:     function completeQueuedWithdrawal(
266:         IDelegationManager.Withdrawal calldata withdrawal,
267:         IERC20[] calldata tokens,
268:         uint256 middlewareTimesIndex
269:     ) external nonReentrant onlyNativeEthRestakeAdmin {
270:         uint256 gasBefore = gasleft();
271:         if (tokens.length != withdrawal.strategies.length) revert MismatchedArrayLengths();
272: 
273:         // complete the queued withdrawal from EigenLayer with receiveAsToken set to true
274:         delegationManager.completeQueuedWithdrawal(withdrawal, tokens, middlewareTimesIndex, true);
---
501:     receive() external payable nonReentrant {
502:         // check if sender contract is EigenPod. forward full withdrawal eth received
503:         if (msg.sender == address(eigenPod)) {
504:             restakeManager.depositQueue().forwardFullWithdrawalETH{ value: msg.value }();
```

However, the `receive()` function is normally called by the `EigenPod` in the call stack originated by the L274 `completeQueuedWithdrawal()` when `receiveAsTokens == true` like in this case. 

This particular instance of reentrancy is not only acceptable but also required to allow ETH redemptions from EigenLayer. The `nonReentrant` modifier, however, prevents it.

All withdrawals that include any amount of ETH will be permanently stuck in EigenLayer and won't be redeemable. Only amounts coming from new deposits can be redeemed and the team will have no way to fill the withdrawal queues.

To unblock them, the team will necessarily have to upgrade OperatorDelegator.

To prove the concept, it's sufficient to upgrade OperatorDelegator on a mainnet fork and initiate a withdrawal that has ETH among the withdrawn strategies.

While it would be too bulky to provide a coded PoC, you can find in this GH Gist the Foundry traces of such failed call on a mainnet fork -> https://gist.github.com/assets/145972240/0f2500e1-1f93-4daf-8a5f-509da79f2e96

## Tools Used
Code review, Foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider removing `nonReentrant` from OperatorDelegator's `receive`, or applying the modifier only in case `msg.sender != eigenPod`.
