# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L75
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L92


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The [`RenzoOracle`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol) contract uses Chainlink oracles to fetch the price of assets, which is then used to calculate the value of tokens deposited by users. The `lookupTokenValue()` function fetches the latest price from the oracle using `latestRoundData()`.

However, Chainlink oracles have a built-in circuit breaker that gets triggered if the price of an asset goes outside a predetermined price band, defined by a `minAnswer` and `maxAnswer`. If the actual price of the asset falls below `minAnswer` or goes above `maxAnswer`, the oracle will keep returning the `minAnswer` or `maxAnswer` instead of the real price.

This could lead to a situation where the oracle is returning an incorrect price that doesn't reflect the true value of the asset. As a result, the `RenzoOracle` contract would calculate the value of user deposits based on this incorrect price. 

In a scenario where an asset experiences a massive crash in value (like LUNA), the oracle price could get stuck at `minAnswer`, allowing users to continue borrowing the asset but at an inflated price compared to its real value. This is similar to what happened to Venus protocol on BSC when LUNA [crashed](https://rekt.news/venus-blizz-rekt/).

## Proof of Concept
1. Collateral asset X has a current price of $100, which falls within the `minAnswer` and `maxAnswer` range of the Chainlink oracle. 
2. The price of Asset X suddenly crashes and falls to $10, which is below the oracle's `minAnswer` of $50.
3. When `RenzoOracle.lookupTokenValue()` fetches the latest price for Asset X, the oracle returns `minAnswer` of $50 instead of the real price of $10.
4. `RenzoOracle` calculates the value of user deposits of Asset X based on the incorrect price of $50 returned by the oracle.
5. Users can now mint ezETH for X at an inflated price of $50 instead of its real value of $10.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a check in `lookupTokenValue()` to verify if the price returned by the oracle is equal to `minAnswer` or `maxAnswer`, and revert if that's the case:

```solidity
(, int256 price, , , ) = oracle.latestRoundData();
(uint80 roundID, int256 minAnswer, int256 maxAnswer, , , , ) = oracle.getRoundData(oracle.getRoundId());

if (price == minAnswer || price == maxAnswer) revert OraclePriceOutsideRange();
```

This will ensure that the protocol doesn't use prices from the oracle if they are outside the valid range and stuck at the min/max thresholds. The `minAnswer` and `maxAnswer` values can be obtained by querying the aggregator contract, as described [here](https://medium.com/cyfrin/chainlink-oracle-defi-attacks-93b6cb6541bf#00ac).


## Assessed type

Oracle

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L308
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L168
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/84ca899c715dbc577af1c8db5965188b061fe464/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L332-L336
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/84ca899c715dbc577af1c8db5965188b061fe464/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L297
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/0139d6213927c0a7812578899ddd3dda58051928/src/contracts/strategies/StrategyBaseTVLLimits.sol#L74-L75
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/mainnet/src/contracts/strategies/StrategyBaseTVLLimits.sol#L80-L81


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The [`OperatorDelegator.completeQueuedWithdrawal()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L265) function serves to finalize a queued withdrawal consisting of different tokens, sending the withdrawn tokens to the `WithdrawQueue` contract up to the buffer amount, and depositing any excess tokens back into the corresponding EigenLayer strategy.

The issue is that the [call](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L168) to `strategyManager.depositIntoStrategy()` used to deposit any amount of excess tokens back into EigenLayer may revert, which would cause the entire `completeQueuedWithdrawal()` transaction to revert.

There are a couple reasons why `depositIntoStrategy()` may revert:
1. In `StrategyManager.depositIntoStrategy()`, the number of shares returned by the strategy is [verified](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/84ca899c715dbc577af1c8db5965188b061fe464/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L297) to be > 0. If the strategy mints shares at less than a 1:1 ratio, this can cause the transaction to revert, as the amount being deposited back may be as small as 1 wei. 
2. EigenLayer's stETH and wBETH [strategies](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts?tab=readme-ov-file#strategies) both implement per-transaction and total deposit limits ([stETH](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/0139d6213927c0a7812578899ddd3dda58051928/src/contracts/strategies/StrategyBaseTVLLimits.sol#L74-L75), [wBETH](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/mainnet/src/contracts/strategies/StrategyBaseTVLLimits.sol#L80-L81)):
	- if the deposit limit of a strategy has been reached, attempting to complete a queued withdrawal containing any amount over the `WithdrawQueue`'s buffer of the strategy's token will fail
	- if the amount being redeposited is large enough, it may surpass the per-deposit limit

This issue forces the `withdrawQueueAdmin` (which is a separate entity from the `nativeEthRestakeAdmin` affected) to set the buffer for the affected token high enough for the full amount being withdrawn to be transferred to the `WithdrawQueue`. This will hence require a third party to intervene and the protocol to handle in an unintended way by increasing the withdraw buffer for one or more tokens.

Furthermore, another entry point that calls `strategyManager.depositIntoStrategy()` and will revert under the same conditions is [`RestakeManager.deposit()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L491), the main deposit function for collateral tokens. Also here, the collateral token being deposited is first used to fill the `WithdrawQueue`'s buffer, so the transaction can revert for any of the reasons outlined above.

## Proof of Concept
Scenario A:
1. The `nativeEthRestakeAdmin` queues a withdrawal for 10 ETH, 10 stETH and 10 wBETH.  
2. After the withdrawal delay passes, `completeQueuedWithdrawal()` is called to process the withdrawals  
3. The 10 ETH are forwarded to the deposit queue  
4. Next, 9 stETH are withdrawn and sent to `WithdrawQueue`, filling its stETH buffer  
5. 1 stETH remains and is attempted to be deposited back into the stETH strategy via `strategyManager.depositIntoStrategy()`  
6. However, the stETH strategy has already reached its total deposit limit  
7. The deposit reverts and causes the entire `completeQueuedWithdrawal()` transaction to revert

Scenario B:
1. A user calls `RestakeManager.deposit()` to deposit 1 wBETH. 
2. All wBETH but 1 wei is used to fill the wBETH buffer in the `WithdrawQueue`.
3. The remaining 1 wei is then attempted to be deposited into the wBETH strategy via `strategyManager.depositIntoStrategy()`.
4. However, it is converted into 0 shares by the strategy.
5. `StrategyManager` verifies that the number of shares minted by the strategy is greater than 0.
6. Since 0 shares were minted, this check fails.
7. The `strategyManager.depositIntoStrategy()` call reverts.
8. This causes the entire `RestakeManager.deposit()` transaction to revert due to no fault of the user's.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider catching any reverts when depositing excess tokens into strategies. In order to ensure that the excess tokens remain in the system and are accounted for in the TVL, the best option may be to send them to the `WithdrawQueue` in the catch clause, regardless of whether the buffer for the given token is already full.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L491


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The deposit function of the DepositQueue contract, enables users to deposit any erc20 assets that is supported into the protocol, getting ezETH tokens in return. 1. Check for if sequencer is down
2.* Consider having off-chain monitoring to identify when the market price moves out of [minAnswer, maxAnswer] range
* better to decrease the heartbeat i.e  MAX_TIME_WINDOW 
3. Wrap chainlink answer in a try/catch block

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L307-L313

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The protocol assumes that the oracle decimals are 18 but that is not always the case. The `RestakeManager::calculateTVLs` function aggregates token values returned from an oracle in oracle decimals and native ETH values in 18 decimals without normalizing their decimal places. This can result in a TVL that is  mathematically incorrect. Such discrepancies can lead to severe issues including:

- Incorrect valuation of deposits, leading to errors in minting of protocol tokens.
- Erroneous withdrawal calculations, potentially allowing users to withdraw more/less value than entitled.
- Miscalculated reward distributions.


## Proof of Concept
The `RestakeManager::calculateTVLs` function integrates TVL calculations from multiple sources with differing decimal precisions. First it calls the `RenzoOracle::lookupTokenValue`, which always return price in oracle decimals, to calculate the return values :

```js
    function lookupTokenValue(IERC20 _token, uint256 _balance) public view returns (uint256) {
...

        return (uint256(price) * _balance) / SCALE_FACTOR;//@note supposedly balance is always in 10**18 decimals this should always return in oracle decimals
    }
```

```js
...
// Renzo Oracle returns values in oracle decimals 
operatorValues[j] = renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
    collateralTokens[j], operatorBalance
);
operatorTVL += operatorValues[j]; // Adding token values in oracle decimals
```

Then adds eth value using `getStakedETHBalance` which will always be in 18 decimals (since `stakedButNotVerifiedEth += msg.value;` represents the eth value):

```js
...

// Code segment showing mixed decimal calculations
uint256 operatorEthBalance = operatorDelegators[i].getStakedETHBalance();
operatorValues[operatorValues.length - 1] = operatorEthBalance;
operatorTVL += operatorEthBalance;  // Adding ETH value in 18 decimals directly

```

In cases where oracle decimals is different from 18 it can lead to a wrong total TVL.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider normalizing the decimal values in the function `RenzoOracle::lookupTokenValue` using the `decimals` function of the `AggregatorV3Interface`.





## Assessed type

Decimal

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L13
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L52


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The stale period 86400 + 60 seconds used for the oracle price validation is too short for some tokens like `ezETH` for example on Arbitrum. This could lead to the protocol consuming stale prices on Arbitrum.

## Proof of Concept
In both `RenzoOracle` and `RenzoOracleL2`, the hearbeat period `MAX_TIME_WINDOW` is set to `86400 + 60; // 24 hours + 60 seconds`. In the functions `RenzoOracleL2::getMintRate` and `RenzoOracle::lookupTokenValue`, a validation checks sees if the price data fed by Chainlink's price feed aggregators is stale depending if the period of 24 hours + 60 seconds has passed. Example :

```js
    function getMintRate() public view returns (uint256, uint256) {
        (, int256 price, , uint256 timestamp, ) = oracle.latestRoundData();
        if (timestamp < block.timestamp - MAX_TIME_WINDOW) revert OraclePriceExpired();
```

The problem is that depending on the token and the chain, the same period can be considered too small or too stale.

Let's consider the ezETH/ETH oracles on different chains:

- On Ethereum, the oracle will update the price data every [~24 hours](https://data.chain.link/feeds/ethereum/mainnet/ezeth-eth).
- On Arbitrum, the oracle will update the price data every [~6 hours](https://data.chain.link/feeds/arbitrum/mainnet/ezeth-eth-exchange-rate).
- On Linea, the oracle will update the price data every [24 hours](https://data.chain.link/feeds/linea/mainnet/ezeth-eth).
...

This means that on Arbitrum, 24 hours can be considered too large for the stale period which will cause the function `RenzoOracleL2::getMintRate` to return stale data.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

It is recommanded to store a mapping that would record the hearbeat parameter for the stale period of each token and for every different chain.





## Assessed type

Oracle

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L192-L199
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L182-L184


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The funds of the Renzo protocol need to participate in the re-staking of the EigenLayer protocol to generate income. If an attacker interferes with and prevents the Renzo protocol from staking to the EigenLayer, it will prevent the Renzo protocol from generating income.

## Proof of Concept
The key to the attack is that all deposits made by Renzo will be prioritized to meet the withdrawal buffer of the WithdrawQueue contract. To put it in a metaphor, a malicious attacker is equivalent to digging a black hole in the WithdrawQueue contract, which will absorb all new deposits into the WithdrawQueue contract as much as possible, thereby preventing Renzo from depositing funds into EigenLayer.

Taking Native ETH as an example, the ETH deposited by users into the Renzo protocol will be first held in the DepositQueue contract until the ETH held in the DepositQueue contract reaches 32 ETH. Only then will the Renzo protocol deposit the 32 ETH into the EigenLayer protocol

Suppose the value of the withdrawalBufferTarget for Native ETH in the WithdrawQueue contract is equal to 100 ether, and the Renzo team has perfectly filled the withdrawalBufferTarget when the project was launched.

1. Ethereum mainnet: Because the Ethereum mainnet can observe the transaction records of the mempool, the attacker observes that Alice is about to deposit X ETH into the Renzo protocol. At this time, the attacker conducts a front-run to initiate a preemptive transaction, depositing X ETH into the Renzo protocol and immediately applying for withdrawal. At this time, the WithdrawQueue contract will generate X amount of buffer that needs to be filled. Alice's transaction is executed after the attacker, so her X ETH flows to the WithdrawQueue contract. In this way, the attacker prevents X ETH from being deposited into the EigenLayer protocol.

2. L2 network (Arbitrum, Base chain, etc.): Although L2 networks cannot preempt transactions, attackers can find the amount of ETH deposited into Renzo every T period (such as one hour) from historical transactions and calculate the average value R. Note that R < 100 (100 represents the value of withdrawalBufferTarget). Then the attacker executes an attack every T period, first depositing R amount of ETH in the same transaction and then immediately applying for withdrawal. The purpose of this is to ensure that as much as possible, the ETH deposited into the Renzo protocol will flow to the WithdrawQueue contract within T period. The higher the accuracy of T period, the more likely it is to prevent more ETH from being deposited into the EigenLayer protocol

Other attack methods that are not native to ETH follow the same logic. Next, let's analyze the cost of the attacker:

1. Because the attack is to apply for withdrawal immediately after depositing in a transaction, the attacker's funds will not be lost, and the only real loss is the gas fee, which is sufficiently low in the L2 network
2. The Renzo protocol requires a 7-day delay before a withdrawal request can be made, so an attacker with sufficient funds can prevent more ETH from being deposited into the EigenLayer protocol. This amount of funds is approximately equal to the total ETH deposits generated by the Renzo protocol over a 7-day period. I found sample data from the Renzo website, which shows that the amount of ETH deposited into Renzo on January 29, 2024 was 66.54k, and the amount of ETH deposited into Renzo 7 days later, on February 4, 2024, was 80.79k. The cumulative amount of ETH over these 7 days was 14.25k
3. Obviously, ordinary individuals cannot meet this funding scale, although the attack threshold requirements are high, it is not theoretically impossible to achieve. For example, some financial institutions that have competitive relationships with Renzo have the ability to launch attacks. Therefore, theoretically speaking, there is a risk that Renzo will be attacked. The most important thing is that the attacker does not have to achieve a 100% attack. An attacker that can affect 50% or 10% of Renzo's funds and prevent them from interacting with EigenLayer will also cause some degree of damage to Renzo.

In summary, it is recommended to consider this attack strategy as a medium-severity risk.


## Tools Used
Manual audit

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
After limiting user deposits, a short period of time is required before applying for withdrawals to prevent simultaneous deposits and withdrawal requests in the same transaction









## Assessed type

DoS

price oracle will not work as intended 

## Proof of Concept
#### 1.NO checking for l2 sequencer is active or not 

When using Chainlink with L2 chains like Arbitrum, smart contracts must check whether the L2 Sequencer is down to avoid stale pricing data that appears fresh - Chainlink’s official documentation provides an example implementation. 

[*renzo code implementation*](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L50-L58)


#### 2.Unhandled Oracle Revert Denial Of Service

Calls to Oracles could potentially revert, which may result in a complete Denial-of-Service to smart contracts which depend upon them. Chainlink multisigs can immediately block access to price feeds at will, so just because a price feed is working today does not mean it will continue to do so indefinitely. Smart contracts should handle this by:

wrapping calls to Oracles in try/catch blocks and dealing appropriately with any errors,
providing functionality to replace or update oracle feeds after they are configured.
If a configured Oracle feed has malfunctioned or ceased operating, but the smart contract does not have any alternative data source, nor does the contract allow updates to data sources, that contract will be permanently bricked.


[*renzo code implementation*](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L51)

````Solidity
75:         (, int256 price, , uint256 timestamp, ) = oracle.latestRoundData();
76:         if (timestamp < block.timestamp - MAX_TIME_WINDOW) revert OraclePriceExpired();
77:         if (price <= 0) revert InvalidOraclePrice();
78: 
79:         // Price is times 10**18 ensure value amount is scaled
80:         return (uint256(price) * _balance) / SCALE_FACTOR;
81:     }
````

### Issue
There is potential volatility on collateral LST tokens being exchanged for ezETH. These collateral token price may drop against the ETH. The protocol did not put any slippage protection in regards of this situation. User may be put into a disadvantage position and received unfavorable number of minted ezETH.


## Impact
Can lead to unfavorable ezETH minting rates and potential economic losses to users

## Proof of Concept
This could be the scenario
1. User A deposits an LST token with the price of 3,100 usd.
2. Suddenly this LST token drops to 2,900 usd. This could be cause of penalties imposed due to malicious behavior or network downtime.
3. The protocol pick-up the 2,900 usd price in minting ezETH token.
4. User A receives of lower number of ezETH since the collateral drop its price.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Put a parameter input in deposit function in which a user can decide the minimum output it can receive from minting so user can control the slippage.




## Assessed type

As per current market condition, not all LSTs are equal in terms of pricing, so there is a high chance this price difference can be use as arbitrage opportunity to drain the high valued assets from the protocol to the malicious user.

## Proof of Concept
This could be the scenario of the exploit.
1. User A deposited a higher valued LST of 1 wbETH amounting 3,100 usd.
2. User B sees the transaction of User A and immediately backruns it by depositing a lower valued LST of 1 stETH amounting 3,000 usd.
3. User A receives a minted 1.06 ezETH in exchange of deposited 1 wbETH.
4. User B receives a minted 1.02 ezETH in exchange of deposited 1 stETH.
5. User B seeing the price difference, immediately withdraws 1.02 ezETH but the actual collateral token to be withdraw is in the form of wbETH.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L362-L393
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L534-L537


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Under specific conditions, OperatorDelegators included in a further index may never receive deposits despite the set allocation. OperatorDelegators are discouraged to participate.

A small number of OperatorDelegators threatens the stability of the protocol and is inconsistent with the operational assumptions.

## Proof of Concept
During the deposit in `RestakeManager`, current TVLs are calculated [#L500-504](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L500-L504). Based on them, it is determined to which `operatorDelegator` the funds should be transferred through the `chooseOperatorDelegatorForDeposit` [#L534](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L534-L537) function.

The `chooseOperatorDelegatorForDeposit` [#L362-L393](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L362-L393) function selects the FIRST `OperatorDelegator` with the TVL below the threshold OR returns the FIRST one in the list, as stated in the comment.

This approach under specific conditions will create unfair distribution.

Look at the example below:
1. We have 3 `OperatorDelegator`, each of them have the same allocation (1/3). The first deposit is 0,6 ETH. It automatically goes to the `operatorDelegator` located at the first index[0].

**Total TVL before deposit:** 0 ETH
**Before deposit:** Operator 1: 0/0 ETH         Operator 2: 0/0 ETH         Operator 3: 0/0 ETH
**After deposit:** Operator 1: 0,6/0,2 ETH         Operator 2: 0/0,2 ETH         Operator 3: 0/0,2 ETH
**Total TVL after deposit:** 0,6 ETH

2. As we can see, OperatorDelegator 1 exceeds their threshold, and the others are waiting for the next deposits. Now, someone deposits 3 ETH.

**Total TVL before deposit:** 0,6 ETH
**Before deposit:** Operator 1: 0,6/0,2 ETH         Operator 2: 0/0,2 ETH         Operator 3: 0/0,2 ETH

The OperatorDelegator 2 at index[1] is taken into account as the first one that does not have the threshold filled. So the situation changes to the following:

**After deposit:** Operator 1: 0,6/1,2 ETH         Operator 2: 3/1,2 ETH         Operator 3: 0/1,2 ETH
**Total TVL after deposit:** 3,6 ETH

3. The next deposit, regardless of its size, will again go to OperatorDelegator 1, index[0] as it will be below the threshold (0,6/1,2), which constantly increases with each deposit. Even though OperatorDelegator 3 has not received any funds yet.

If the deposit is large enough, it will increase the threshold of OperatorDelegator no. 2 index[1] and the funds can be handled by only 2 of the 3 OperatorDelegators.

**This scenario only illustrates this problem on a small scale. The more operators there are and the more diverse the deposits and withdrawals, the more significant the problem may be.**


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Choose OperatorDelegator for deposit proportionally based on the lowest allocation utilization to create incentives for new OperatorDelegators that rank further down the index[]. The funds should go to the OperatorDelegator who has the largest gap between the established allocation and the actually deposited capital.

Use a similar approach when selecting OperatorDelegator to withdraw, but in reverse. Pick OperatorDelegator with the highest allocation utilization rate.


## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Under specific conditions, user deposits will always revert.

## Proof of Concept
When a user deposits funds through `RestakeManager`, the function checks the withdraw buffer and fill it if it is below the buffer target determined by `bufferToFill`. 

If it needs to be filled, line [RestakeManager#L547](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L547) checks whether the transferred `_amount` is less than or equal to `bufferToFill`.
```solidity
bufferToFill = (_amount <= bufferToFill) ? _amount : bufferToFill;
```
The case where `_amount` is equal to `bufferToFill` is incorrectly handled as after subtraction the `_amount` value will be 0 [RestakeManager#L549](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L549C13-L549C37).
```solidity
_amount -= bufferToFill;
```
That leads to a revert during `operatorDelegator.deposit` line [RestakeManager#L562](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L562), as it will not be able to pass the requirement for `tokenAmount` in [OperatorDelegator#L147](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L147)
```solidity
        if (address(tokenStrategyMapping[token]) == address(0x0) || tokenAmount == 0)
```

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Handle separately the case in which the entire `_amount` goes towards filling the `bufferToFill` (`_amount == bufferToFill`). If the amount equals 0 after paying `bufferToFill`, do not try to deposit it to `operatorDelegator`, allocate the appropriate amount of tokens to the user.


## Assessed type

Token-Transfer

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L229


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Holders of wBETH and other tokens that will be accepted by Renzo can compensate for their losses resulting from price drop (e.g. slashing) using the funds of Renzo users. Very quickly after this system weakness will be discovered by the first attacker, it can be automated and exploited by bots as an arbitrage opportunity creating a growing loss for Renzo depositors.

## Proof of Concept
Renzo creates a system that allows for restaking various tokens and receive their Liquid Restaking Token (LRT) EzETH in return. Example ERC20 used by the protocol ezETH, stETH, wBETH.

Users depositing their funds into Renzo are encouraged by the rewards of staking and re-staking through EigenLayer, but they also bear the risk of penalties and slashing of their deposited funds.

However, in case of wBETH, the 3rd party users who are not associated in any way with Renzo ecosystem can take advantage of such LRT and make Renzo users bear their losses.

Keeping in mind these things:

- value of assets like wBETH
- there are price drops for assets like wBETH, wstETH, cbETH, but most of the time these are temporary,
- things that can cause price drops for assets like wBETH include: slashing, lower demand / lack of trust for particular asset, withdrawal caused by people who accumulated big rewards over time,
- lower demand / lack of trust is unpredictable, however, big withdrawals can be monitored and slashing is a process spread over time, so there is a time when you know the value of asset will drop,
- liquid staking providers like LIDO etc., protects themselves from "withdrawal before slashing" by making withdrawal process long enough so that slashing can affect the users who request to withdraw,
- user within Renzo ecosystem can deposit asset1 (wBETH) to get ezETH, and then request to withdraw asset2 (ETH).

Consider the following scenario (values used for ease of calculation and to illustrate the attack, real values will be presented later in this description):

1. 200 ETH is deposited inside Renzo by users and 200 ezETH were minted.

2. The attacker (wBETH staker) has 100 wBETH (price is e.g. 1 wBETH = 2 ETH, their wBETH is worth 200 ETH)

3. The attacker knows through monitoring slashing events and big withdrawalas that price will drop soon.

4. The attacker deposit their 100 wBETH to Renzo to get 200 ezETH (as current price is still 1 wBETH = 2 ETH)

Total value locked on Renzo will increase from 200 ETH to 400 ETH (200 eth and 100 wBETH). Users posses 200 ezETH, Attacker posses 200 ezETH.

5. Price of wBETH now drops by 50% (so now 1 wBETH = 1 ETH)

Total value locked on Renzo will decrease from 400 ETH to 300 ETH (as 100 wBETH is now worth only 100 ETH). That causes value drop for ezETH value (1 ezETH = 0,75 ETH).

6. The attacker decides to request withdraw all of their wBETH by burning only ~134 ezETH (instead of 200 ezETH) so 66 ezETH will remain for them. They use them to another withdraw of ~50 ETH by burning another 66 ezETH.

Attacker gets 200 wBETH back (current price is 100 ETH) and additional 50 ETH.

Attacker buys additional wBETH for their additional 50 ETH, so know they have 250 wBETH (from another source, outside protocol)

Now price recover, so its again 1 wBETH = 2 ETH.

Attacker now have 250 wBETH worth 500 ETH, and Renzo users have 150 ETH (lost 50 ETH, as attacker delegeted their risk to Renzo users).

However, the price will not drop by 50%. The real numbers could be up to 10%.

wBETH (https://coinmarketcap.com/currencies/wrapped-beacon-eth/)
there are price drops (https://coinmarketcap.com/currencies/wrapped-beacon-eth/historical-data/)

Looking also at 2 examples of similar assets to those that are considered (cbETH and wstETH) we can observe the following:

cbETH (https://coinmarketcap.com/currencies/coinbase-wrapped-staked-eth/)
there are price drops, based on data from last 365 days the biggest percentage drop in price occurred on March 11, 2023, with a drop of approximately 8.25%
(https://coinmarketcap.com/currencies/coinbase-wrapped-staked-eth/historical-data/)

wstETH (https://coinmarketcap.com/currencies/lido-finance-wsteth/)
there are price drops, based on data from last 365 days the biggest percentage drop in price occurred also on March 11, 2023, with a drop of approximately 9.28% (https://coinmarketcap.com/currencies/lido-finance-wsteth/historical-data/)


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Set a minimum period for the user between their deposit and withdrawal so that they cannot take advantage of price fluctuations. Right know, their redeem amount is calculted as soon as withdraw is called.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L491
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Loss of capital of users who withdraw stETH. Their LST rewards will be miscalculated. Loss will constantly grow over time.

## Proof of Concept
The general questions section in the readme.md states that the ERC20s used by the protocol are ezETH, stETH, and wBETH.
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/README.md#scoping-q--a

However, stETH is a rebase token and the amount of stETH in a user/platform balance will not be constant - it changes daily as staking rewards arrive.

The current deposit/withdraw flow does not handle rebasing tokens at all.

In the case of wrapped tokens such as used here wBETH, although the exact `amountToRedeem` amount is calculated during the withdrawal request [WithdrawQueue#L229](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L229) user will continue to earn part of rewards as their value is determined by price that increases over time.

Even though the user has to wait 7 days (according to the readme) for a claim, the same `amountToRedeem` of wBETH will be worth more after this 7 days.

In the case of stETH, rebase token the exact `amountToRedeem` will be calculated in the same way. However, rebase token value remains 1:1 and its value changes through balance updates, not increasing the price.

Here, after 7 days, this `amountToRedeem` will not be updated. Users who decide to withdraw stETH will always lose their accumulating rewards before they will be able to claim.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider the non-rebasing wrapped version of stETH instead (wstETH) or re-calculate amountToRedeem to adjust it's balance.  
https://help.lido.fi/en/articles/5231836-what-is-lido-s-wsteth 



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L55


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The main impact is that the RenzoOracleL2.sol contract will out of service permanently if the Chainlink aggregator returns a price that is less than
1 ETH, even though the price is not stale. Precisely the getMintRate function contains an unnecessary check on the returned price, which could leave the oracle in a state of Denied Service. 

## Proof of Concept

Consider the following block [excerpt](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L50) from the getMintRate() function.

```
uint256 _scaledPrice = (uint256(price)) * 10 ** (18 - oracle.decimals());
        if (_scaledPrice < 1 ether) revert InvalidOraclePrice();
        return (_scaledPrice, timestamp);
```

Now ezETH Token contains 18 decimals.

So if a call to the aggregatorV3 interface returns a price of 0.99 ETH

price = 990_000_000_000_000_000 Wei

scaled price becomes

uint256 _scaledPrice = price * 10 ** (18 - 18)

_scaledPrice = price

Therefore

the conditional

```
if (_scaledPrice < 1 ether) revert InvalidOraclePrice();
```

will revert since the _scaledPrice is less than 1 ETH and the oracle will not be able to return an answer and remain is a DOS state until the price increases.


## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

I would Recommend the scaled price check be removed, a check for stale price is sufficient.


## Assessed type

Oracle

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Factory.sol#L82
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Factory.sol#L147


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Ambiguous abi encoding of the salt in the _deployXERC20(...) function leads to a hash calculation collision, which in turn leads to a collision in create3 contract deployment for the same user. This will be a major problem for users that wish to use the factory to deploy multiple tokens that could most likely have ambiguous names and symbols as a hash collision will also mean contract deployment collision.

## Proof of Concept

Consider a user named Alice, who wants to deploy two XERC20 contracts

```
--------------------------------------
           | CONTRACT A | CONTRACT B |
_______________________________________
  _name    |  "craz"    |   "c"      |
______________________________________
  _symbol  |    "y"     | "razy"     |
---------------------------------------
```


Now lets consider the excerpt from the [_deployXERC20(...)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Factory.sol#L147) function

```
 bytes32 _salt = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(_name, _symbol, msg.sender));
```

As we can see from above the contract uses the Non-standard packed mode as a result

abi.encodePacked("craz","y",msg.sender) == abi.encodePacked("c","razy",msg.sender)

and the keccak256 hash of either will cause a collision.

Meaning when the [create3](https://github.com/transmissions11/solmate/blob/c892309933b25c03d32b1b0d674df7ae292ba925/src/utils/CREATE3.sol#L49) calls the following line

```
proxy := create2(0, add(proxyChildBytecode, 32), mload(proxyChildBytecode), salt)
```

The deployment will fail as the salt has already been used.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

I would recommend the salt generation use only a single dynamic type to prevent collisions.


## Assessed type

en/de-code

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/optimism/OptimismMintableXERC20Factory.sol#L89
https://github.com/transmissions11/solmate/blob/c892309933b25c03d32b1b0d674df7ae292ba925/src/utils/CREATE3.sol#L49


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Ambiguous abi encoding of the salt in the _deployOptimismMintableXERC20 function leads to a hash calculation collision, which in turn leads to a collision in create3 contract deployment for the same user. This will be a major problem for users that wish to use the factory to deploy multiple tokens that could most likely have ambiguous names and symbols as a hash collision will also mean contract deployment collision.

## Proof of Concept

Consider a user named Alice, who wants to deploy two OPTIMISM XERC20 contracts

```
--------------------------------------
           | CONTRACT A | CONTRACT B |
_______________________________________
  _name    |  "craz"    |   "c"      |
______________________________________
  _symbol  |    "y"     | "razy"     |
---------------------------------------
```


Now lets consider the excerpt from the [_deployOptimismMintableXERC20(...)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/optimism/OptimismMintableXERC20Factory.sol#L89) function

```
 bytes32 _salt = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(_name, _symbol, msg.sender));
```

As we can see from above the contract uses the Non-standard packed mode as a result

abi.encodePacked("craz","y",msg.sender) == abi.encodePacked("c","razy",msg.sender)

and the keccak256 hash of either will cause a collision.

Meaning when the [create3](https://github.com/transmissions11/solmate/blob/c892309933b25c03d32b1b0d674df7ae292ba925/src/utils/CREATE3.sol#L49) library calls the following line

```
proxy := create2(0, add(proxyChildBytecode, 32), mload(proxyChildBytecode), salt)
```

The deployment will fail as the salt has already been used.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

I would recommend the salt generation use only a single dynamic type to prevent collisions.





## Assessed type

en/de-code

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/TimelockController.sol#L368-L370
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L168


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the `_execute` function of the `TimelockController` contract, a low-level `call` is used to send Ether and execute arbitrary code at a target address. However, if the target account does not exist, the `call` will return `true` even though the transaction did not have the intended effect. This can lead to silent failures where the transaction appears to succeed but no action is actually performed.

A similar issue was acknowledged [here](https://solodit.xyz/issues/m-07-low-level-transfer-via-call-can-fail-silently-code4rena-rolla-rolla-contest-git) and it was of medium severity.

## Proof of Concept
```solidity
function _execute(address target, uint256 value, bytes calldata data) internal virtual {
        (bool success, ) = target.call{ value: value }(data);
        require(success, "TimelockController: underlying transaction reverted");
    }
```

Per the Solidity docs:

> The low-level functions call, delegatecall and staticcall return true as their first return value if the account called is non-existent, as part of the design of the EVM. Account existence must be checked prior to calling if needed."

Please find the documentation here: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/develop/control-structures.html#error-handling-assert-require-revert-and-exceptions


There's another instance of the issue;

Another instance is in the `DepositQueue` contract, specifically in the `receive()` function. Just as described above, the function does not check the return value of the low-level call when transferring the fee amount to the `feeAddress`.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L168

```solidity
(bool success, ) = feeAddress.call{ value: feeAmount }("");
if (!success) revert TransferFailed();
```

The `TransferFailed()` error is only thrown if the low-level call itself fails (i.e., it runs out of gas or the call stack depth is exceeded). However, if the `feeAddress` is a contract that doesn't accept plain ETH transfers (i.e., it doesn't have a `receive()` or `fallback()` function), the call will succeed but the ETH transfer will fail silently.

This means that the fee amount will be deducted from the `msg.value`, but it won't actually be transferred to the `feeAddress`. As a result, the fee will be permanently lost, and the `totalEarned` will be incorrectly updated with the remaining rewards.





## Tools Used
Manual review
[Solidity doc](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/develop/control-structures.html#error-handling-assert-require-revert-and-exceptions)
[Past Audit](https://solodit.xyz/issues/m-07-low-level-transfer-via-call-can-fail-silently-code4rena-rolla-rolla-contest-git)

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Check for the account's existence prior to transferring.


For the second instance, consider using the `transfer()` function instead of a low-level call to transfer the fee amount.




## Assessed type

call/delegatecall

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/2024-04-renzo/contracts/Bridge/L2/PriceFeed/CCIPReceiver.sol#L5-L7


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
CCIP Router addresses cannot be updated in `CCIPReceiver.sol`.
Router address deprecation will cause the protocol to stop working and it might temporarily DOS users who continue to interact with old controllers.

I reported this issue as "Medium" because of the impacts stated above

## Proof of Concept

```solidity
import {
    CCIPReceiver
} from "@chainlink/contracts-ccip/src/v0.8/ccip/applications/CCIPReceiver.sol";
```

On contracts that inherit from CCIPReceiver just like `CCIPReceiver.sol`, router addresses need to be updatable. Chainlink may update the router addresses just as they did before. This issue introduces a single point of failure that is outside of the protocol's control.

[An example of a contract](https://github.com/smartcontractkit/ccip-tic-tac-toe/blob/main/contracts/TTTDemo.sol#L81-L83) that uses CCIP gotten from [Chainlink docs](https://docs.chain.link/ccip/examples#ccip-tic-tac-toe).

On 8th of December, 2023, [Chainlink documents notified users about router address updating on testnet](https://docs.chain.link/ccip/release-notes#v120-release-on-testnet---2023-12-08)

> CCIP v1.0.0 has been deprecated on testnet. You must use the new router addresses mentioned in the [CCIP v1.2.0 configuration page](https://docs.chain.link/ccip/supported-networks/v1_2_0/testnet) before January 31st, 2024.

On Testnets, router contracts in v1.0.0 and v1.2.0 are different. It means that router contract addresses can change from version to version. So CCIPReceivers should accommodate this. Mainnet is on v1.0.0 which means its router addresses can change with an update.



## Tools Used

Manual review
Chainlink docs (Check all the links above)


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Implement a function to update the _router address. Just like this:

```solidity
function updateRouter(address routerAddr) external onlyOwner {
        _router = routerAddr;
    }
```


## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L491-L576
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L263


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`RestakeManager::deposit()` and `WithdrawQueue::withdraw()` have no slippage protection. `deposit()` receives amount collateral from the user and mints them `ezETH`, and `withdraw()` does the opposite. Both calculations, `collateral → ezETH` and `ezETH → collateral`, rely on oracles to convert everything to ETH denomination, meaning that the amount received in return may vary indefinitely while the request is waiting to be executed.

## Proof of Concept

As you can see, none of the functions have a slippage parameter that allows the user to specify a minimum amount they expect to receive. This means that the user has no control over how much `ezETH` or collateral they will receive in return.

[RestakeManager.sol#L491-L576](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L491-L576)
```solidity
function deposit(
    IERC20 _collateralToken,
    uint256 _amount,
    uint256 _referralId // @audit no minAmountOut
) public nonReentrant notPaused {
    ...
}
```

[WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L263](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L263)
```solidity
function withdraw(uint256 _amount, address _assetOut) external nonReentrant {
    ...
}
```

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add `minAmountOut` to `deposit()` and `minAmountOut` to `withdraw()` because it calculates `amountToRedeem` there.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Validators could be staked using duplicated signatures

## Proof of Concept
Staking multiple validators in stakeEthFromQueueMulti does not check for duplicate signatures across validators. This allows the same signature to be reused for different pubkeys.

Steps to Reproduce

Call stakeEthFromQueueMulti with:

An array of 2 different operatorDelegator addresses
2 different pubkey values
An array of 2 identical signature values
2 depositDataRoot values
The contract will stake both validators without error, reusing the same signature for both pubkeys



## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The contract should check that each signature in the array is unique and reject the transaction if a duplicate is found. Signatures should have a 1-to-1 mapping with pubkeys.

Invalid Validation

## Impact
There's no way to identify which is native token or not in the contract potentially leading to loss of funds

## Proof of Concept
The initialize function in the XERC20Lockbox contract takes three parameters: _xerc20 (the address of the XERC20 contract), _erc20 (the address of the ERC20 token), and _isNative (a boolean indicating whether the ERC20 token is the native gas token of the chain or not).

However, there is no explicit validation or check within the initialize function to ensure that the _erc20 address corresponds to the actual native token of the chain when _isNative is set to true. Similarly, there is no validation to ensure that the _erc20 address corresponds to a non-native ERC20 token when _isNative is set to false.
## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use a special value to represent the native token, and validating that the xerc20 address matches this value when _isNative is true.

Using `.transfer` forwards 2300 gas which may not be enough if the recipient is a contract because the 2300 gas is only enough to emit an event. ` .transfer` forwards a fixed gas amount of 2300 with the assumption that it will prevent callbacks into the contract via reentrance to mitigate the reentrancy vulnerabilities. This is false as gas price aren't fixed and are subject to change.

Other occurrence of using `.transfer` and `.send` to send ETH 
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts%2FDelegation%2FOperatorDelegator.sol#L485

```solidity
        if (_withdrawRequest.collateralToken == IS_NATIVE) {
            payable(msg.sender).transfer(_withdrawRequest.amountToRedeem);
```
## Impact
`recoverNative` () will fail if the receiver is a contract and the gas price changes, if the gas price gets reduced it opens room for reentrance and if the gas price gets increased the transfer will fail as the forwarded gas won't be enough to complete the transaction.

if the `to` address isn't an EOA  but a contract the contract can call back(re-enter)into the contract if the gas price changes in a favourable way and drain the contract of the remaining Eth , or fail if the gas price changes in a non favourable way locking Eth in the contract.
## Proof of Concept
```solidity
function recoverNative(uint256 _amount, address _to) external onlyOwner {
//@audit - This forwards 2300 gas, which may not be enough if the recipient is a contract and gas costs change.
        payable(_to).transfer(_amount);
    }
```
The purpose of The `recoverNative` is to send back any ETH mistakenly sent to the contract or any ETH that fails to be brigded back to the respective sender the function can only be called by the` owner`, if the `to` address isn't an EOA  but a contract the contract can call back(re-enter)into the contract if the gas price changes in a favourable way and drain the contract of the remaining Eth , or fail if the gas price changes in a non favourable way locking Eth in the contract.

Manual Review

Use `.call` which forwards all available gas and include a non reentrancy modifier

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts%2FWithdraw%2FWithdrawQueue.sol#L242-L248


# Vulnerability details

When creating a `withdrawRequest ` a struct is created with the necessary information to be used when claiming, 
```solidity
   withdrawRequests[msg.sender].push(
            WithdrawRequest(
                _assetOut,
                withdrawRequestNonce,
                amountToRedeem,
                _amount,
                block.timestamp
            )
        );
```
This struct contains information such as the `_assetOut` `withdrawRequesutNonce` `amountToRedeem` _`amount` `block.timestamp`. 
The issue here is that when claiming the request creation time wasn't assigned to `createdAt` which is used to compare the cool down 
```solidity
if (block.timestamp - _withdrawRequest.createdAt < coolDownPeriod) revert EarlyClaim();
```
`createdAt` will default to zero allowing user withdraw immediately after the creation of withdraw request.

## Impact
Users are able to bypass coolDown allowing them to withdraw at anytime.

## Proof of Concept
Users that want to withdraw calls `witdraw` in the `witdrawQueue` contract which creates a withdrawal index for the user with a struct containing the time of creation which will later be used to compare the cool down, however the `block.timestamp` when the request index is created is not assigned to `createdAt`, the struct saves the time with the default `block.timestamp` .

```solidity
   withdrawRequests[msg.sender].push(
            WithdrawRequest(
                _assetOut,
                withdrawRequestNonce,
                amountToRedeem,
                _amount,
                block.timestamp
            )
        );
```
But when `claim` is called it compares the time with `createdAt` which doesn't belong in the struct and is effectively zero allowing the bypass of the cool down period
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts%2FWithdraw%2FWithdrawQueue.sol#L287
```solidity
if (block.timestamp - _withdrawRequest.createdAt < coolDownPeriod) revert EarlyClaim();
```
 because `createdAt` is zero, while `block.timestamp` will always be greater than `coolDownPeriod` 
```solidity
if (block.timestamp  < coolDownPeriod) revert EarlyClaim();
```
`createdAt` is zero, the cooldown period effectively gets bypassed, allowing users to withdraw immediately without waiting for any cooldown period.
## Tools Used
Manual Review 
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Assign `createdAt` to `block.timestamp` when the withdraw Request is created.

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L245-L250
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L289-L301
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L13
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L50-L57


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

```
As per docs and sponsor confirmation staleness only allowed up to 1 day only. 

```
Deposits are permitted using price data that is up to 2 days and 60 seconds old. This allowance for utilizing stale price information can lead to inaccuracies in deposit valuations, potentially resulting in overestimations or underestimations of user deposit amounts due to outdated price data. 

## Proof of Concept

```solidity
FILE: 2024-04-renzo/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol

// Fetch price and timestamp of ezETH from the configured price feed
        (uint256 _lastPrice, uint256 _lastPriceTimestamp) = getMintRate();

        // Verify the price is not stale
        if (block.timestamp > _lastPriceTimestamp + 1 days) {
            revert OraclePriceExpired();
        }

```

```solidity
FILE: 2024-04-renzo/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol

function getMintRate() public view returns (uint256, uint256) {
        // revert if PriceFeedNotAvailable
        if (receiver == address(0) && address(oracle) == address(0)) revert PriceFeedNotAvailable();
        if (address(oracle) != address(0)) {
            (uint256 oraclePrice, uint256 oracleTimestamp) = oracle.getMintRate();
            return
                oracleTimestamp > lastPriceTimestamp
                    ? (oraclePrice, oracleTimestamp)
                    : (lastPrice, lastPriceTimestamp);
        } else {
            return (lastPrice, lastPriceTimestamp);
        }
    }

```

```solidity
FILE: 2024-04-renzo/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle
/RenzoOracleL2.sol

13: uint256 public constant MAX_TIME_WINDOW = 86400 + 60; // 24 hours + 60 seconds


52: if (timestamp < block.timestamp - MAX_TIME_WINDOW) revert OraclePriceExpired();

```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L50-L57

### Explanation

Based on the current implementation, the oracle extends a freshness threshold of (timestamp < block.timestamp - MAX_TIME_WINDOW) ``1 day + 60 seconds``. Concurrently, the ``_deposit`` function performs its own check, verifying if the timestamp exceeds the last recorded price ``timestamp`` by more than a (block.timestamp > _lastPriceTimestamp + 1 days) ``1 day``. This dual-layer check functions correctly when using ``lastPrice`` and ``lastPriceTimestamp``. However, an issue arises when the price is directly fetched from the oracle (``oraclePrice`` and ``oracleTimestamp``). In this scenario, since the oracle already allows for a staleness of ``1 Day + 60 seconds``, and the ``_deposit`` function further allows an additional ``1 Day`` from the ``oracleTimestamp``, the system inadvertently accepts a price that could be up to ``2 days + 60 seconds old``, thus potentially compromising the accuracy and reliability of the price data used in transactions.

### Steps

This setup means that even though the Oracle first records a price as valid for 1 day and 60 seconds, the _deposit function extends this period by another day, thereby making the price potentially acceptable for up to 2 days + 60 seconds:

Original Oracle Timestamp: T
Price valid in Oracle until: T + 1 day + 60 seconds
Price potentially accepted in _deposit until: T + 1 day + 60 seconds + 1 day (T + 2 days + 60 seconds)

### POC 

Assume the current date and time is May 10, 2024, at 12:00 PM UTC. 

- Step 1: Oracle Timestamps the Price

Oracle Timestamp: May 8, 2024, at 11:59 AM UTC.
Oracle Price Valid Until: May 9, 2024, at 12:00 PM UTC + 60 seconds (i.e., May 9, 2024, at 12:01 PM UTC).

- Step 2: Deposit Function Checks for Staleness

The _deposit function retrieves the price at May 10, 2024, 12:00 PM UTC with the Oracle timestamp of May 8, 2024, at 11:59 AM UTC.

The function checks:
if (block.timestamp > _lastPriceTimestamp + 1 day)
In this case, if (May 10, 2024, 12:00 PM UTC > May 8, 2024, 11:59 AM UTC + 1 day)
This equates to if (May 10, 2024, 12:00 PM UTC > May 9, 2024, 11:59 AM UTC)
The price is still considered valid in the _deposit function up until May 9, 2024, 11:59 AM UTC + 1 day, which is May 10, 2024, 11:59 AM UTC.

Outcome:
The price is still acceptable for use in the _deposit function on May 10, 2024, at 12:00 PM, which is almost 2 days and 1 minute after the Oracle initially timestamped it. This scenario reveals that the price, although expired by the Oracle's definition, is still considered fresh by the _deposit function for an extra day.

## Tools Used
Manual Audit

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Remove (timestamp < block.timestamp - MAX_TIME_WINDOW) ``1 day + 60 minutes`` check from ``RenzoOracleL2`` oracle contract. Only check in the _deposit() function. So that this will applicable for both ``oraclePrice``, ``oracleTimestamp`` and ``lastPrice``,``lastPriceTimestamp`` values.







## Assessed type

Oracle

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L106
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L302


# Vulnerability details

EigenLayer Strategies can be updated, that's why Renzo have a `setTokenStrategy()` function, which allows setting & updating of the strategies:
```solidity
    function setTokenStrategy(IERC20 _token, IStrategy _strategy) external nonReentrant onlyOperatorDelegatorAdmin {
        if (address(_token) == address(0x0)) revert InvalidZeroInput();
        tokenStrategyMapping[_token] = _strategy;
        emit TokenStrategyUpdated(_token, _strategy);
    }
```
While updating the strategy, previous strategy's balance is not recorded. If there is update in strategy, `getTokenBalanceFromStrategy()` will reduce for the updated strategy's asset.  And as the `getTokenBalanceFromStrategy()` is used in the calculation of TVLs, the TotalTVL value will be decreased which will increase the ezETHAmountToMint.

## Proof of Concept
I'll use the `calculateMintAmount()` formula to proof the concept.
Consider this:
- Total TVL = 10_000 ethers (8000 ethers and 2000 stETH Tokens)
- NewValueAdded = 10
- ezETH TotalSupply = 9500
- ezETHMintAmount will be = `9499999999999999990`

But now admin updates the stETH strategy, 2000 stETH balance gone:
- Total TVL = 8000 ethers
- NewValueAdded = 10
- ezETH TotalSupply = 9500
- ezETHMintAmount will be = `11874999999999993353`

As the TVL drops, ezETHMintAmount increases.

I would encourage you to copy-paste this code in remix and play with different values to understand the depth of the issue:
```solidity
contract Calculate {
    uint256 constant SCALE_FACTOR = 10 ** 18;
    function calculateMintAmount(uint256 _currentValueInProtocol, uint256 _newValueAdded, uint256 _existingEzETHSupply) external pure returns (uint256) {
        uint256 inflationPercentaage = (SCALE_FACTOR * _newValueAdded * 10 ** 18) / (_currentValueInProtocol * 10 ** 18 + _newValueAdded * 10 ** 18);
        uint256 newEzETHSupply = (_existingEzETHSupply * 10 ** 18 * SCALE_FACTOR) / (SCALE_FACTOR - inflationPercentaage);
        uint256 mintAmount = newEzETHSupply - _existingEzETHSupply * 10 ** 18;
        return mintAmount;
    }
} 
```

## Impact
Wrong Calculation of `ezETH` minting amount

## Tools Used
[Shaheen's Jurat-e-Rayindana](https://twitter.com/0x_Shaheen/status/1722664258142650806)

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Whenever the strategy for the asset is being updated, the previous deposited amount for that strategy should be stored and taken into account while calculating `ezETH`'s amount to mint.

### Reference
Same issue was reported in C4's last LRT Protocol [Audit](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-11-kelp-findings/issues/197)


## Assessed type

Math

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `bridgeTo` function of the `LockboxAdapterBlast.sol` contract performs token transfers and approvals without checking the return values of the `SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom` and `SafeERC20.safeApprove` functions. Also, the `bridgeTo` function calls the deposit function on the Lockbox contract interface without proper checks on the return value. 
This oversight can lead to incomplete transactions, failed interactions with other contracts, and internal state inconsistencies, resulting in potential loss of user funds and unexpected contract behavior.

## Proof of Concept
The vulnerability arises in the `bridgeTo` function of the `LockboxAdapterBlast.sol` contract. Below are the relevant lines of code:

```
 SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom(IERC20(_erc20), msg.sender, address(this), _amount);
 SafeERC20.safeApprove(IERC20(_erc20), lockbox, _amount);
 IXERC20Lockbox(lockbox).deposit(_amount);
 SafeERC20.safeApprove(IERC20(xerc20), blastStandardBridge, _amount);
```
In all cases, the return values of the `safeTransferFrom`,`safeApprove` and `deposit` functions are not checked for success. This can lead to loss of funds if the token transfer or approval fails

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To mitigate this vulnerability, the following steps are recommended:

- Check Return Values: Ensure that return values of token transfer and approval functions are properly checked for success before proceeding with further actions.
- Implement Error Handling: Implement appropriate error handling mechanisms to revert the transaction or take corrective actions in case of failure.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol?plain=1#L473-L576


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `RestakeManager::deposit` function does not have any mechanisms in place to prevent malicious dust transactions that could cause legitimate transactions to revert. There are no explicit checks or limits on transaction sizes or amounts, which could lead to potential disruption of normal user transactions.

Malicious actors could submit dust transactions to the `RestakeManager` contract, with negligible amounts, to cause legitimate transactions to fail. Attackers could do this to every transaction. This will disrupt the normal operation of the protocol and negatively impact users. 


## Proof of Concept
A very common scenario:

Alice is a legitimate user of the protocol, who wants to deposit a large amount of tokens into the protocol to earn rewards. Bob, on the other hand, is a malicious actor who wants to disrupt Alice's transactions by leveraging the lack of dust transaction prevention in the protocol.

Step 1: Observe Alice's Pending Transactions
Bob closely monitors the mempool for any pending transactions submitted by Alice to the `RestakeManager` contract. He identifies Alice's large deposit transaction that is waiting to be included in a block.

Step 2: Front-run Alice's Transaction with Dust Transactions
Knowing that the `RestakeManager` contract does not have any mechanisms to prevent dust transactions, Bob quickly submits multiple small, malicious transactions to the contract, depositing negligible amounts of the same token that Alice is trying to deposit.

Step 3: Cause Alice's Legitimate Transaction to Revert
When Alice's large deposit transaction is processed, the `RestakeManager` contract will first execute Bob's dust transactions. Since the contract does not have any checks or limits on transaction sizes, these dust transactions will be accepted and processed.

However, the execution of the dust transactions can potentially cause the contract's internal state to become inconsistent or exceed certain limits (e.g., the maximum number of OperatorDelegators or collateral tokens). As a result, when Alice's legitimate, large deposit transaction is executed, it will revert due to the protocol's inability to handle the state changes caused by the malicious dust transactions.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement checks to prevent transactions with non-material amounts from affecting the contract's state or execution flow.






## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol?plain=1#L491-L576


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `deposit` function in `RestakeManager.sol` does not have any mechanisms in place to protect against replay attacks. Replay attacks occur when a valid transaction is maliciously repeated or copied to perform unauthorized actions. This vulnerability could allow an attacker to steal funds by replaying a victim's failed transactions.

Without proper replay attack protection, an attacker could potentially replay a victim's failed transactions to siphon funds from the protocol. This could lead to significant financial losses for the victims and undermine the overall security of the protocol.

## Proof of Concept

The attacker observes Alice, the victim, attempting to deposit tokens into the protocol using the `deposit()` function.

The attacker intercepts Alice's failed transaction and obtains the transaction data.

The attacker waits for a brief period, then resubmits the same transaction data to the `deposit()` function.

Since the protocol does not have any mechanisms to prevent replay attacks, the protocol will execute the transaction again, effectively draining Alice's funds.

The attacker can repeat this process until Alice's entire balance is drained from the protocol.

The attacker can do this over and over to any and all users.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement nonce-based or other mechanisms to ensure that each transaction can only be executed once, preventing replay attacks.








## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol?plain=1#L168-L191


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the `xRenzoDeposit.sol` smart contract, the `depositETH` function is not equipped with any safeguards against replay attacks. Replay attacks involve the malicious duplication of a legitimate transaction, which can lead to unauthorized actions being performed. This vulnerability could potentially enable an attacker to steal funds by re-enacting a transaction that initially failed for the victim.

This `depositETH` function lacks safeguards against replay attacks, and an adversary could exploit this vulnerability by repeating a user's unsuccessful transactions. This malicious activity could result in substantial monetary losses for the victims and jeopardize the security framework of the protocol. The financial impact can be significant, as an attacker can potentially steal large amounts of user funds by exploiting this vulnerability across multiple victims.

## Proof of Concept

The attacker observes Alice, the victim, attempting to deposit ETH into the protocol using the `depositETH()` function.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol?plain=1#L101-L157


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `initialize()` function in the `RestakeManager` contract is marked as public initializer, which allows any account to call this function before the intended deployer.

Manipulation of Role Assignments:

The attacker can set the `IRoleManager` contract address to one they control, effectively granting themselves the "restake manager admin" and "deposit/withdraw pauser" roles.
This would give the attacker the ability to call the following admin-only functions:

setPaused(bool _paused): The attacker can pause or unpause the deposit and withdrawal functionality, potentially freezing user funds.

addOperatorDelegator(IOperatorDelegator _newOperatorDelegator, uint256 _allocationBasisPoints): The attacker can add new operator delegators to the protocol and set their allocations, potentially diverting user funds.

removeOperatorDelegator(IOperatorDelegator _operatorDelegatorToRemove): The attacker can remove legitimate operator delegators, disrupting the protocol's functionality.

setOperatorDelegatorAllocation(IOperatorDelegator _operatorDelegator, uint256 _allocationBasisPoints): The attacker can adjust the allocation of operator delegators, potentially diverting user funds.

setMaxDepositTVL(uint256 _maxDepositTVL): The attacker can set the maximum deposit TVL, limiting user participation in the protocol, or increasing it to infinity.

addCollateralToken(IERC20 _newCollateralToken) and removeCollateralToken(IERC20 _collateralToken): The attacker can add or remove supported collateral tokens, disrupting the protocol's functionality.


Disruption of Protocol Functionality:

The attacker can set the `IEzEthToken`, `IRenzoOracle`, `IStrategyManager`, `IDelegationManager`, and `IDepositQueue` contract addresses to ones they control, effectively hijacking the protocol's core functionality.
This would allow the attacker to manipulate token minting and burning, pricing mechanisms, delegation management, and the deposit/withdrawal process, leading to significant financial losses for users.


Disabling Protocol Pausing:

The attacker can set the paused state to false, preventing the protocol from being paused in the future, even by legitimate admins.
This would make it more difficult to mitigate any issues or attacks on the protocol.


## Proof of Concept

The attacker observes the deployment of the RestakeManager contract and quickly calls the `initialize()` function before the intended deployer.

The attacker sets the `IRoleManager` contract address to one they control, effectively granting themselves the "restake manager admin" and "deposit/withdraw pauser" roles.

The attacker can now call the admin-only functions mentioned above to manipulate the protocol's state, add malicious operator delegators, adjust TVL limits, and disrupt the overall functionality of the `RestakeManager` contract.

Users attempting to interact with the protocol will be subject to the attacker's manipulations, potentially leading to the loss of their funds or disruption of their expected interactions.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use the factory pattern to allow only the factory to call the initializer or ensure it is not front-runnable by calling `initialize` directly in the deploy script.



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol?plain=1#L193-L236


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
(I am reuploading this vulnerability because I accidently withdrew the previous one when I went to update it.)

The `queueWithdrawals` function in the `OperatorDelegator` contract contains an unbounded loop that iterates through the entire array of tokens and token amounts. If the array is large, it can consume a significant amount of gas, which can lead to a Denial-of-Service (DoS) condition.

An Admin can provide a large array of tokens and/or token amounts when calling the `queueWithdrawals` function, causing the transaction to consume an excessive amount of gas. This can result in the transaction exceeding the block gas limit and reverting, making the contract unusable or blocking other transactions from being processed. As a result, the protocol's functionality and availability can be disrupted. 

The Admin does not have to be malicious, an admin can be benevolent and still accidently trigger the Denial of service if the arrays added are too large.

## Impact
The `_ccipReceive` function in the `CCIPReceiver.sol` contract does not have any mechanism to validate the origin of the CCIP message, leaving it vulnerable to replay attacks across different chains.

The `_ccipReceive` function has two checks, which are:
`if (_ccipSender != xRenzoBridgeL1) revert InvalidSender(xRenzoBridgeL1, _ccipSender);` -  checks if the _ccipSender is the same as the xRenzoBridgeL1 address to verify the sender.

and `if (_ccipSourceChainSelector != ccipEthChainSelector)
revert InvalidSourceChain(ccipEthChainSelector, _ccipSourceChainSelector);` - checks if the _ccipSourceChainSelector matches the ccipEthChainSelector to verify the source chain.

These checks are a good start, but they are not sufficient to fully protect against replay attacks across different chains.

The key issue is that these checks only verify the origin of the message on the current chain. They do not provide any protection against a valid message being replayed on a different chain.

For example, an attacker could intercept a valid CCIP message on one chain, and then replay that same message on a different chain, where the `_ccipSender` and `_ccipSourceChainSelector` would still pass the checks, even though the origin is different.

An attacker could intercept a valid CCIP message on one chain and replay it on a different chain, resulting in unauthorized actions, such as updating the price feed for their benefit or triggering other sensitive operations. Bob then replays the CCIP message on chain B, where the `CCIPReceiver` contract is also deployed.

Since the `_ccipReceive` function does not validate the origin of the message, it will execute the price update without any checks, allowing Bob to potentially manipulate the price feed.

Implement a mechanism to validate the origin of the CCIP message, such as using a nonce or a chain ID.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `sendPrice` function in the `xRenzoBridge.sol` contract is responsible for sending the current price of `ezETH` to the L2 contracts, such as the `CCIPReceiver.sol` and `ConnextReceiver.sol`. This function is marked as `onlyPriceFeedSender`, which means only authorized entities with the `onlyPriceFeedSender` role can call it.

However, despite this role-based access control, the function is still vulnerable to front-running attacks. The issue arises due to the nature of the Ethereum blockchain, where transactions are processed in the order of the highest gas price, rather than the order in which they were submitted.

The exploitation of this vulnerability can have severe consequences:

The attacker can manipulate the price feed, undermining the integrity of the entire cross-chain functionality.

Users who mint `xezETH` tokens based on the manipulated price feed can receive an incorrect, inflated amount of tokens, leading to financial losses.

Attackers can manipulate price feed with flashloans to deposit a smaller amount of assets and receive a larger amount of `xezETH` tokens, effectively stealing funds from other users.

## Proof of Concept
The authorized `onlyPriceFeedSender` entity, such as the `xRenzoBridge` contract, submits a transaction to call the `sendPrice` function and update the price feed.

An attacker, Bob, observes the pending transaction and quickly obtains a large amount of ETH through a flash loan.

Bob submits his own transaction to call the `sendPrice` function, with a higher gas price than the authorized transaction.

Bob's transaction, being processed first, can manipulate the price data before it is sent to the `CCIPReceiver.sol` and `ConnextReceiver.sol` contracts.

Bob can then use the manipulated price feed to deposit a smaller amount of assets and receive an inflated amount of `xezETH` tokens, effectively stealing funds from other users.

Bob can withdraw the xezETH tokens and repay the flash loan, keeping the profit.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement anti-front-running measures, such as a commit-reveal scheme or the use of a decentralized oracle network, to make it more difficult for attackers to front-run the authorized price feed updates.

The user receives the slightly lower amount of xezETH tokens due to the rounding error.

The user deposits another 1 ETH, and the rounding error is repeated, further compounding the issue.

Over multiple deposits, the rounding errors can accumulate, leading to users receiving a significantly lower amount of xezETH tokens than expected.

Manual Review

Implement Precise Arithmetic: Replace the integer division in the xezETH amount calculation with a more precise arithmetic mechanism, such as using a decimal library or fixed-point math, to minimize rounding errors.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Factory.sol?plain=1#L147
