# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L265


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`OperatorDelegator.completeQueuedWithdrawal()` perform an external call to [delegationManager](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/15b679b08e7a3589ff83a5e84076ca4e0a00ec0b/src/contracts/core/DelegationManager.sol#L305) contract which finalize any queued withdrawals initiated by the operatorDelegator. This function passes `receiveAsToken` parameter `true`, so the podOwnerShares in EigenPodManager/StrategyManager will be redeemable for the underlying token. 

If the withdrawal is from the [beaconChainETHStrategy](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/15b679b08e7a3589ff83a5e84076ca4e0a00ec0b/src/contracts/core/DelegationManager.sol#L750-L755), it processes a transfer of the amount of beacon chain ETH to the `withdrawer`(i.e. operatorDelegator), which causes the `nonReentrant` check to be triggered for the [second time](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L501). The txn reverts and any queued withdrawal from the stategies cannot be completed further. 

## Proof of Concept
Step-by-step execution flow,
1. NativeEthRestakeAdmin call `OperatorDelegator.queueWithdrawals()` making a full or partial withdrawal from the beacon chain, note the `withdrawer` is the OperatorDelegator itself
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L228-L229

2. Before the withdrawal can be completed, podOwner call the permissionless `EigenPod.verifyAndProcessWithdrawal` function to prove that a withdrawal occured on the beacon chain, 
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L414

3. After the delay has been passed, the nativeEthRestakeAdmin call `completeQueuedWithdrawal()` to finalize the withdrawal, also where the first time reentrancy guard activates(marks `_status = _ENTERED`) 

```solidity
        // complete the queued withdrawal from EigenLayer with receiveAsToken set to true
        delegationManager.completeQueuedWithdrawal(withdrawal, tokens, middlewareTimesIndex, true);
```
4. Since the `receiveAsTokens==true`, the delegationManager `withdrawSharesAsTokens` via the `EigenPodManager`,
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/15b679b08e7a3589ff83a5e84076ca4e0a00ec0b/src/contracts/core/DelegationManager.sol#L751

5. `EigenPodManager` checks for any ETH deficit, and updates the amount accordingly. Finally, the `EigenPod.withdrawRestakedBeaconChainETH()` is called, to `_sendETH` to the `withdrawer` address. 
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/15b679b08e7a3589ff83a5e84076ca4e0a00ec0b/src/contracts/pods/EigenPod.sol#L424C14-L424C44

6. `receive()` function on the `withdrawer`(i.e. OperatorDelegator) will be triggered to the ETH transfer. Since this function is also guarded by the `nonReentrant` modifier, the _status won't be `_NOT_ENTERED` anymore. 

Consequently, the entire withdrawal transaction will revert due to a unexpected reentrancy.

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Remove `nonReentrant` modifer from the `receive()` function. 


## Assessed type

Reentrancy

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L293-L297


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `getMintRate()` returns the ezETH price which is used to calculate the xezETH amount to mint to the depositor. This function uses **CCIPReceiver** which get collateral price directly from L1 and also another oracle price feed(which is generally our **RenzoOracleL2** contract). 

Amoung the two price feed, the `getMintRate()` returns the most recently updated price of ezETH,

*File: xRenzoDeposit.sol*
```solidity
function getMintRate() public view returns (uint256, uint256) {
    ...snip...	
    if (address(oracle) != address(0)) {
        (uint256 oraclePrice, uint256 oracleTimestamp) = oracle.getMintRate();
        // @audit-info its using the most recently updated price below 
        return
            oracleTimestamp > lastPriceTimestamp
                ? (oraclePrice, oracleTimestamp)
                : (lastPrice, lastPriceTimestamp);
    } else {
        return (lastPrice, lastPriceTimestamp);
    }
}
```
However, the issue is if either of oracle hardcoded the lastTimestamp to current `block.timestamp`, the `getMintRate()` will always return the price corresponding to that price feed. Currently, the one of the affected token is `wBETH`. 

Here is the oracle contract for wBETH used by RenzoOracleL2(further used by `xRenzoDeposit` contract as second price feed). It can be seen here that the `latestRoundData()` internally call `_getWBETHData()` which harcoded the updatedAt to `block.timestamp`.
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Oracle/Binance/WBETHShim.sol#L12 


As an impact, if the price diverge by more than 10%, then `xRenzoDeposit` contract will reflect those price during minting of the xezETH token, which could possibly be avoided if the price from `CCIPReceiver` contract was used, as it has the in-built check for price divergence. 

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L293
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L51

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use RenzoOracleL2 as a backup price feed, in case something bad happen with CCIPReceived price, the `updatePriceByOwner()` could mitigate the pricing problem,

Oracle

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The price of ezETH is susceptible to manipulation, which can result in user losses or prevent deposits to L2.

## Proof of Concept

The calculation formula for the price of ezETH is `totalTVL / totalSupply`. If the totalTVL increases, it will cause the price of ezETH to rise. Attackers can initiate donation attacks on the WithdrawQueue, causing totalTVL to increase while totalSupply remains unchanged, resulting in a rapid increase in the price of ezETH.

For the L2 deposit contract `xRenzoDeposit`, if the price fluctuates by more than 10%, it is considered invalid. Therefore, users can control the price of ezETH through donation attacks and make a profit of 10% or prevent L2 from accepting normal deposits.


https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RateProvider/BalancerRateProvider.sol#L28-L41

Manual Review

There isn't a great solution to this problem, but when there's a significant price change, perhaps we could try using 110% of the previous price.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L121-L149


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Deposits are vulnerable to inflation attacks, resulting in user losses.

## Proof of Concept

The formula for calculating the shares received by a user upon deposit is: `totalSupply(share) / (1 - (deltaAsset/(totalAsset+deltaAsset))) - totalSupply(share)`. 

However, in reality, this formula is equivalent to: `deltaAsset * SupplyShare / totalAsset`.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L121-L149

Therefore, if a user donates to Withdraw, causing the totalAsset price to rise, this will result in the next user receiving significantly fewer shares than expected upon deposit, leading to losses.

Proof of Concept (PoC):

1. User B wants to deposit 100,000 tokens.
2. User A discovers B's transaction to deposit 100,000 tokens in the mempool and deposits 1 token first, obtaining 1 share.
3. User A then donates 49,999 tokens to the WithdrawQueue contract.
4. The share calculation for User B's deposit of 100,000 tokens is: 1 / (1 - (100,000 / (50,000 + 100,000))) - 1 => 2.999999 - 1 = 1.
5. User A withdraws 75,000 tokens.



## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add minShare parameter.


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L290-L309


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

completeQueuedWithdrawal cannot run properly and, in severe cases, may result in an inability to withdraw funds correctly.

## Proof of Concept

When OperatorDelegator withdraws funds, it first calls `queueWithdrawals` and then `completeQueuedWithdrawal`. However, when `completeQueuedWithdrawal` is called, a portion of the withdrawn amount is sent to the WithdrawQueue contract, and the remaining amount is deposited back into the strategy manager.

During this process, when depositing into the strategy manager, the calculation of shares is also performed based on the deposited amount. However, if the `tokenAmount` is too small, the calculated shares will be 0, causing the entire transaction to revert.

The deposit process into `strategyManager.depositIntoStrategy` is as follows:

`strategyManager.depositIntoStrategy -> _depositIntoStrategy -> StrategyBase.deposit` 

https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/15b679b08e7a3589ff83a5e84076ca4e0a00ec0b/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L323-L342

`depositIntoStrategy` calls the strategy, but all strategies inherit from `StrategyBase`, and the deposit implementation in `StrategyBase` is as follows:

https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/15b679b08e7a3589ff83a5e84076ca4e0a00ec0b/src/contracts/strategies/StrategyBase.sol#L96-L123

The calculation for `newShare` is: `amount * virtualShareAmount / virtualPriorTokenBalance`. If `newShare` is 0, it will revert.

The reason for a too-small `tokenAmount` is that some amount is transferred to the WithdrawQueue contract, and the remaining amount may not be enough to generate 1 share in the strategy manager, causing `completeQueuedWithdrawal` to fail to run properly.

In severe cases, when only `completeQueuedWithdrawal` can provide funds for the WithdrawQueue to withdraw, users' funds will be stuck in the contract. The only way to withdraw is to send funds to the contract, but this will also result in some loss of funds.

Therefore this will result in core functionality not functioning properly

poc :

EigenLayer deployment address information:

https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts?tab=readme-ov-file#deployments

https://etherscan.io/address/0x93c4b944D05dfe6df7645A86cd2206016c51564D

can verify using the `underlyingToSharesView` function of the on-chain StrategyBase contract. If the input amount is 1 and the return value is 0, the transaction will fail because it does not meet the following conditions.

```solidity
require(newShares != 0, "StrategyBase.deposit: newShares cannot be zero");
```

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

It is recommended to use similar logic to ETH when re-depositing

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L565-L569


# Vulnerability details



## Impact
Standard inflation attack. First depositor can steal funds from subsequent depositors.

## Proof of Concept
In `RestakeManager.deposit()` the [amount of ezETH to mint](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L565-L569) is calculated by [`RenzoOracle.calculateMintAmount()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L123-L149). While written on a novel form this calculation simplifies to the standard `mintAmount = _existingEzETHSupply * _newValueAdded / _currentValueInProtocol` (albeit with the occasional extra wei rounding down; consider simplifying this). [`mintAmount == 0` reverts](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L146) so the best we can do for profit is to round down from `2` to `1`. That is, if we deposit one wei so `_existingEzETHSupply = 1`, and then inflate `_currentValueInProtocol` to half the next depositor's `_newValueAdded` (because of the extra rounding mentioned above we can inflate to exactly half rather than `1` above half). This can be done by [a direct transfer of tokens](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L319) or [ETH](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L352). Then `mintAmount` will be rounded down from a theoretical just below `2` to `1` and the next depositor thus receives only half the shares needed to represent his deposit. The attacker can then withdraw his share (out of a total two shares) of all deposited value (three times the donated amount), i.e. 1.5 times his investment. This is locked in on calling `WithdrawQueue.withdraw()` so the timeout period has no effect on the feasibility of this attack, except that the attacker will have to wait to receive the funds.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider making an initial deposit on deployment. Note that the inflation attack can also be used to DoS subsequent depositors and does not need to target a specific depositor, so the protective deposit must be atomic with or prior to deployment to preclude this.


## Assessed type

ERC4626

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L246
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L299-L309


# Vulnerability details



## Impact
Claiming withdrawals may change the ezETH price. This can be used extract profit from the protocol, at the cost of other holders.

## Proof of Concept
The price of ezETH is essentially `TVL / totalSupply`, i.e. depositing `d` worth of collateral will mint `d * totalSupply / TVL` ezETH ([`RenzoOracle.calculateMintAmount()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L123-L149)). When requesting to withdraw `w` ezETH the reverse calculation is made, i.e. `w * TVL / totalSupply` ([`RenzoOracle.calculateRedeemAmount()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L152-L164)). [These values are set at the time of the withdrawal request](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L217-L224), such that the amount of collateral token and amount of ezETH to burn are fixed. [Only later upon `claim()` are the tokens transferred and the ezETH burned](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L299-L309).

The values used in the deposit calculation are also not affected by any pending withdrawals, but the [current TVL](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L302-L321) and the [current ezETH supply](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L568) are used.

Suppose the value of the collateral token to be withdrawn has deviated from the average collateral value, i.e. the price of ezETH, since the withdrawal request was made. If it is greater than the average then upon `claim()` correspondingly more value will be removed from the TVL than ezETH burned from the total supply, and the price of ezETH will decrease. Conversely, if the value of the collateral token has become less than the average of the collateral values then the price of ezETH will increase.

This can be abused in all kinds of ways. It gives an attacker some measure of control over the price of ezETH. He can make withdrawal requests and then choose to claim them such that the price is manipulated in his favour, depending on the integrations with Renzo. The attacker can frontrun another claim (not necessarily his own) with a deposit such that he experiences an immediate profit from the price movement.

For example, let's say `2` ezETH has been minted against `1` tokA and `1` tokB, and that all current prices are `1`. Suppose `0.5` ezETH is requested to be withdrawn against tokA. This will schedule the burning of `0.5` ezETH and the transfer of `0.5` tokA. Suppose then the price of tokA increases to `1.1` and the price of tokB increases to `1.25`. Before `claim()` the price of ezETH is `(1.1 + 1.25) / 2 = 1.175`, but after `claim()` the price would be `(0.55 + 1.25) / 1.5 = 1.2`. Now, if an attacker deposits `1` ETH's worth (of any token) just before `claim()` is called, he will receive `1 / 1.175 ≈ 0.8512` ezETH. After `claim()` the price will then be `(0.55 + 1.25 + 1) / 2.3512 ≈ 1.1910`. Immediately withdrawing this again would give him `0.8512 * 1.1910 ≈ 1.014` ETH worth of collateral.
Note that by sandwiching the `claim()` with a deposit and withdrawal the attacker was able to reduce the price of ezETH (up to future additional price changes) and extract a profit.
The more volatile the collateral tokens, and especially if they move in opposite directions, the more profit can be extracted.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider calculating the amount of collateral token to be transferred at the time of `claim()` instead. It could then be possible to also choose which token to withdraw from in `claim()`. That is, a withdraw request would simply be a request to withdraw an amount of ezETH, with the rest to be decided upon `claim()`.


## Assessed type

MEV

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L507
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L229


# Vulnerability details



## Impact
A discrepancy in oracle price deviation between two assets can be exploited for arbitrage; one can deposit the relatively overvalued asset and withdraw for the relatively undervalued asset.

## Proof of Concept
The price of ezETH is based on a sum of oracle prices of multiple assets. The oracles will be slightly inaccurate; in the case of the Chainlink stETH/ETH feed the deviation threshold [is 0.5%](https://data.chain.link/feeds/ethereum/mainnet/steth-eth), which means that it may be up to 0.5% more or less than the true price.
[The deposit is valued according to the oracle price](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L507), and [so is the amount of tokens received on withdrawal](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L229).

Suppose `2000` ezETH has been minted against `1000` tokA and `1000` tokB, and that the current true prices of tokA and tokB are `1`. However, suppose the oracle returns a price of tokA as `1.005` and of tokB as `0.997`. This means that ezETH will be priced at `(1005 + 997) / 2000 = 1.001` An attacker can exploit this by depositing tokA and withdrawing tokB. Suppose the attacker buys `100` tokA for `100` ETH (according to its true price) and deposits this. This will be valued as `100 * 1.005 = 100.5` ETH by the oracle and he will get `100.5 / 1.001 ≈ 100.4` ezETH. (This does not change the price of ezETH.) If he then immediately withdraws the ezETH, but now for tokB, he will get a value of `100.4 * 1.001 = 100.5` ETH, which in tokB is–according to the oracle–`100.5 / 0.997 ≈ 100.8` tokB, which is also truly worth `100.8` ETH.
The attacker was thus able to acquire `100.8` ETH worth of tokB by depositing only `100` ETH worth of tokA.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Note that this attack depends on a differential deviation between assets. It would not work if there was only one asset, or if they deviate identically.
The maximum extractable value in percentage is the maximum possible deviation between any two assets. Consider eliminating the profitability of this attack by taking exactly this percentage as a fee on either deposit of withdrawal, e.g. if the deviation threshold of tokA is 0.5% and of tokB is 0.3% then charge a 0.8% fee. This fee might either be taken by the protocol or just implemented as a reduced amount of ezETH minted or tokens withdrawn, effectively returning it to other holders.


## Assessed type

MEV

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L76
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L93


# Vulnerability details

There will be a guarantee of stale price due to the hardcoded `uint256 constant MAX_TIME_WINDOW = 86400 + 60; // 24 hours + 60 seconds`. This mean that pricefeed checks only if the pricefeed is updated 1 day ago instead of the respective token's heartbeat duration.

The heartbeat duration for [STETH/ETH is 24 hour](https://data.chain.link/feeds/ethereum/mainnet/steth-eth)
The heartbeat duration for [BETH/USD is 15 Minutes](https://data.chain.link/feeds/bsc/mainnet/beth-usd)
The heartbeat duration for [ezETH/ETH is 24 hour](https://data.chain.link/feeds/ethereum/mainnet/ezeth-eth)


The staled price from [bots-automation](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/4naly3er-report.md#m-6-chainlinks-latestrounddata-might-return-stale-or-incorrect-results) reasoning from stale price is completely different from my report, hence the submission of issue.

## Impact
Staled data due to wrong update timestamp check.

## Proof of Concept
```solidity
        if (timestamp < block.timestamp - MAX_TIME_WINDOW) revert OraclePriceExpired();
```

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ensure that latest heartbeat duration is based on token's actual heartbeat from Chainlink.

Allow admin to set gas price via a mutator method.

The `WithdrawalQueue::withdraw()` and `WithdrawalQueue::claim()` did not enforce the Openzeppelins `whenNotPaused` modifier. This means that if the admin were to call the `WithdrawalQueue::pause()`, it does not affect the withdraw flow. ```

--    function claim(uint256 withdrawRequestIndex) external nonReentrant {

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L300
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L137


# Vulnerability details

Renzo has a buffer that acts as a pool of assets to support withdrawal requests. There is a need for buffer in order to support withdrawal of assets.

The withdrawQueue contract get filled by 3 ways -> 
1) New Deposits
2) Daily Rewards Coming in the Protocol.
3) Manual withdrawal from EigenLayer. Permissioned call from OperatorDelegator.

If options 1 and 2 are not sufficient to fulfill withdraw requests of Users then admin accounts will manually unstake from EigenLayer through 2 step process: 
1) OperatorDelegator.queueWithdrawals
2) OperatorDelegator.completeWithdrawals

```solidity
// OperatorDelegator.sol
    function completeQueuedWithdrawal(
        IDelegationManager.Withdrawal calldata withdrawal,
        IERC20[] calldata tokens,
        uint256 middlewareTimesIndex
    ) external nonReentrant onlyNativeEthRestakeAdmin {
    -- SNIP --
                    restakeManager.depositQueue().fillERC20withdrawBuffer( //@audit
                        address(tokens[i]),
                        bufferToFill
                    );
    -- SNIP --
```
The `fillERC20withdrawBuffer` is called to fill up ERC20 withdraw buffer. However the function call will revert because that function required to be called by the restake manager admin. In Renzo, each and every roles are unique and have their own functionalities to perform.  This means that whenever there is a need to fill up the buffer, the 3rd option will not be able to do so, bricking the protocol if there isn't enough assets to cover the withdrawal requests.

Furthermore, the Operator will not be able to unstake delegated funds from Eigenlayer. [Assets remain frozen due to the inability to complete the steps required for withdrawal.](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/docs/core/DelegationManager.md#undelegating-and-withdrawing)

```solidity
// DepositQueue.sol
    /// @dev Allows only the RestakeManager address to call functions
    modifier onlyRestakeManager() {
        if (msg.sender != address(restakeManager)) revert NotRestakeManager();
        _;
    }

    function fillERC20withdrawBuffer(
        address _asset,
        uint256 _amount
    ) external nonReentrant onlyRestakeManager { //@audit
    -- SNIP --
```
## Impact
1) Buffer will never be filled in the case of supporting withdrawal requests.
2) Operator unable to unstake delegated assets from Eigenlayer, causing assets to be frozen.

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Remove the access control for only restake manager, leaving the function similar to a donation function.
```diff
    function fillERC20withdrawBuffer(
        address _asset,
        uint256 _amount
--    ) external nonReentrant onlyRestakeManager {
++    ) external nonReentrant {
```


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L355


# Vulnerability details

Delegated staking protocols may be exposed to a [known vulnerability](https://ethresear.ch/t/deposit-contract-exploit/6528), where a malicious operator front-runs a staker’s deposit call to the Beacon chain deposit contract and provides a different withdrawal credentials. This issue impacts Reno as well.

## Impact
Even though operators are trusted by the DAO, there's a risk associated with incoming ETH deposits potentially reaching the ETH_DEPOSIT_SOFT_CAP of 3200 ETH. This sizable amount could serve as a strong incentive for an operator to turn malicious and execute an attack, with the cost of the attack being only 1 ETH per validator.

In practice, incoming deposits could surpass the soft cap, possibly in multiples of 3200 ETH. This scenario could unfold if several rebalances are initiated without delay, allowing for the depositing of all the ETH within a few blocks.

Should such an attack occur, all deposited funds would be lost.

This vulnerability also affected several LST/LRT protocols, see [Lido](https://research.lido.fi/t/mitigations-for-deposit-front-running-vulnerability/1239) and [EtherFi](https://246895607-files.gitbook.io/~/files/v0/b/gitbook-x-prod.appspot.com/o/spaces%2FG3Lk76lfvw9ecPIg0mK8%2Fuploads%2FFgdNivH2FNNe7JwkZXtd%2FNM0093-FINAL-ETHER-FI.pdf?alt=media&token=5aa1a2dc-33c7-430d-a2cb-59f56d2cfd2b) reports.
## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L355
```solidity
        eigenPodManager.stake{ value: msg.value }(pubkey, signature, depositDataRoot);
```

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The Lido discussion thoroughly explores potential solutions. My suggestions are:

To ensure that validator key entries submitted by a node operator are approved by the DAO, require the operator to deposit 1 ETH, along with the correct protocol-controlled WC, for each public key used in these deposit data entries. Upon approval of the validator keys, refund the operator the deposited 1 ETH.

Alternatively, emulate Lido's approach by establishing a committee of guardians tasked with monitoring the deposit contract and issuing a signed off-chain message to authorize deposits.

Rio should also consider measures to reduce incentives for malicious operator behavior, such as:
1) Limiting the maximum ETH deposit amount per transaction.
2) Implementing a brief delay between rebalances, even if the soft cap is reached, to prevent the chaining of rebalances for depositing a large amount of ETH.


## Assessed type

Token-Transfer

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Lockbox.sol#L131
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Lockbox.sol#L125-L136


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
There is an unprotected call to a function sending Ether to an arbitrary address, this line [(bool _success, ) = payable(_to).call{ value: _amount }("");](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Lockbox.sol#L131) sends Ether to the address specified by the `_to` variable, which is not validated or checked in any way. An attacker could potentially drain the contract's funds by calling the `_withdraw` function with a malicious address.

### Vulnerability & Description
The function takes two inputs:

 * `_to`: the address to which the funds will be sent
 * `_amount`: the amount of funds to be sent

It performs the following steps:

1. Emits a Withdraw event with the `_to` address and `_amount`
2. Burns the specified `_amount` of tokens from the sender's balance using `XERC20.burn(msg.sender, _amount)`
3. If `IS_NATIVE` is true, sends Ether to the `_to` address using `payable(_to).call{ value: _amount }("")`
4. If `IS_NATIVE` is false, transfers ERC20 tokens to the `_to` address using `ERC20.safeTransfer(_to, _amount)`

The [(bool _success, ) = payable(_to).call{ value: _amount }("");](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Lockbox.sol#L131), which sends Ether to the `_to` address without any validation or checks allows an attacker to drain the contract's funds by calling the `_withdraw` function with a malicious address.

The call function is used to send Ether to the `_to` address, which can lead to a reentrancy attack. If the `_to` address is a contract, it can execute a fallback function, which can call the `_withdraw` function, potentially draining the contract's funds.

## Proof of Concept
The function's behavior deviates from the expected outcome, as it allows an attacker to manipulate the `_to` address and drain the contract's funds.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Lockbox.sol#L125-L136

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use the **transfer** function instead of **call** to send Ether, as it includes additional security measures to prevent reentrancy attacks. Validate and sanitize the `_to` address to ensure it is a legitimate recipient.

Use the address **payable** type instead of **address** to ensure that the `_to` address is a payable address.

```solidity
// Vulnerable code
(bool _success, ) = payable(_to).call{ value: _amount }("");

// Mitigated code
_to.transfer(_amount);
```


## Assessed type

Reentrancy

title: TimelockController's `isOperationDone` function could lead to reentrancy attacks.
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/TimelockController.sol#L176-L178
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/TimelockController.sol#L32
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/TimelockController.sol#L177
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/TimelockController.sol#L327


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
This is vulnerable to readonly-reentrancy function (if read in other function) [TimelockController.isOperationDone(bytes32)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/TimelockController.sol#L176-L178) 
```solidity
    function isOperationDone(bytes32 id) public view virtual returns (bool) {
        return getTimestamp(id) == _DONE_TIMESTAMP;
    }
```
State variables read that were written after the external call(s):
- TimelockController._timestamps
[(contracts/TimelockController.sol#32)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/TimelockController.sol#L32) was read at `getTimestamp(id) == _DONE_TIMESTAMP`
[(contracts/TimelockController.sol#177)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/TimelockController.sol#L177) This variable was written at (after external call):
- _afterCall(id) ([contracts/TimelockController.sol#327](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/TimelockController.sol#L327))

The issue is that the function reads the `_timestamps` state variable, which is written to after an external call, if another function calls `isOperationDone` and then modifies the `_timestamps` variable, it could potentially cause a reentrancy vulnerability.

Here's a breakdown of the issue:

  * `isOperationDone` function checks if an operation is done by checking if the timestamp for that operation is equal to the `_DONE_TIMESTAMP` ([line 177](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/TimelockController.sol#L177)).
  * The `_timestamps` variable is read in the `getTimestamp` function ([line 177](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/TimelockController.sol#L177)), which is a separate function that retrieves the timestamp for a given ID.
  * However, the `_timestamps` variable is written to in the `_afterCall` function ([line 327](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/TimelockController.sol#L327)), which is called after an external call.

If an attacker can call a function that modifies the `_timestamps` variable after the external call, they could potentially re-enter the `isOperationDone` function and cause unintended behavior.

## Proof of Concept
In a scenario where an attacker Creates a user account (e.g., attacker) and a target contract (e.g., TargetContract) that will interact with the TimelockController contract.

  * Call the execute function on the TimelockController contract with the attacker account, passing in the target contract's address, a value, payload, predecessor, and salt. This will trigger the `_afterCall` function, which writes to the `_timestamps` variable.
```solidity
contract.execute(targetContract, 0, payload, predecessor, salt);
```
  * Immediately call the `isOperationDone` function with the same `id` parameter used in the execute function. This will read the `_timestamps` variable, which was just modified.
```solidity
bool isDone = contract.isOperationDone(id);
```
**Expected behavior:** The `isOperationDone` function should return false, as the operation has not yet been marked as done.

**Actual behavior:** Due to the reentrancy vulnerability, the `isOperationDone` function returns true, indicating that the operation is done, even though it has not been marked as done.

With the `isOperationDone` function returning true, the attacker can now exploit this behavior to manipulate the contract's logic. For example, they can call the TargetContract's functions, thinking that the operation is done, while in reality, it has not been marked as done.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ensure that the `_timestamps` variable is not modified after the external call, or to use a different approach to check if an operation is done. Use a separate mapping to store the operation status instead of relying on the `_timestamps` variable.
```solidity
mapping(bytes32 => bool) private _operationStatus;

function isOperationDone(bytes32 id) public view virtual returns (bool) {
    return _operationStatus[id];
}
```
Alternatively, use the `block.timestamp` directly in the `isOperationDone` function to avoid relying on the `_timestamps` variable.
```solidity
function isOperationDone(bytes32 id) public view virtual returns (bool) {
    return block.timestamp == _DONE_TIMESTAMP;
}
```


## Assessed type

Reentrancy

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L204-L217
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L227-L271


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The deposit and _deposit functions in the xRenzoDeposit contract show discrepancies in the recorded and actual amounts of tokens handled. The issue arises because the `Deposit` event logs the original amount of tokens transferred (`_amountIn`) prior to the deduction of the bridge fee, meaning that the event logs do not accurately reflect the actual token amount that influences the minting of xezETH. As a result, users reviewing transaction logs are misled about the amount of tokens actually used for operations.


## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L204C10-L271C1

The deposit function transfers tokens from the user's address to the contract using:
 
   depositToken.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), _amountIn);

 This operation transfers _amountIn tokens from the user to the contract.

 Inside the _deposit` function, a bridge fee is deducted from `_amountIn`:
 
   uint256 bridgeFee = getBridgeFeeShare(_amountIn);
   _amountIn -= bridgeFee;
   bridgeFeeCollected += bridgeFee;

Here, the bridge fee is subtracted from _amountIn, which reduces the amount available for further processing.

The `Deposit` event logs the original transferred amount rather than the net amount after fee deduction:
 
   emit Deposit(msg.sender, _amountIn, xezETHAmount);

The event inaccurately logs the initial amount, not considering the fee deduction, thus not reflecting the true amount used for minting xezETH.

Users and auditors analyzing the transaction logs will see the original amount sent (_amountIn) as logged in the `Deposit` event, which does not match the actual net amount used after deducting the bridge fee. 

## Tools Used
Visual Studio Code
Manual Inspection

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Modify the `Deposit` event to log the net amount of tokens after deducting the bridge fee. 

 emit Deposit(msg.sender, _amountIn - bridgeFee, xezETHAmount);


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L316-L321


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Using the wrong index for the collateral token array causes incorrect calculation of TVL or blocks deposits into the protocol.

## Proof of Concept
When calculating TVL, the code includes ERC20 token balances from the WithdrawQueue. However, this isn't done correctly. Instead of getting the balance of `collateralTokens[j]`, it uses the price of `collateralTokens[i]` for calculation. Since the prices of these tokens can differ, this leads to inaccurate calculations.
```solidity
if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
        collateralTokens[i],
        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
    );
}
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/1c7cc4e632564349b204b4b5e5f494c9b0bc631d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L316-L321

Additionally, if the number of operator delegators exceeds the number of collateral tokens, it causes an out-of-bounds error for `collateralTokens[i]`. As a result, the `calculateTVLs` function always reverts, preventing any deposits into the protocol.

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update the code to use the correct index for collateral tokens:
```solidity
if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
        collateralTokens[j],
        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
    );
}
```





## Assessed type

Context

title: Deposits of rebasing stETH can revert
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L491-L576
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L143-L154
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L323-L342


# Vulnerability details

Due to the rebasing mechanism in stETH, stETH transfers will frequently result in [1-2 wei less](https://docs.lido.fi/guides/lido-tokens-integration-guide/#1-2-wei-corner-case) than the expected transfer amount. 

In Renzo, depositing into the Restake Manager leads to a string of token transfers.

```
caller ---> RestakeManager ---> OperatorDelegator ---> Strategy
```

Every transfer will result in 1-2 wei less stETH for the recipient. However, each transfer expects to transfer the same amount. If one of the contracts (RestakeManager or OperatorDelegator) do not have extra stETH, the deposit will revert. This is the most likely outcome since RestakeManager and OperatorDelegator are not meant to hold token balances beyond the length of a function executing. Also, the Operator Delegator would [deposit its token balances](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L307-L309) back to Eigenlayer every time it completes a queued withdrawal, emptying its balance of stETH.


## Impact
This issue prevents users from depositing stETH into Renzo since it will frequently fail.

## Proof of Concept
Below are the relevant steps in a transaction that reproduces the issue:
1. Alice deposits 1000 stETH into Restake Manager. The 1000 stETH are [transferred](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L540) from Alice to Restake Manager. The Restake Manager only receives 998 stETH.
2. The Restake Manager then [deposits](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L562) 1000 stETH into the Operator Delegator. The Delegator [transfers](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L151) the 1000 stETH from the Restake Manager to itself. The transaction could revert here if the Restake Manager did not have 1-2 extra wei on top of the 998 stETH received from Alice. The Operator Delegator receives only 998 stETH.
3. The Operator Delegator [deposits](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L168) the 1000 stETH into the Eigenlayer Strategy Manager. The Strategy Manager then [transfers](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L330) the 1000 stETH from the Delegator to itself. The transaction reverts here since the Operator Delegator only has 998 stETH because its balance of stETH was recently emptied with a [`completeQueuedWithdrawal()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L306-L309). 

## Tools Used
Manual Review, Foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider calculating for the deposit amount by subtracting the token's post-balance with the token's pre-balance on every transfer. This should be the deposit amount used in RestakeManager's deposit() and OperatorDelegator's deposit(). 


## Assessed type

Token-Transfer

raw_row.title: Insolvency due to inaccurate Withdrawal Queue TVL

title: Insolvency due to inaccurate Withdrawal Queue TVL
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L316-L321
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L500-L504
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L594-L609
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L652
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L217-L224
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RateProvider/BalancerRateProvider.sol#L31-L40


# Vulnerability details

The Restake Manager [calculates the total TVL](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L316-L321) in the protocol including the Withdrawal Queue's TVL.
```solidity
function calculateTVLs() public view returns (uint256[][] memory, uint256[] memory, uint256) {
    // ... snip ...
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < odLength; ) {
        // ... snip ...
        for (uint256 j = 0; j < tokenLength; ) {    
            // ... snip ...
            if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
                totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
                    collateralTokens[i],
                    collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
                );
            }
    // ... snip ...
```

There is a mistake, however, in the token being passed to `lookupTokenValue()` when computing for the Withdrawal Queue's TVL. It uses the index `i` instead of the index `j`, which means the token value being looked up every time is of the same token. This leads to inaccurate TVL calculations for the Withdrawal Queue. 

For example, there are 3 collateral tokens wbETH, mETH and stETH:
1. wbETh is the first collateral token in the `collateralTokens` array.
2. The calculation for the total token value in the Withdrawal Queue will be `wbETH price * wbETH balance + wbETH price * mETH balance + wbETH price * stETH`.
3. The following prices will bloat the Withdrawal Queue's TVL because wbETH is more expensive than the other tokens:
- wbETH - $3,339.50
- stETH - $3,008.83
- mETH  - $3,100.56

## Impact
Users observing this behavior can exploit it to mint more ezETH tokens and withdraw more collateral tokens at the expense of other users. This is essentially stealing other users' deposits. This can be done for the life of the protocol unless the issue is fixed.

## Proof of Concept
`calculateTVLs()` is used in the deposit and withdraw functions to compute for the mint and redeem amounts.
- [RestakeManager.deposit()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L500-L504)
- [RestakeManager.depositEth()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L594-L609)
- [WithdrawQueue.withdraw()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L216-L224)

The TVL is inversely correlated with the mint amounts and it is correlated with the withdrawn amounts. To exploit this issue, consider the following scenario:

- Users deposit collateral when the Withdraw Queue's withdraw buffer is empty or close to it to maximize the amount of ezETH minted to them.
- Users withdraw collateral when the Withdraw Queue's withdraw buffer is full of the collateral tokens to maximize the amounts withdrawn.
- Multiple iterations of bloated withdrawals and mints will lead to losses for other users.

## Tools Used
Manual Review, Foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The fix is changing the index `i` to index `j` when doing the lookup for the token's collateral value.

```diff
            if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
                totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
-                   collateralTokens[i],
+                   collateralTokens[j]
                    collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
                );
            }
```





## Assessed type

Loop

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L405-L424
https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/15b679b08e7a3589ff83a5e84076ca4e0a00ec0b/src/contracts/pods/DelayedWithdrawalRouter.sol#L127-L137

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L459-L463


# Vulnerability details

There are Native ETH Restake Admin operations in the Operator Delegator that send funds to the Delayed Withdrawal Router.
1. [`withdrawNonBeaconChainETHBalanceWei()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L432-L437)
2. [`startDelayedWithdrawUnstakedETH()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L459-L463)
3. [`verifyAndProcessWithdrawals()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L405-L424)
4. [`startDelayedWithdrawUnstakedETH()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L459-L463)
5. [`activateRestaking()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L101-L103)

Once there are funds in the Delayed Withdrawal Router, anyone can [claim these withdrawals](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/15b679b08e7a3589ff83a5e84076ca4e0a00ec0b/src/contracts/pods/DelayedWithdrawalRouter.sol#L111-L115) after the set delay. When the protocol computes for its [TVL](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L274-L358), it does not include any of its Operator Delegators' ETH that is in the Delayed Withdrawal Router. This presents an MEV opportunity.

## Impact
Users can extract value at the expense of other depositors by sandwiching the `claimDelayedWithdrawals()` call whenever funds are in the Withdrawal Router.

## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenario:
1. Funds are sent to the Delayed Withdrawal Router by the Native ETH Restake Admin.
2. Once the [delayed withdrawal](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/15b679b08e7a3589ff83a5e84076ca4e0a00ec0b/src/contracts/pods/DelayedWithdrawalRouter.sol#L100-L105) can be claimed, a user can do the following in:
  - Deposit tokens to mint as much ezETH as possible.
  - Claim the delayed withdrawal in the Delayed Withdrawal Router.
  - [Withdraw](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206) and eventually [claim](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279) using as much ezETH as possible.

## Tools Used
Manual Review, Foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider including the total amount in delayed withdrawals and the `nonBeaconChainETHBalanceWei` for each pod as part of the TVL calculation. Delayed Withdrawal Router's [`getUserDelayedWithdrawals()`](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/15b679b08e7a3589ff83a5e84076ca4e0a00ec0b/src/contracts/pods/DelayedWithdrawalRouter.sol#L127-L137) can be used for getting the delayed withdrawals.








## Assessed type

MEV

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L75


# Vulnerability details

## Summary

When utilizing Chainlink in L2 chains like Arbitrum, it's important to ensure that the prices provided are not falsely perceived as fresh, even when the sequencer is down. This vulnerability could potentially be exploited by malicious actors to gain an unfair advantage.

## Vulnerability Detail

If the Arbitrum Sequencer goes down, oracle data will not be kept up to date, and thus could become stale. However, users are able to continue to interact with the protocol directly through the L1 optimistic rollup contract.

As a result, users may be able to use the protocol while oracle feeds are stale. This could cause many problems, but as a simple example:

- A user has an account with 100 tokens, valued at 1 ETH each, 
- The Arbitrum sequencer goes down temporarily
- While it's down, the price of the token go up to 1.1 ETH each token.
- Because of the stale price, A user Withdraw it and take profit amout of  `1.1 * 100 = 110 ETH = 10 ETH`

## Impact

If the Arbitrum sequencer goes down, the protocol will allow users to continue to operate at the previous (stale) rates.

```
    /// (e.g. a value of 100 would return as 100 * 10^18)
    function lookupTokenValue(IERC20 _token, uint256 _balance) public view returns (uint256) {
        AggregatorV3Interface oracle = tokenOracleLookup[_token];
        if (address(oracle) == address(0x0)) revert OracleNotFound();

        (, int256 price, , uint256 timestamp, ) = oracle.latestRoundData();//@audit sequencer oracle
        if (timestamp < block.timestamp - MAX_TIME_WINDOW) revert OraclePriceExpired();
        if (price <= 0) revert InvalidOraclePrice();

        // Price is times 10**18 ensure value amount is scaled
        return (uint256(price) * _balance) / SCALE_FACTOR;  
    
    }
```

## Tools Used

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L318


# Vulnerability details

## Cause
The `calculateTVLs` function uses [uses `i` (the index of the operator delegator)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L318) instead of `j` (the index of the collateral token) to access the `collateralTokens` array when calculating the token value of the withdrawal queue balance causing the wrong oracle price to be used for the calculation.

## Impact
Because `i` is 0 when `withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded` is false, the calculation will always use the price of the first token for all tokens in the withdrawal queue. For all tokens except the first, the TVL calculation will be incorrect and exploitable:

- When `OperatorDelegator.completeQueuedWithdrawal` is called, it changes the TVL without changing the supply by moving the balance from a correctly [accounted location (`queuedShares`) ](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L281)to an [incorrectly accounted one (`WithdrawalQueue`)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L300).
- When `RestakeManager.deposit` is called, it mints an amount of ezETH based on [correct token price](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L507) but then moves the tokens [into the withdrawal queue](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L555) where they are accounted for with the incorrect price.
- When `WithdrawalQueue.claim` is called, incorrectly acounted tokens reduce the TVL by an incorrect amount, because the change in shares due [to `burn`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L299) does not correspond to the change in TVL due to previously incorrectly accounted tokens that now are [transferred out](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L305).

Currently, token 0 is wBETH and token 1 is stETH, with a price difference of 4%, meaning that stETH balances in the withdrawal queue are overvalued in the TVL calculation. When more tokens are enabled, larger price differences will be possible. Accumulating tokens (e.g., ANKRETH & rETH) are much more expensive than rebasing ones (stETH, frxETH), with price differences of up to 15%.

This makes the TVL calculation exploitable by frontrunning. A transaction that moves a balance from an incorrectly accounted location to a correctly accounted one changes the TVL, which in turn affects the ezETH share price. This directly changes the deposit and withdrawal prices, as well as the [`getRate()` price value used by the Balancer pool](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RateProvider/BalancerRateProvider.sol#L29).  

Sandwiching this predictable change between either two opposite Balancer trades or a pair of deposit and withdraw actions allows an attacker to steal funds from ezETH holders.

## Proof of Concept

Scenario 1:
1. An attacker buys ezETH for ETH via Balancer, which uses `getRate()` price that uses the TVL calculation.
2. When `OperatorDelegator.completeQueuedWithdrawal` is called, withdrawing a large amount of `stETH`,  the `stETH` balance is moved from a correctly accounted location (`queuedShares`) to an incorrectly accounted one (`WithdrawalQueue`). This increases the TVL due to using `wBETH` price for calculating the `stETH` value added to the WithdrawalQueue.
3. Attacker sells the ezETH for ETH via Balancer, which uses the increased `getRate` price to realize a risk free profit.

A variety of similar exploits involving both Balancer traders, and deposit and withdrawals are made possible. Both for exploiting the TVL in  deposit flow, for the `completeQueuedWithdrawal` flow, and for the withdrawal flow. They can involve sandwiching large transactions of other users, or using attacker's funds to trigger the deposit and withdrawal flows directly.

## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use the correct index `j` instead of `i` when accessing `collateralTokens` in the `totalWithdrawalQueueValue` calculation:

```diff
totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
--    collateralTokens[i],
++    collateralTokens[j],
    collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
);
```

This will ensure that the correct token prices are used for each token in the withdrawal queue.











## Assessed type

Oracle

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L236


# Vulnerability details

## Cause
The [withdraw request ensures that sufficient funds are available](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L236) in the buffer, and the buffer [cannot be overfilled](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L299). At the same time, new deposits are withdrawable immediately at no cost. An attacker willing to DoS user withdrawals can frontrun all users' withdrawal transactions (of asset A) with their own transaction of deposit(asset B) + withdraw(asset A). Alternatively, the attacker can also backrun all buffer refills from deposits or EigenLayer withdrawals or rewards.

## Impact
A well-capitalized attacker can indefinitely DoS protocol withdrawals at no cost and exploit this to also achieve a depeg of ezETH relative to its underlying value, profiting from it. By preventing withdrawals, the attacker breaks the arbitrage cycle for ezETH's price. Due to the inability to withdraw funds, users willing to withdraw will have to trade out of ezETH instead via DEX or CEX. At the same time, arbitrageurs will not be able to complete withdrawals either, so they will not buy the ezETH sold by users. This will cause the ezETH price to depeg relative to its value.

The attack is highly likely because the attacker can directly profit from the depeg by preemptively shorting ezETH where available.

In addition to the depeg and DoS impacts, the protocol's indefinite withdrawal DoS will result in locking all users' funds for the duration of the attack, and will cause users to lose funds by having to trade out of ezETH at a reduced price.

Moreover, because only new deposits and EigenLayer withdrawals and rewards are used to replenish the buffers, increasing the buffer size by the admin and trying to fill the buffers at a higher pace via withdrawing additional funds from Eigenlayer will be delayed by at least 7 days (due to Eigenlayer's withdrawal delay). This allows the first 7 days of DoS to require only minimal capital that would need to, at most, match the organic pace of new deposits, which will also be greatly diminished by the attack.

After the same 7 days however, the previously queued withdrawals by the attacker become claimable, and available for recycling back into the attack.

## Proof of Concept
1. The attacker shorts ezETH (and REZ) - this is the profit motive.
2. A user submits a withdrawal request for asset A.
3. The attacker frontruns with a deposit of asset B and a withdrawal request for asset A. This "takes" the assets in the buffer.
4. The user's withdrawal request reverts due to insufficient assets available in the buffer.
5. After some time, ezETH depegs below its underlying value due to the inability to complete price arbitrage and increased selling pressure from users trading out instead of withdrawing.
6. Users' funds are locked for some users, and other users lose value by trading at a below-value price.
7. The attacker profits by closing the shorts.

## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use the buffer for serving withdrawal claims, but allow withdrawal requests to be queued without the buffer requirement:

```diff
-    /// @dev mapping of claimReserve (already withdraw requested), indexed by token address
-    mapping(address => uint) public claimReserve;

    function withdraw(uint256 _amount, address _assetOut) external nonReentrant {
        ...
-        // revert if amount to redeem is greater than withdrawBufferTarget
-        if (amountToRedeem > getAvailableToWithdraw(_assetOut)) revert NotEnoughWithdrawBuffer();

    function claim(uint256 withdrawRequestIndex) external nonReentrant {
        ...
+        // revert if amount to redeem is greater than withdrawBufferTarget
+        if (_withdrawRequest.amountToRedeem > getAvailableToWithdraw(_withdrawRequest.collateralToken)) {
+            revert NotEnoughWithdrawBuffer();
+        }
```


## Assessed type

MEV

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L220-L224


# Vulnerability details


## Cause

Deposit and withdrawal requests can be done immediately with no costs or fees, and both use the current oracle prices and TVL calculation ([deposit](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L499-L504), and [withdraw](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L217)). Crucially, the [withdrawal amount is calculated at withdrawal request submission time](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L220C1-L224C11) instead of at withdrawal claim time. Any small change in either ezETH value or in the price of a collateral token can be exploited at no cost by MEV. Specifically, if the price increases, a deposit is made before the increase, and a withdrawal request immediately after.

Additionally, in case of a supported LST's sudden change in price (for example due to price manipulation, an exploit of that LST, due to consensus layer penalties (slashing), or liquidity issues), external holders of that LST may frontrun the change, deposit the LST into Renzo, and immediately request a withdrawal of another asset (e.g., native ETH). In such situations, Renzo functions as a **zero-slippage zero-fees oracle-price-based DEX** for LSTs and ETH up to the TVL cap for the affected LST. Zero-slippage zero-fee oracle-price-based designs are notoriously vulnerable to both oracle manipulation and oracle latency attacks if not carefully prevented.

## Impact

The newly introduced frontrunning vector, due to incurring only gas fees, and no fee that is proportional to the size of the "trade", allows profitably exploiting most TVL and oracle price changes, and exploiting previously exploitable updates (vie Balancer's [usage of `getRate()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RateProvider/BalancerRateProvider.sol#L28C1-L41C6)) even more profitably via the new vector.

The impact is that value that otherwise should be distributed to ezETH holders is constantly lost to MEV. 

Additionally, ezETH holders lose value due to facilitating asset swaps with no slippage and no fees based on outdated oracle prices.

## Proof of Concept

Scenario 1 (MEV, price increase):

1. A transaction that will increase the TVL value without minting or burning ezETH, such as a Chainlink oracle update or EigenLayer rewards withdrawal, is observed.
2. An attacker sandwiches the transaction by depositing asset A right before it (minting ezETH to themselves).
3. The attacker completes the sandwich by submitting a withdrawal request for asset A after the "target" transaction. This sends the ezETH to WithdrawQueue, and credits the attacker with a larger amount of A than was just deposited, corresponding to the updated price of ezETH.
4. The attacker realizes an immediate, same block profit - a larger amount of the same asset, due to the price increase and credit of future withdrawal amount, and no fee being charged.
5. Value that would otherwise be distributed to holders of ezETH was lost to the attacker.

Scenario 2 (malicious):

1. Asset A experiences a sharp price decline due to slashing, exploit, or other factors.
2. An attacker borrows LST asset A from on-chain lending protocols. This is done to reduce the assets available for others to short the price manipulation of the next step.
3. The attacker buys up even more of the LST on CEX and DEX, running up the price of that asset, such that a manipulated price is reported by oracles.
4. The attacker deposits all asset A into Renzo, being credited with an outsized amount of ezETH due to the inflated price of the collateral.
5. The attacker immediately submits a withdrawal request of asset B, which upon conversion uses the inflated value of asset A in Renzo's TVL.
6. 7 days later, upon withdrawal claiming, the attacker withdraws the inflated amount of asset B.

Scenario 3 (MEV, price decrease, zerp-slippage zero-fees DEX):

1. A supported LST experiences a sudden change in price due to factors such as price manipulation, an exploit of that LST, consensus layer penalties (slashing), or liquidity issues.
2. Existing external holders of the LST, or arbitrageurs borrowing the asset, frontrun the transaction that changes the oracle price by depositing the LST into Renzo, and immediately requesting a withdrawal of another asset (e.g., native ETH or another LST). Using Renzo as a zero-slippage oracle-price-based DEX.
3. After the withdrawal delay, the attackers claim their withdrawal, receiving the other asset at the pre-change price, effectively exploiting the ezETH holders.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The redemption conversion should be performed at both request and claim time. If it results in a lower redeem value, that value should be used for the claim instead of the initial redeem amount. Additionally, a rate limit or a short delay on deposits with similar protection can be added as well.

```diff
function claim(uint256 withdrawRequestIndex) external nonReentrant {
    ...
+   // All the code converting from ezETH amount to amountToRedeem as is done in withdraw()

+   if (amountToRedeem < _withdrawRequest.amountToRedeem) {
+       _withdrawRequest.amountToRedeem = amountToRedeem;
+   }
}
```


## Assessed type

MEV

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L289-L310


# Vulnerability details


## Cause

The `calculateTVLs` function in the `RestakeManager` contains [two nested loops](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L289-L310): one loop for each operator delegator (OD), and an internal loop for each token. In each internal loop:

- The [OD's `getTokenBalanceFromStrategy`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L302) function is called for the token, which in turn calls the [Eigenlayer strategy](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L332) for the shares balance.
- The [`renzoOracle`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L307) is called for the token value, which in turns [calls the respective oracle](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L75).
- Additionally, memory is allocated for all the results and intermediate call outputs, incurring high quadratic memory expansion costs.

Due to the the nested loop structure, the gas consumption in the case of several operator delegators, and several tokens used is quadratic: `n-OD x n-Tokens`. Crucially, this method is called in most user flows: [deposits](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L500-L504), [withdrawals](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L217), and [Balancer trades](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RateProvider/BalancerRateProvider.sol#L31). 

## Impact

An even small number of operators and supported tokens will render the protocol unusable, up to running out of block gas limit.

Currently, with 1 OD and 2 tokens, `calculateTVLs` consumes approximately 450K gas (see the [example transaction](https://app.blocksec.com/explorer/tx/eth/0x5366d8b097cc2d2c27c45d97266b1fa6d76606e735c4a261efa7b43aff87de42) gas profiling section).

For reasonable values, such as 12 ODs and 12 tokens ([Eigenlayer supports 12 tokens](https://app.eigenlayer.xyz/restake)), there would be **144** nested loop iterations instead of just 2 iterations in the current version and configuration. A simple extrapolation, without adding the cost of operations added in the new version, and without estimating the additional quadratic memory expansion costs, would suggest that 144 iterations, instead of the current 2, would cost 32M gas (450K * 144 / 2), exceeding the block gas limit.

However, an earlier limiting factor will be encountered because `calculateTVL` is called in most user interactions with Renzo:  [deposit](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L500-L504), [withdrawal](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L217), and [Balancer trade](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RateProvider/BalancerRateProvider.sol#L31). Thus, exceeding even 1M-2M gas on L1 will render most protocol methods practically unusable for users.

## Proof of Concept
1. With 1 OD and 2 tokens, `calculateTVLs` consumes approximately 450K gas (see the [example transaction](https://app.blocksec.com/explorer/tx/eth/0x5366d8b097cc2d2c27c45d97266b1fa6d76606e735c4a261efa7b43aff87de42) gas profiling section)
2. For reasonable values, such as 12 ODs and 12 tokens currently supported by EigenLayer, there would be **144** nested loop iterations instead of the current 2 . 
3. A simple extrapolation, would suggest that 144 iterations, instead of the current 2, would cost 32M gas (450K * 144 / 2), exceeding the block gas limit. Moreover, this is an underestimate, due to not adding the cost of operations added in the new version (relative to the deployed one), and without estimating the additional quadratic memory expansion costs.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Instead of "pulling" operator delegator token balances, a "pushing" pattern can be used:
- Instead of "pulling" token TVLs from each component, the aggregated TVL sums should be maintained and "pushed" by each OD when its TVL changes (on OD deposits and withdrawals). This way, during admin's OD operations, the RM's TVL cache and each token's total protocol balance is updated. 
- Then, total token balances can be used to calculate TVL from `RenzoOracle.lookupTokenValues` once, which will result in a single loop over the tokens only.
- For enabling `chooseOperatorDelegatorForDeposit` a Set of ODs that can accept a deposit (are below allocation) can be maintained via "push" updates.

This will remove all loops during the calculation, except for the loop needed to iterate over the token oracles (once).

Alternatively, an off-chain custom TVL oracle can be used, for example, via a custom Chainlink oracle.


## Assessed type

DoS

# Vulnerability details


## Cause

The `WithdrawQueue` contract [defines a pausing functionality](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L139-L149) but does not use it for the user-controlled [`withdraw`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206) and [`claim`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279) functions. This is in contrast to the pausing functionality that is used for [deposits](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L495) and [ezETH](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/token/EzEthToken.sol#L64-L66) transfers.

Crucially, during the withdrawal `claim()` function, [ezETH is burned (not transferred)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L299), meaning that it cannot be paused using ezETH's pausing functionality as a workaround. This is because ezETH's pausing functionality is limited to transfers and [does not pause minting or burning](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/token/EzEthToken.sol#L68-L69).

## Impact

In case of an issue that requires pausing the protocol, for example, during a configuration change, an upgrade, or the mitigation of another issue, funds in the `WithdrawQueue` will remain vulnerable and may leave the protocol incorrectly, causing a loss of funds to ezETH holders.

Additionally, if ezETH itself is not paused, withdrawal requests will also be callable, potentially taking advantage of [possibly incorrectly calculated redemption values](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L217-L233), causing loss of value to ezETH holders.

## Proof of Concept

N/A

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Use the `whenNotPaused` modifier on the `withdraw()` and `claim()` functions:

```diff
-    function withdraw(uint256 _amount, address _assetOut) external nonReentrant {
+    function withdraw(uint256 _amount, address _assetOut) external nonReentrant whenNotPaused {

-    function claim(uint256 withdrawRequestIndex) external nonReentrant {
+    function claim(uint256 withdrawRequestIndex) external nonReentrant whenNotPaused {
```


## Assessed type

Access Control

title: A negative LST rebase may cause `getAvailableToWithdraw` to revert blocking deposits and withdrawals

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L158


# Vulnerability details


## Cause

 `WithdrawQueue`'s [`getAvailableToWithdraw` function may underflow and revert](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L158) if stETH (or another rebasing LST) experiences a negative rebase. This is because when `IERC20(_asset).balanceOf(address(this)) - claimReserve[_asset]` is 0 (or nearly 0), a negative rebase will result in stETH balance being lower than `claimReserve`. 
 
 A negative rebase is [expected to happen due to slashing, inactivity leaks, or a Lido issue in the case of stETH](https://docs.lido.fi/guides/lido-tokens-integration-guide#risks). Other rebasing LSTs may also expirience a negative rebase during the course of normal operation.

## Impact

This will cause the following user flows to revert:

- [`RestakeManager.deposit`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L543)
- [`WithdrawQueue.withdraw`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L236)

This will also cause the following admin flow to revert:

- [`OperatorDelegator.completeQueuedWithdrawal`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L286)

Crucially, because user deposits will revert and `OperatorDelegator.completeQueuedWithdrawal` will revert, it will not be possible to refill the buffer. This is because refilling the buffer always calls the method to calculate the transfer amount, which will revert for this asset.

For the issue to resolve, unclaimed withdrawals will need to be claimed. However, due to the 7-day delay imposed on unclaiming, this may take up to 7 days. Even then, because[ a claim transaction may only be submitted by the original withdrawer (msg.sender check)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L284), a user may prolong the DoS maliciously or inadvertently by not claiming their withdrawal.

Even if the buffer is not near 0 (when balance and reserve are equal to each other), an attacker may frontrun a negative rebase with a deposit and a withdrawal to "take the buffer" bringing it to 0, such that after their action, the protocol will stop functioning for this asset, possibly until the attacker claims their withdrawal. This will result in a prolonged DoS.

## Proof of Concept

1. The buffer for stETH is at (or near) 0 following a withdrawal request "taking" it by increasing the `claimReserve`, either in the course of normal operations or maliciously.
2. A negative rebase reduces the stETH supply held by the `WithdrawQueue`.
3. All subsequent calls to the buffer views for stETH will revert, preventing refilling it.
4. User deposits, withdrawals, and admin's claiming of EigenLayer withdrawal (`OperatorDelegator.completeQueuedWithdrawal`) involving stETH all revert until a sufficient amount of withdrawals is claimed to reduce the `claimReserve`.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Check if the subtraction will underflow and report 0 in that case:

```diff
    function getAvailableToWithdraw(address _asset) public view returns (uint256) {
        if (_asset != IS_NATIVE) {
-            return IERC20(_asset).balanceOf(address(this)) - claimReserve[_asset];
+            uint256 balance = IERC20(_asset).balanceOf(address(this));
+            return (balance > claimReserve[_asset]) ? balance - claimReserve[_asset] : 0;
```


## Assessed type

DoS
