# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L92


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
The discrepancy between ezETH/ETH oracle price and market price can be used for arbitrage opportunities

## Vulnerability detail
The value of `stETH` deposited into the protocol is priced using chainlink oracle. The current deviation and heartbeat of `stETH/ETH` are `0.5%` and `86400s`. This means stETH price will not be updated it the price doesn't deviate `0.5%` in 24 hours. This difference between market price and oracle price can be used to perform arbitrage

Consider this scenario
  
1. Lets say the price of 1 stETH/ETH is 1 in oracle. And the market price of stETH/ETH is also 1
2. Now if the market price of stETH/ETH becomes 0.996. But as the deviation doesn't cross 0.5% the price will not get updated. 
3. So an attacker with lot of upfront capital finds this arbitrage opportunity to buy stETH for market price in an AMM
4. Lets say has 100 ETH. He gets 100.4 stETH for the market price
5. He then deposits the 100.4 stETH in renzo. The price in renzo is still 1, so he gets 100.4 value of ETH (100.4 ETH value worth of ezETH is minted)
6. Attacker gets profit of 0.4 ETH value from arbitrage

The `0.5%` deviation might seem less here. But attacker can front run oracle updates to exploit the above scenario which have more deviation thus more profit.
For ex: if the oracle price for stETH/ETH is 1 and it changes to 0.98, now the attacker can front run the oracle update to perform the above attack. Here attacker used 2% deviation to get more profit.

The delay implemented for withdraws can gaurd against using a flash loan to perform this attack. But its still possible for attacker to perform arbitrage using upfront capital

Refer to this for more info
https://medium.com/angle-protocol/angle-research-series-part-1-oracles-and-front-running-d75184abc67

## Impact
Attacker can make profit using arbitrage opportunity.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider implementing a deposit fee to mitigate against arbitrage opportunities. Ideally, this fee would be larger than the oracle's maximum price deviation so that it is not possible to profit from arbitrage.



## Assessed type

Oracle

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details

The `bool success = payable(tx.origin).send(gasRefund);` function intends to transfer the refund amount to `tx.origin` (the sender of the transaction) but it is not equipped to handle changes in the underlying `.send()` due to its limitation of a fixed gas price of 2300. ## Impact
The use of `.send()` instead of `.call` may cause the function to revert, if the gas price is above 2300, because of the limitation with `.send()` which may lead to denial service.

`bool success = payable(tx.origin).send(gasRefund);`

The `.send()` function intends to transfer an ETH amount with a fixed amount of 2300 gas. However, these function is not be equipped to handle changes in the underlying functions which may use higher amounts of gas in the future. If the recipient Fallback Function Consumes More Than 2300 Gas, `.send()` may revert. Hence, the vault and the contract owner will not be able to call certain sensitive functions.

https://vscode.dev/github/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L481-L493

Manual Review

use the `.call()` function to transfer ether and prevent some of the limitations of .send(), with the checks-effects-interactions (CEI) pattern utilized rightly. Careful considerations needs to be made to prevent reentrancy.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L312


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the withdrawalQueue.sol, the ``withdraw()`` is used to start the withdrawal process for a user, which is then finalized using ``claim()``. However, this is an issue for the protocol and users because:

- The protocol includes collateral funds already rrequested in the ``withdraw`` process in it's TVL when calculating
- The tokens to be burnt are not burnt in the initial ``withdraw`` function. 
- The amount to be sent to the sent to the user is set before the actual transfer is made.

Since the ``_withdrawRequest.amountToRedeem`` is set in the ``withdraw``, and there exists a time delay of ``coolDownPeriod`` before finalization, it is expected that price will flunctuate during the wait period. 
When the price flunctuation between that period is suffiently large, the protocol will over pay the user using the old amount that was previously set. This causes a deficit in the protocol since the caculated TVL used for other transactions included these tokens used as collateral
When the price drops sufficiently, the user looses a large part of their funds since the amount has been previously set.Considering that withdrawal requests cannot be reversed, the user has no choice but to complete the transaction. Meanwhile, the live prices are being used for deposits and TVL caculations.




Also by not finalizing withdrawals, a user can start multiple withdrawal process, all using the same TVL and therefore the ``calculateRedeemAmount`` rate, instead of a decreased rate after each withdrawal application.

## Proof of Concept
```solidity
    function claim(uint256 withdrawRequestIndex) external nonReentrant {
        // check if provided withdrawRequest Index is valid
        if (withdrawRequestIndex >= withdrawRequests[msg.sender].length)
            revert InvalidWithdrawIndex();

        WithdrawRequest memory _withdrawRequest = withdrawRequests[msg.sender][
            withdrawRequestIndex
        ];
        if (block.timestamp - _withdrawRequest.createdAt < coolDownPeriod) revert EarlyClaim();

```

## Tools Used
Manual Review, Josephdara

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Since this is an economic impact bug, I would like to suggest a few solutions.
- Don't add collateral tokens already requested for to the TVL. Since ezETH is already transferred from the user.
- Do the actual exchange rate calculation inside ``claim()``
- Implement a slippage parameter to determine a minimum amount expected, and reverse the transfer if the final amount is less than slippage

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/Oracle/RenzoOracleL2.sol#L50


# Vulnerability details

## Description
 The getMintRate function in the RenzoOracleL2 contract is intended to revert if the price of ezETH is less than 1 ether. However, due to the scaling implementation, when the oracle's reported price is exactly 1 ether and the oracle has a non-zero decimal count, the _scaledPrice calculation results in a value less than 1 ether. This triggers the InvalidOraclePrice revert condition even though the actual price is 1 ether.



## Function(s) Affected
 getMintRate

## Code Snippet

    uint256 _scaledPrice = (uint256(price)) * 10 ** (18 - oracle.decimals());
    if (_scaledPrice < 1 ether) revert InvalidOraclePrice();

## Proof of Concept (PoC)

1. Deploy an oracle with decimals() returning a value greater than 0 (e.g., 8).
2. Set the oracle price to exactly 1 ether (e.g., price = 10**8 to represent 1 ether with 8 decimals).
3. Call getMintRate.
4. Observe that _scaledPrice becomes 10**(18 - 8), which is less than 1 ether.
5. The condition if (_scaledPrice < 1 ether) is met, and the transaction reverts with InvalidOraclePrice.

## Impact
 This bug can prevent valid price feeds from being accepted, potentially halting operations that rely on the getMintRate function.

## Recommendation
 Adjust the scaling logic to ensure that a reported price of exactly 1 ether does not result in a scaled price less than 1 ether. One possible solution is to add a conditional check for this edge case or modify the scaling formula.


## Assessed type

Oracle

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L327-L335


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `TVL` is calculated less than the actual value. This may lead to loss of funds for users.

## Proof of Concept

The `OperatorDelegator.getTokenBalanceFromStrategy()` function returns the token balance of the `operatorDelegator`. It also includes the amount of the tokens in the withdrawl queue of the eigen layer. However, `queuedShares[address(this)]` is used instead of `queuedShares[address(token)]` in the following code. 
`queuedShares[address(this)]` is always 0, so the amount of the tokens in the withdrawl queue of the eigen layer is never added. 

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L327-L335

```solidity
    function getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(IERC20 token) external view returns (uint256) {
        return
@>          queuedShares[address(this)] == 0
                ? tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this))
                : tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) +
                    tokenStrategyMapping[token].sharesToUnderlyingView(
                        queuedShares[address(token)]
                    );
    }
```

As a result, the `TVL` is calculated less than the actual value. This leads to loss of fund for withdrawing users, when there are many tokens in the withdrawl queue of the eigen layer.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

```diff
    function getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(IERC20 token) external view returns (uint256) {
        return
-           queuedShares[address(this)] == 0
+           queuedShares[address(token)] == 0
                ? tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this))
                : tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) +
                    tokenStrategyMapping[token].sharesToUnderlyingView(
                        queuedShares[address(token)]

```

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L491-L576


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The protocol could be unable to receive the desired amount of deposits due to the requested withdrawal amounts being factored into the deposit limitation checks, even though the actual utilized assets are insufficient

## Proof of Concept

As you can see at `L510` of the `RestakeManager.deposit()` function, there is a check to ensure the deposit amount does not cause an overflow of the deposit limitation. However, this check does not consider the requested withdrawal amounts.

In fact, all assets in the `WithdrawQueue` contract, including the requested withdrawal amounts (`claimReserve`s), are included in the `totalTVL` calculation. But these assets were already determined to be claimed at a later time, so it is improper to include them in the deposit limitation check.

As a result, protocol could be unable to receive the desired amount of deposits due to the requested withdrawal amounts being factored into the deposit limitation checks, even though the actual utilized assets are insufficient

```solidity
    function deposit(
        IERC20 _collateralToken,
        uint256 _amount,
        uint256 _referralId
    ) public nonReentrant notPaused {
        [...]

        // Enforce TVL limit if set, 0 means the check is not enabled
510     if (maxDepositTVL != 0 && totalTVL + collateralTokenValue > maxDepositTVL) {
            revert MaxTVLReached();
        }

        [...]
    }
```

This problem also occurs in `RestakeManager.depositETH()` function.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The requested withdrawal amounts held in the `WithdrawQueue` contract should not be included in the `maxDepositTVL` check.


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206-L263


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Attackers can interrupt any withdrawing from `WithdrawQueue` contract, by front-running.

## Proof of Concept

Let's consider following scenario:
1. Bob, the malicious user, fully fills `stETH` withdraw buffer of `WithdrawQueue` contract.
2. Everytime anybody tries to withdraw their `stETH` by calling `WithdrawQueue.withdraw()` , Bob withdraws all buffer by front-running. Then, the available amount to withdraw becomes 0, leading to the reversal of former's transaction.
3. And after that, if someone tries to deposit `stETH`, Bob fully fills `stETH` withdraw buffer again by front-running. Then, Bob is able to withdraw all that buffer anytime, facilitates the interrupting any following withdrawings.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

There should be a cooldown mechanism between depositting and withdrawing.


## Assessed type

DoS

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/v0.2.1-goerli-m2/src/contracts/pods/DelayedWithdrawalRouter.sol#L99-L104


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Attackers can take a part of rewards by front-running the call to `DelayedWithdrawalRouter.claimDelayedWithdrawals()` of EigenLayer.

## Proof of Concept

Rewards that are generated in EigenLayer are sent to `DelayedWithdrawalRouter` contract of EigenLayer first. After a delay, the rewards can be claimed by calling the permissionless function `DelayedWithdrawalRouter.claimDelayedWithdrawals()` of EigenLayer. This call will instantly increase the TVL of the protocol.

An attacker can take advantage of this to steal a part of the rewards. Let's consider following scenario:
1. Initial sate:
    - Total supply of `ezETH`: `1,000e18`,
    - TVL: `1,000 ETH`,
    - Exchange rate: 1.
2. The protocol is about to call the `DelayedWithdrawalRouter.claimDelayedWithdrawals()` function of EigenLayer and receive `50 ETH` as the reward.
3. The attacker deposits `9,000 ETH` by front-running. Then the state becomes:
    - Total supply of `ezETH`: `10,000e18`,
    - TVL: `10,000 ETH`,
    - Exchange rate: 1,
    - The attacker's `ezETH` balance: `9,000e18`.
4. After the protocol's transaction, the state becoems:
    - Total supply of `ezETH`: `10,000e18`,
    - TVL: `10,500 ETH`,
    - Exchange rate: 1.05,
    - The attacker's `ezETH` balance: `9,000e18`.

Finally, the attacker's asset becomes `1.05 * 9,000 = 9450 ETH`, results in taking `45 ETH`, that is the `90%` of protocol's reward.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Recommend not send `DepositQueue` contract all the reward at once. It would be better distribute the reward following linear function on time.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Factory.sol#L135


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Malicious proxyAdmin can upgrade xerc20 token implementation and steal fund from user.

## Proof of Concept

When deploying [deployXERC20](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/xERC20/contracts/XERC20Factory.sol#L135), we are calling 

```solidity
 /**
     * @notice Deploys an XERC20 contract using CREATE3
     * @dev _limits and _minters must be the same length
     * @param _name The name of the token
     * @param _symbol The symbol of the token
     * @param _minterLimits The array of limits that you are adding (optional, can be an empty array)
     * @param _burnerLimits The array of limits that you are adding (optional, can be an empty array)
     * @param _bridges The array of bridges that you are adding (optional, can be an empty array)
     * @param _proxyAdmin The address of the proxy admin - will have permission to upgrade the lockbox (should be a dedicated account or contract to manage upgrades)
     * @return _xerc20 The address of the xerc20
     */

    function deployXERC20(
        string memory _name,
        string memory _symbol,
        uint256[] memory _minterLimits,
        uint256[] memory _burnerLimits,
        address[] memory _bridges,
        address _proxyAdmin
    ) external returns (address _xerc20) {
        _xerc20 = _deployXERC20(
            _name,
            _symbol,
            _minterLimits,
            _burnerLimits,
            _bridges,
            _proxyAdmin
        );

        emit XERC20Deployed(_xerc20);
    }

```

note, 

> _proxyAdmin The address of the proxy admin - will have permission to upgrade the lockbox (should be a dedicated account or contract to manage upgrades)

and this is how the xerc20 token is deployed

```solidity

        bytes memory _creation = type(TransparentUpgradeableProxy).creationCode;

        // Constructor in Proxy takes (logic, admin, data)
        bytes memory _bytecode = abi.encodePacked(
            _creation,
            abi.encode(xerc20Implementation, _proxyAdmin, initializeBytecode)
        );

        _xerc20 = CREATE3.deploy(_salt, _bytecode, 0);

        EnumerableSetUpgradeable.add(_xerc20RegistryArray, _xerc20);
```

the lock box contract enforce that when withdraw, the token must be burnt,

but Malicious proxyAdmin can upgrade lock box implementation and steal fund directly (one of the way is minting a lot of tokens).

consider any user can deploy xerc20 token and lock box contract, the proxy admin can be anyone and may not be trusted.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

N/A

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/Connext/integration/LockboxAdapterBlast.sol#L93


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Unverified calldata allows an attacker to steal ERC20 tokens from users who have approved the contract to spend their tokens.

## Vulnerability Details

The bridgeTo function combines both Lockbox deposit and Blast bridge's BridgeERC20To call. As seen below, the function makes a call to Blast L1StandardBridge with an unverified calldata. This calldata can be the 'transferFrom' of a previously approved user. This allows an attacker to steal tokens from users who have approved the contract to spend their tokens.

[LockboxAdapterBlast.sol#L93](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/Connext/integration/LockboxAdapterBlast.sol#L93)
```
        L1StandardBridge(blastStandardBridge).bridgeERC20To(
            xerc20,
            _remoteToken,
            _to,
            _amount,
            _minGasLimit,
@>          _extraData
        );
```

An example of an exploit caused by unverified calldata is the Paraswap [exploit](https://medium.com/neptune-mutual/analysis-of-the-paraswap-exploit-1f97c604b4fe) where the attacker used a malicious calldata input to steal the tokens of users who had previously approved the contract to spend their tokens.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

[The Graph solved this by whitelisting users who can use calldata](https://etherscan.io/address/0xd41ca6a1d034d178c196dfa916f22f7d1a1b8222#code#F1#L294). Whitelist users who can use calldata or verify that the calldata provided by users isn't malicious.

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L302-L304
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L327-L335


# Vulnerability details

`RestakeManager:calculateTVLs()` loops trough the registered OperatorDelegators and adds up their token balances (deposited) to compute the TVL of the whole system.

The token balance of a single OperatorDelegator is retrieved by this line:

```js
uint256 operatorBalance = operatorDelegators[i].getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(
    collateralTokens[j]
);
```

The issue is found in how `OperatorDelegator:getTokenBalanceFromStrategy()` handles 0-address strategies (not-set):

```js
function getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(IERC20 token) external view returns (uint256) {
    return
        queuedShares[address(this)] == 0
            ? tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this))
            : tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) +
                tokenStrategyMapping[token].sharesToUnderlyingView(
                    queuedShares[address(token)]
                );
}
```

If `tokenStrategyMapping[token] = address(0)` the call to `userUnderlyingView` will revert... making impossible to execute `RestakeManager:calculateTVLs()`.


## Impact

No one will be able to mint ezETH if at lest one OperatorDelegator does not support a registered collateral token.

I believe this issue to be considered as a medium since it can temprorarly block the protocol but can be easily resolved by contacting the OperatorDelegator causing it.

## Proof of Concept

The screenshot below was taken after running a Foundry test suite in which I deployed an OperatorDelegator without setting his strategy for stETH.
After running deposit(stETh, 1e18) it failed:

https://drive.google.com/file/d/1HZEjbjcxTBj_70QZo00GK2tDoeSbO9E4/view?usp=sharing

## Tools Used

- Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Make `OperatorDelegator:getTokenBalanceFromStrategy()` return 0 if the token is not supported.

```diff
function getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(IERC20 token) external view returns (uint256) {
+   if (tokenStrategyMapping[token] == address(0)) return 0;
    return
        queuedShares[address(this)] == 0
            ? tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this))
            : tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) +
                tokenStrategyMapping[token].sharesToUnderlyingView(
                    queuedShares[address(token)]
                );
}
```













## Assessed type

# Vulnerability details

* In order to keep track of the user's withdrawal requests, the mapping is used, where the key is a user, and the value - `withdrawRequestIndex`, which itself holds a request. After claiming the request, it should be removed from the mapping to avoid a double claim. Currently, it's done in the following way:
  * ```Solidity
     // delete the withdraw request
        withdrawRequests[msg.sender][withdrawRequestIndex] = withdrawRequests[msg.sender][
            withdrawRequests[msg.sender].length - 1
        ];
        withdrawRequests[msg.sender].pop(); 

        // burn ezETH locked for withdraw request
        ezETH.burn(address(this), _withdrawRequest.ezETHLocked);
    ```

However, the system assumes that the `withdrawRequests[msg.sender][withdrawRequests[msg.sender].length - 1]` will retrieve the last requested withdrawal, which is not true. In fact, it might be an empty slot, since the `withdrawRequestIndex` is not tied to a specific user. 

## Impact
* There is a possibility to accidentally remove two separate requests by only claiming one of them.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
- Long term:
  - Consider removing an appropriate slot in a mapping.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L71-L81
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L85-L98


# Vulnerability details

Chainlink aggregators come with a built-in circuit breaker that triggers when the price of an asset surpasses a pre-set range. Additionally, it's essential to note the `minPrice` and `maxPrice` parameters of the Chainlink oracle, ensuring these limits are not breached.

For comprehensive documentation on `minPrice` and `maxPrice`, please consult the Chainlink API reference. This matter has already been covered in: 

https://solodit.xyz/issues/missing-checks-for-chainlink-oracle-spearbit-connext-pdf

https://solodit.xyz/issues/m-02-missing-check-for-the-maxmin-price-in-the-chainlinkoraclesol-contract-code4rena-moonwell-moonwell-git

## Impact
In the event of a market crash, there's a risk of receiving incorrect pricing data, potentially enabling adversaries to borrow based on this inaccurate valuation. This could lead to accumulating harmful debt within the protocol.

## Proof of Concept
The function `lookupTokenValue` in `RenzoOracle.sol` checks only that `price` to be non-positive for reverting:

```
if (price <= 0) revert InvalidOraclePrice();
```

Nevertheless, it fails to verify minimum and maximum price thresholds. Let's examine a potential vulnerability:

Token X, configured with a minimum price of 10, undergoes a decline in value to 1. Despite this plunge, the aggregator persistently indicates 10, allowing users to borrow against Token X under the impression that it's valued at 10, when in reality, it's only worth a fraction of that.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The `RenzoOracle.sol` must ensure that the returned answer falls within the designated `minPrice` and `maxPrice` boundaries.

```solidity
require(price < _maxPrice, "Upper price bound breached");
require(price > _minPrice, "Lower price bound breached");
```



## Assessed type

Oracle

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L193
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L244-L245

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L289-L301
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L139-L201
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L605-L609
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L193


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Detail

When users mint `xezETH` on L2 (layer 2), they need to deposit their ETH/WETH into the `xRenzoDeposit` contract. The assets are later bridged to L1 (layer 1, i.e. Ethereum) via Connext and deposited into `restakeManager`. At the end of this deposit, some amount of `xezETH` is burned on L1, but the burned amount may be less than the initially minted amount.

The issue arises because the burned amount of `xezETH` is calculated based on the amount of WETH bridged, using the price on L1 at `restakeManager`'s deposit time. This price is likely to be higher than the initial minting price of `xezETH` on L2 due to the following reasons:

1. Over time, the price of `ezETH` with respect to ETH will increase as the Renzo protocol receives rewards from both EigenLayer and Renzo's operators.
2. There is a time lag between users depositing their ETH/WETH on L2 and the assets being received on L1 and deposited into the `restakeManager` contract.

If the burning price is higher than the minting price, the amount of `xezETH` burned is fewer than the amount of `xezETH` initially minted. As `xezETH` is a xERC20 token that can cross-chain with zero slippage via Connext, if users bridge all their `xezETH` from L2 to L1 and want to unwrap them to `ezETH`, there will not be enough `ezETH` in the Lockbox contract for them to unwrap.

## Impact

More `xezETH` tokens are minted than intended, resulting in two issues:

1. The surplus supply of `xezETH` cannot be unwrapped to `ezETH`, and in the scenario where all users want to exit, the last users cannot redeem their `xezETH` into the underlying asset.
2. The actual value of a `xezETH` token is lower than a `ezETH` token, which opens up arbitrage opportunities not intended by the protocol.

I believe the risk rating for this issue is high because it violates an invariance: during the cross-chain scenario of the xezETH token, the minted amount should match the burned amount.

## Proof of Concept
```solidity
        // Fetch price and timestamp of ezETH from the configured price feed
        (uint256 _lastPrice, uint256 _lastPriceTimestamp) = getMintRate();
```
```solidity
        // Calculate the amount of xezETH to mint - assumes 18 decimals for price and token
        uint256 xezETHAmount = (1e18 * amountOut) / _lastPrice;
```

When a user deposits native ETH into the `xRenzoDeposit` contract on Layer 2, the amount of minted `xezETH` is calculated using the price from [`getMintRate()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L289-L301), which gets the current mint rate from the oracle or the price previously set by the receiver.

```solidity
        // Calculate how much ezETH to mint
        uint256 ezETHToMint = renzoOracle.calculateMintAmount(
            totalTVL,
            msg.value,
            ezETH.totalSupply()
        );
```

```solidity
        // Burn it - it was already minted on the L2
        IXERC20(address(xezETH)).burn(address(this), xezETHAmount);
```
Later, the sweeper calls the [`xRenzoDeposit.sweep()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L414-L449) function to bridge these assets to L1 via Connext. When L1 receives these assets, the [`xRenzoBridge.xReceive()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L139-L201) function is triggered, depositing the assets into the `restakeManager` contract and receiving `ezETH` in return using the rate calculated in [`renzoOracle.calculateMintAmount()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L605-L609). Then, the same amount of `xezETH` is burned.

However, since the price of `xezETH` with respect to ETH is likely to increase over time from when `xezETH` is minted on L2 to when `xezETH` is burned on L1, the burned price may be higher than the mint price back on L2, resulting in fewer `xezETH` being burned than needed.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
During the L2 native restaking process, record the amount of minted `xezETH` on L2 in a variable and encode it into the Connext cross-chain message when bridging. When the L1 component receives the message, decode the amount of `xezETH` minted from the message and burn the exact same amount of `xezETH`. This ensures a balanced minting and burning of the `xezETH` xERC20 token.





## Assessed type

Token-Transfer

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L235-L236
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L156-L162


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details

Renzo's withdraw flow is a two-step process:

1. The user initiates a withdraw request by calling `WithdrawQueue.withdraw()`.
2. After a certain cool-down period, the user completes the withdraw by calling `WithdrawQueue.claim()`.


```
// revert if amount to redeem is greater than withdrawBufferTarget
if (amountToRedeem > getAvailableToWithdraw(_assetOut)) revert NotEnoughWithdrawBuffer();
```
When making a withdraw request, the withdraw amount cannot exceed the available-to-withdraw amount in the `WithdrawQueue`.

```
    function getAvailableToWithdraw(address _asset) public view returns (uint256) {
        if (_asset != IS_NATIVE) {
            return IERC20(_asset).balanceOf(address(this)) - claimReserve[_asset];
        } else {
            return address(this).balance - claimReserve[_asset];
        }
    }
```
The available-to-withdraw amount is determined by the contract balance, subtracting the `claimReserve[_asset]` value. The `claimReserve[_asset]` value is increased in `WithdrawQueue.withdraw()` and decreased in `WithdrawQueue.claim()`.

A whale can exploit this by making a large deposit, and then calling `WithdrawQueue.withdraw()` to deplete the available withdrawn amount in the WithdrawQueue. This would prevent other users from making withdraw requests. The cost for the whale is minimal, as they can retrieve their funds from `WithdrawQueue.claim()` after the cool-down period. Moreover, they can choose not to claim the assets after the cool-down period, thereby extending the attack.

However, the team would need to manually unstake assets from EigenLayer and refill the `WithdrawQueue`, which takes about a week. This leaves the `WithdrawQueue` with insufficient available withdrawn amounts during this period.

New deposits from users and protocol rewards to fill the `WithdrawQueue` can alleviate the situation, but only to a limited extent.

## Impact
Whales can deplete the available withdrawn amount in the `WithdrawQueue`, preventing other users from making satisfactory withdraw requests during the time it takes for the team to complete the withdraw from EigenLayer and refill the `WithdrawQueue` (about 1 week).

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Set an upper limit per user in the `claimReserve`, so that if a user wants to withdraw more, they need to first claim to leave some room in `claimReserve` for new withdraw requests.


## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L316-L321


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
The `RestakeManager.calculateTVLs` function contains a section that computes the Total Value Locked (TVL) for the Liquidity Stake Tokens (LSTs) in the `withdrawQueue`. This calculation is performed by iterating over the LSTs in the `withdrawQueue` and determining their values using `renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue`. 
```
                // record token value of withdraw queue
                if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
                    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
                        collateralTokens[i],
                        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
                    );
                }
```
However, there's an error in the token address indexing: the correct token address should be `collateralTokens[j]`, not `collateralTokens[i]`.

Since the `totalWithdrawalQueueValue` is designed to be calculated only once (as indicated by the `withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded` boolean variable in a loop), the index `i` would be zero when computing the `totalWithdrawalQueueValue`. Consequently, the `RestakeManager.calculateTVLs` function uses the price of the first LST to calculate the value of all LSTs for the TVL in `withdrawQueue`. This leads to an inaccurate calculation of the Total TVL in the protocol.

## Impact
The TVL derived from `RestakeManager.calculateTVLs` is vital to the entire Renzo protocol because it sets the price of ezETH. However, due to the incorrect calculation, the TVL uses the price of the first LST to determine the value of all LSTs for the TVL in `withdrawQueue`. 

If the price of the first LST is below average, the calculated TVL will be lower than it should be. This will result in a lower ezETH price, allowing depositors to profit as the mint price of ezETH is lower than it should be. Conversely, if the price of the first LST is above average, the calculated TVL will be higher than it should be. This will lead to a higher ezETH redeem price, benefiting users who withdraw from the protocol.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Correct the index typo:
```diff
- collateralTokens[i]
+ collateralTokens[j]
```


## Assessed type

Math

The total TVL is inaccurate because of an incorrect calculation of the `totalWithdrawalQueueValue`.

The function `renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(IERC20 _token, uint256 _balance)` provides the value of `_balance` denominated in the underlying currency for the specified `_token`. The `renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue()` function's initial parameter should be `collateralTokens[j]`.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Total TVL calculation depends on this, thus `RestakeManager.calculateTVLs()` returns incorrect value.

## Proof of Concept
The mapping `queuedShares` tracks token shares within the withdrawal queue of EigenLayer. Its definition is `mapping(address => uint256) public queuedShares`. Proper representation would involve accessing it as `queuedShares[address(token)]`. However, within the function, it's depicted as `queuedShares[address(this)] == 0`, which is always True. Consequently, the ternary operator always returns the token balance without considering the queued shares for that specific token.

## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Replace `queuedShares[address(this)] == 0` with `queuedShares[address(token)] == 0`.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L219-L233
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L152-L164


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If EigenPod is in deficit due to slashing (or inactivity leak), repayments of native ETH will allow users that withdraw before a Renzo admin unstakes from EigenLayer to get a better exchange price for their ezETH at the expense of all other users in the system.

From [EigenLayer docs](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/docs/core/EigenPodManager.md#depositing-into-eigenlayer) it can be seen that it's possible for an EigenPod to be in deficit (owe more to EigenLayer than it currently holds in a validator): 
>  Pod Owner's beacon chain ETH balance decreases (maybe due to slashing), and someone provides a proof of this to EigenPod.verifyBalanceUpdates. In this case, the Pod Owner will have negative shares in the EigenPodManager.

Which results in the negative shares being repaid out of the withdrawn assets. 

On the Renzo side this would imply that in the event of a slashing or [inactivity leak](https://docs.ethstaker.cc/ethstaker-knowledge-base/help/downtime-explained) (due to validator being offline) the `WithdrawQueue` would receive `32 ETH - deficit` after an admin unstakes from EigenLayer to fill the withdrawal buffer by executing the following call sequence (as mentioned by the sponsor in the competition chat): 

```
1. OperatorDelegator::queueWithdrawals
2. OperatorDelegator::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals
3. OperatorDelegator::completeWithdrawals
```

The greater effect of this is that it decreases the value of ezETH tokens in the following calculation used to determine how much a user should receive: 
```solidity
    function calculateRedeemAmount(
        uint256 _ezETHBeingBurned,
        uint256 _existingEzETHSupply,
        uint256 _currentValueInProtocol
    ) external pure returns (uint256) {
       // @audit _currentValueInProtocol decreases after unstaking is completed in EigenLayer
        uint256 redeemAmount = (_currentValueInProtocol * _ezETHBeingBurned) / _existingEzETHSupply;
       ...
}
```

This implies that users that submitted their withdrawal request before the withdrawal from EigenLayer will be unaffected by this price change whereas users that submit their request after will have their ezETH exchanged at a lower price. 

Given that the withdrawal from EigenLayer is an asynchronous process( requiring at least [`minWithdrawalDelayBlocks`](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/dev/docs/core/DelegationManager.md#completequeuedwithdrawal) to have passed) a user could frontrun the call by the admin to `completeWithdrawals` in order to get a better withdrawal price. If there is sufficient liquidity in the withdrawal buffer to execute this malicious user's withdrawal the subsequent loss to the protocol would be `amount * (originalPrice - priceAfterNativeETHUnstake)`. 

## Proof of Concept
1. Alice submits a withdrawal request but there is insufficient liquidity in the withdrawal buffer to complete her request so it reverts at [L236](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L236)
2. Seeing this the Renzo admin with the `NATIVE_ETH_RESTAKE_ADMIN` role calls `OperatorDelegator::queueWithdrawals` to fill the withdrawal buffer to allow Alice to withdraw her ETH. 
3. While the ETH was staked in EigenLayer, the Renzo validator experienced a period of downtime, resulting in a deficit due to inactivity leak that must be repaid as the ETH is withdrawn from EigenLayer, resulting in `32 ETH - deficit` ETH being sent to the withdrawal buffer.
4. Bob has a bot monitoring the mempool for any calls to `queueWithdrawals` that would return less than 32 ETH to Renzo and so frontruns the admin's call to `completeWithdrawals` to withdraw his stake before the decrease in price of ezETH. Note that he doesn't need to withdraw native staked ETH, he could withdraw an LST asset which has greater liquidity in the withdrawal buffer.  
5. Bob profits `amount * (originalPrice - priceAfterNativeETHUnstake)` more than he would have if he withdrew under normal conditions.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Introduce a mechanism into the `WithdrawQueue::withdraw` function which checks if there is a deficit in the EigenLayer stake and accounts for this deficit in the TVL calculation. 


## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L139-L202


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`Users` will loose some of their `deposits`

## Proof of Concept
The `xRenzoBridge.sol` accepts users `collateral` from the `bridge` and `deposits` it into `Renzo` using the `xReceive()`
The `xReceive()` function takes all the `collateral` and `deposit` it into `Renzo`
The major problem is that an attacker can disrupt this whole process by sending `ether` directly into the bridge contract as the calculations regarding how much to deposit for user is given as 
```solidity
        uint256 ethAmount = address(this).balance - ethBalanceBeforeWithdraw;
``` 
Lets say `User A` intends on depositing `1 ether`, before `xReceive()` is `executed`, the attacker directly sends in `0.5` or `1 ether` into the `xRenzoBridge` contract. This will indeed cause the user to loose half or all of their `ether` because the `amount` that is gonna be sent to the `Restaking manager` contract is the `ethAmount`
```solidity
  restakeManager.depositETH{ value: ethAmount }();
``` 
Over time this will lead to `accumulated` `ether` in the contract that will `unbalance` other users expected deposit `amount`. Leading to a bad user experience overall.
            
## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Tho the protocol implements a `sweep` function that periodically `sweeps` accidental ETH value sent to the contract, alot of damage would have been done before the `sweep` function will be called. 
A more efficient method will be to include a minimum deposit amount parameter to allow to set the minimum deposit amount that will be deposited per deposit and in a situation whereby it is less than the minimum amount set, then the whole transaction will revert. This will be a more forward approach.





## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

In the [claim](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279) function, there is check as follows:

Let's say  cooldownPeriod=2 days,
There are 5 withdrawal requests waiting the cooldown period.After 2 days passed,No other withdrawal request is initiated and Bob(the owner of last withdrawal request) calls claim function with withdrawRequestIndex=5, assuming the other 4 persons that made withdrawal request have not claimed yet,Bob will not be able to claim even if enough time has passed. He won't be able to do that because the others haven't claimed yet and the arrays length still stays same,which potentially may cause Bob losing some profit based on how late he will be able to do the claim.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use ">" instead of ">="

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L317-L319


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `totalWithdrawalQueueValue` in `calculateTVLs` is calculated incorrectly, causing the TVL to be inconsistent with the actual value, which in turn affected the `mint` and `burn` of ezETH.

## Proof of Concept
When calculating `totalWithdrawalQueueValue`, the first argument `collateralTokens[i]` used an incorrect index, it should be `j` instead of `i`, where `i` is the index of OD, not the token.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L317-L319
```solidity
        for (uint256 i = 0; i < odLength; ) {
            ...
            for (uint256 j = 0; j < tokenLength; ) {
            ...
                    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
                        collateralTokens[i], // @audit wrong index i->j
                        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
```

This causes `totalWithdrawalQueueValue` to record `token[i].price * token[j].amount + token[i].price * token[j+1].amount`, instead of `token[j].price * token[j].amount + token[j+1].price * token[j+1].amount`.

## Tools Used
Vscode
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
`collateralTokens[i]` -> `collateralTokens[j]`


## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L327-L335
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L231-L232
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegatorStorage.sol#L60-L61


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`getTokenBalanceFromStrategy` cannot record the queued shares, causing `calculateTVLs` to calculate a TVL smaller than the actual value, thereby affecting ezETH's `mint` and `burn`.

## Proof of Concept
The condition `queuedShares[address(this)] == 0` is used in `getTokenBalanceFromStrategy` to check if there is a queuedShare.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L327-L335
```solidity
    function getTokenBalanceFromStrategy(IERC20 token) external view returns (uint256) {
        return
            queuedShares[address(this)] == 0
                ? tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this))
                : tokenStrategyMapping[token].userUnderlyingView(address(this)) +
                    tokenStrategyMapping[token].sharesToUnderlyingView(
                        queuedShares[address(token)]
                    );
    }
```

The issue here is that the index should be `address(token)` instead of `address(this)`. The index of `queuedShares` is the token address, not the user address.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegatorStorage.sol#L60-L61
```solidity
    /// @dev mapping of token shares in withdraw queue of EigenLayer
    mapping(address => uint256) public queuedShares;
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Delegation/OperatorDelegator.sol#L231-L232
```solidity
            // track shares of tokens withdraw for TVL
            queuedShares[address(tokens[i])] += queuedWithdrawalParams[0].shares[i];
```

Therefore, `queuedShares[address(this)] == 0` is always satisfied, and the value of `tokenStrategyMapping[token].sharesToUnderlyingView(queuedShares[address(token)])` cannot be recorded into the TVL.

## Tools Used
vscode
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
`queuedShares[address(this)] == 0` -> `queuedShares[address(token)] == 0`


## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol#L77
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/PriceFeed/CCIPReceiver.sol#L44


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If Chainlink updates the routers to new addresses, [CCIPReceiver.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/PriceFeed/CCIPReceiver.sol) and [xRenzoBridge.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L1/xRenzoBridge.sol) will stop working properly because these contracts lack logic to update the routers' addresses, which will also stop [xRenzoDeposit.sol's updatePrice()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L310) function from working.

## Proof of Concept
As you can see on [Chainlink's docs](https://docs.chain.link/ccip/release-notes#v100-deprecated-on-mainnet---2024-04-01), if Chainlink's team updates the routers, the addresses of the routers will change and the previous ones will be deprecated.
> CCIP v1.0.0 is no longer supported on mainnet. You must use the new router addresses listed in the CCIP v1.2.0 configuration page.

For example, if a [CCIPReceiver](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/PriceFeed/CCIPReceiver.sol) can't update router's address, it will revert on new router's messages, which are price feeds from L1. That will cause L2's [xRenzoDeposit.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L310) to use stale prices and put users and the protocol to risk.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a function to [CCIPReceiver.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/PriceFeed/CCIPReceiver.sol) that lets the owner update the router's address
```solidity
    function updateRouter(address _router) external onlyOwner {
        if (_router == address(0)) revert InvalidZeroInput();
        i_ccipRouter = _router;
    }
```

Other

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/549f774626b71dd13a427561d4743535a9cc0dca/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L139-L141
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/549f774626b71dd13a427561d4743535a9cc0dca/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L147-L149


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The following `WithdrawQueue.pause` and `WithdrawQueue.unpause` functions are meant to pause and unpause functions of the `WithdrawQueue` contract. However, none of the `WithdrawQueue` contract's functions have the `whenNotPaused` modifier. As a result, calling these `WithdrawQueue.pause` and `WithdrawQueue.unpause` functions are not effective, and the `WithdrawQueue` contract's functions of interest that need to be paused during an emergency cannot be paused when needed.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/549f774626b71dd13a427561d4743535a9cc0dca/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L139-L141
```solidity
    function pause() external onlyWithdrawQueueAdmin {
        _pause();
    }
```


https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/549f774626b71dd13a427561d4743535a9cc0dca/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L147-L149
```solidity
    function unpause() external onlyWithdrawQueueAdmin {
        _unpause();
    }
```

## Proof of Concept
The following steps can occur for the described scenario.
1. A very volatile market condition occurs that causes a bank run.
2. The `WithdrawQueueAdmin` wants to temporarily pause the `WithdrawQueue.withdraw` and `WithdrawQueue.claim` functions until the market becomes more stable.
3. The `WithdrawQueueAdmin` calls the `WithdrawQueue.pause` function.
4. However, because such `WithdrawQueue.pause` function call is not effective, the `WithdrawQueue.withdraw` and `WithdrawQueue.claim` functions cannot be paused.
5. The bank run continues that negatively affects the protocol.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The `whenNotPaused` modifier can be added to the `WithdrawQueue` contract's functions of interest.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L316-L321


# Vulnerability details

# Description
During the calculation of the total TVL, the function initiates a loop over the `operatorDelegators` array using `i` as the index, followed by a nested loop over the `collateralTokens` array using `j` as the index. The issue arises when computing the token values in the withdrawQueue, where `i` is incorrectly used as the index instead of `j`. Consequently, the function consistently references the first collateral token for calculating token values in the withdrawQueue, resulting in an inaccurate total TVL calculation.

## Impact
An inaccurate calculation of the total TVL poses several critical risks within the system. Given that the minting or redeeming of ezETH is contingent upon the total TVL, any miscalculation could lead to erroneous minting or redemption actions. This, in turn, jeopardizes the fair distribution of rewards among users and potentially results in financial losses.

Moreover, the totalTVL serves as a pivotal factor in determining the exchange rate between ezETH and ETH within the BalancerRateProvider contract. Any inaccuracies in its calculation could profoundly impact this rate, disrupting the balance and fairness of exchanges between the two assets.

Furthermore, the withdraw function relies on the accurate determination of the totalTVL to calculate the amount of ETH to redeem. An erroneous total TVL calculation here could lead to incorrect redemption amounts, thereby causing financial losses either to the user or the protocol itself.


## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L216-L224

withdraw function in WithdrawQueue.sol:

```
    File: contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol #1

    216        // calculate totalTVL
    217        (, , uint256 totalTVL) = restakeManager.calculateTVLs();
    218
    219        // Calculate amount to Redeem in ETH
    220        uint256 amountToRedeem = renzoOracle.calculateRedeemAmount(
    221            _amount,
    222            ezETH.totalSupply(),
    223            totalTVL
    224        );
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RateProvider/BalancerRateProvider.sol#L29C1-L41C6

getRate function in BalancerRateProvider.sol:

```
    File: contracts/RateProvider/BalancerRateProvider.sol #2

29    function getRate() external view returns (uint256) {
30        // Get the total TVL priced in ETH from restakeManager
31        (, , uint256 totalTVL) = restakeManager.calculateTVLs();
32
33        // Get the total supply of the ezETH token
34        uint256 totalSupply = ezETHToken.totalSupply();
35
36        // Sanity check
37        if (totalSupply == 0 || totalTVL == 0) revert InvalidZeroInput();
38
39        // Return the rate
40        return (10 ** 18 * totalTVL) / totalSupply;
41    }

```

## Recommended Mitigation

To resolve this issue, the function should use the `j` index to reference the correct collateral token in the `collateralTokens` array when calculating the token values in the withdrawQueue. This can be achieved by replacing `collateralTokens[i]` with `collateralTokens[j]` in `RestakeManager.sol`

```diff
        if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
        totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
--          collateralTokens[i],
++          collateralTokens[j],
            collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
        );
    }
```





## Assessed type

Loop

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L546-L575


# Vulnerability details

## Description
During the deposit process, the `deposit` function emits a `Deposit` event. It begins by checking if the `withdrawQueue` buffer for the collateral needs to be filled. If so, it populates it with the `_amount` of collateral deposited by the user. Any surplus collateral is then transferred to an `operatorDelegator`. Subsequently, the `Deposit` event is emitted, indicating the `_amount` of collateral transferred to the `operatorDelegator`. However, this event may be misleading as it signifies the `_amount` transferred to the `operatorDelegator`, not the total amount deposited by the user. This discrepancy could cause confusion for users and off-chain systems relying on this event to track deposits.

## Impact
This issue may lead to confusion for users and off-chain systems relying on this event to track deposits. The event may mislead as it reflects the `_amount` transferred to the `operatorDelegator`, rather than the total amount deposited by the user. It's noteworthy that in the worst-case scenario, if the `bufferToFill` exceeds the `_amount`, there will be a zero token approval and transfer to the `operatorDelegator`, resulting in the `Deposit` event being emitted with an `_amount` of zero.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It is advisable to update the `Deposit` event to reflect the total amount deposited by the user, instead of the amount transferred to the `operatorDelegator`. This adjustment will help mitigate confusion for users and off-chain systems relying on this event to track deposits.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L302-L303


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The use of `payable.transfer()` is heavily frowned upon because it can lead to the locking of funds. The `transfer()` call requires that the recipient has a payable callback, only provides 2300 gas for its operation. This means the following cases can cause the transfer to fail:

    The contract does not have a `payable` callback
    The contract's `payable` callback spends more than 2300 gas (which is only enough to emit something)
    The contract is called through a proxy which itself uses up the 2300 gas

If a user falls into one of the above categories, they'll be unable to receive funds from the vault in a migration wrapper. Inaccessible funds means loss of funds, which is Medium severity.

## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279-L303

303       payable(msg.sender).transfer(_withdrawRequest.amountToRedeem);
```

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Use `address.call{value:x}()` instead.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L318


# Vulnerability details

In the `calculateTVLs()` function there is a loop which iterates over operator delegators and an inner loop which iterates over collateral tokens for every operator delegator. For the first operator delegator, `withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded` is set to `false`, so we pass through if statement with `i = 0`.
```solidity
if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
        collateralTokens[i],
        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
    );
}
```
For the first collateral token, `j == 0`, but if we have more than one token, `totalWithdrawalQueueValue` will be incorrect. We will add  `amount_j * price_i` instead of `amount_j * price_j`.

## Impact
Incorrect `totalTVL` calculation.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```diff
if (!withdrawQueueTokenBalanceRecorded) {
    totalWithdrawalQueueValue += renzoOracle.lookupTokenValue(
        collateralTokens[j],
        collateralTokens[j].balanceOf(withdrawQueue)
    );
}
```

Loop

title: Calculating `amountToRedeem` inside `WithdrawQueue::withdraw()` instead of within `claim()` allows front-running a slashing event while also causing redemption of incorrect amount
warden_comment:
# Lines of code https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L216-L232 # Vulnerability details ## Summary When a user requests a `withdraw()` they also provide the `_assetOut` token (ETH or other ERC20 token). The `amountToRedeem` of this token is [calcuated inside the withdraw() function itself and cached](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L216-L232). This is followed by a [coolDownPeriod post which the claim() function can be called](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L287) to make the [actual transfer](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L301-L309) of `amountToRedeem` to the `msg.sender`.
This use of cached values has multiple repurcussions as detailed in the next section. ## Impact - **Impact-1:** - **_Malicious stakers can front-run a slashing event and submit their withdrawal requests, causing higher penalties for the remaining stakers while escaping themselves_**: Every time a slashing event happens, the TVL decreases. This decrease in TVL impacts the `amountToRedeem` which is obvious from the [calculateRedeemAmount() calculation](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L158) which has `_currentValueInProtocol` term in the numerator. Note that `calculateRedeemAmount()` is [called from inside withdraw() with totalTVL passed as a param for currentValueInProtocol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L220-L224). A malicious user who witnesses any such slashing event can front-run it and call `withdraw()`. Since the TVL has not yet been reduced, he is able to escape the effect of this TVL reduction. This also means that the remaining users who did not front-run have now to proportionally bear a higher amount of TVL loss. This is high impact because this now would become the de-facto behaviour of all stakers and anyone missing out is the one bearing higher losses. - **Impact-2:** - **_Protocol may payout a higher `amountToRedeem` due to usage of stale price_**: Since the `amountToRedeem` is calculated [based on a price lookup using the oracle](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L229) via a call to [lookupTokenAmountFromValue()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L85) from inside of the `withdraw()` function and cached, it may not be the current price when finally `claim()` gets executed after the cooldown period. If the price has meanwhile dropped, the protocol ends up transferring more than the right amount. Conversely, the **_protocol can also use this loophole and engage in malicious behaviour_** in the following way: - The `cooldDownPeriod` can be updated by the admin via a call to [updateCoolDownPeriod()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L129) at any point of time - even between the duration of the user calling `withdraw()` and `claim()`. If the protocol feels the price movement has happened against their interest, they can wait it out by increasing the cooldown period and hoping for a more favourable rate later on.
Although the two aforementioned impacts look mutually exclusive, decided to raise them under this same bug report since they share the same root cause & hence the fix is the same - relocating the TVL & price calculations. Please refer the '_Recommended Mitigation Steps_' section below. ## Proof of Concept https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L216-L232 ## Tools Used Manual code review ## Recommended Mitigation Steps It's recommended to move the calculation of `totalTVL` and `amountToRedeem` out from `withdraw()` and into `claim()` so that rates & values are decided at actual time of disbursement. This will also thwart any attempt to book gains by front-running a slashing event since the TVL would now be calculated after the cooldown period inside `claim()`. ## Assessed type Other

title: totalTVL is incorrectly calculated due to the addition of DepositQueue's entire balance

# Lines of code https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L352 # Vulnerability details ## Summary `calculateTVLs()` calculates the `totalTVL` by adding the entire native ETH held in the deposit queue. This is incorrect since a part of the deposit queue's balance goes towards refunding the gas cost of the admin. In certain situations this results in the protocol paying out more redemption amount than it should at the the time of withdrawal & claim. ## Impact Consider the following flow: - DepositQueue has `32.01 ether` in it at timestamp `t`. - Before the admin calls [stakeEthFromQueue()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L187), a withdrawal request is made by a user by calling `withdraw()`. - `withdraw()` internally calls [calculateTVLs()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L217) to calculate `totalTVL`. Higher the `totalTVL`, higher the `amountToRedeem` transferred to the user in exchange for his `ezETH`. This is because `totalTVL` is used to calculate `amountToRedeem` through a call to [lookupTokenAmountFromValue()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L220-L224) where the `totalTVL` (or `_currentValueInProtocol` as it is known in the param list) [is in the numerator](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L158). - As can be seen inside `calculateTVLs()`, the [deposit queue's balance is added to compute the totalTVL](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L352). This is of course done under the assumption that the entire balance of the deposit queue is anyway going to be staked sooner or later and hence should be a part of `totalTVL`. - Hence the user redeems a certain amount. - At `t + 1` or later `stakeEthFromQueue()` is called. While `32 ether` [is forwarded via restakeManager.stakeEthInOperatorDelegator()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L195), the remaining `.01 ether` [is used to refund the admin's gas cost](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L205) (assuming here that the admin had to spend `.01 ether` as gas cost). - [_refundGas()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Deposits/DepositQueue.sol#L283) of course uses funds from the balance of the `DepositQueue` contract itself for this gas refund. - Thus the **_enitre balance of the deposit queue was never restaked by the protocol_** and hence shouldn't have been considered in advance as part of it's TVL. Hence the protocol just redeemed a higher amount to the user under the assumption that it possesses more TVL than it actually does. Please note that this discrepancy in actual and assumed TVLs would be higher in case where there are more funds in the `DepositQueue` contract and are waiting for `stakeEthFromQueue()` or `stakeEthFromQueueMulti()` to be called, because the gas cost refund could be potentially higher too.

To visualize an extreme case, one could imagine that the user had received the shares when `DepositQueue` had a balance of `32 ether`. He then calls `withdraw()` within a few seconds when `DepositQueue` balance has incremented to `32.01 ether`. The user would receive more amount on redemption and hence will book a profit. On the other hand, upon calling `stakeEthFromQueue()`, the protocol would discover that after covering for admin's gas cost, the TVL has actually gone down from `32.01 ether` to `32 ether`. ## Proof of Concept https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L352 ## Tools Used Manual review ## Recommended Mitigation Steps One way to counter this would be to have a separate contract which handles the funds for any gas refunds. That would enable us to continue using the same `totalTVL` calculation on [L352](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L352). Of course the implementation code inside `_refundGas()` will have to be changed. ## Assessed type Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L146


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
The `deposit()` and `depositETH()` functions mint `ezETH` [based on the returned value](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L565) of the [calculateMintAmount()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L123) function. `calculateMintAmount()` has [a check in place which acts as a partial safeguard](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L146) against inflation attack where it ensures that the minted amount is greater than zero:
```js
        if (mintAmount == 0) revert InvalidTokenAmount();
```

This is however, only partially effective and inflation attack is still possible as described in the next section.

## Impact
Consider the following attack:
- Initially ezETH supply and total TVL are zero.
- Victim attempts to deposit `200 ETH` or `200e18 wei`.
- Attacker front-runs the victim & calls `depositETH()` to deposit `1 wei` and gets `1 ezETH` in return.
- In the same transaction the attacker donates `100 ETH` or `100e18 wei` to the `DepositQueue.sol` contract. This is done because any balance inside `DepositQueue` is considered to be part of `totalTVL` as per the calculation [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L352).
- The ezETH supply currently is `1` while the TVL is `1 + 100e18`. The TVL is 1 more than half of 200e18 where 200e18 is the amount victim wants to deposit.
- The victim's transaction now goes through and [as per the calculations inside calculateMintAmount()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L135-L143) he receives just `1 ezETH`.
- The attacker now back-runs and calls [withdraw()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206) to redeem his `1 ezETH`. Since he owns half of the ezETH supply, he is able to redeem 50% of totalTVL which is approximately `300e18 / 2 = 150e18`, thus making a profit of `50e18 wei` or `50 ETH`.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Oracle/RenzoOracle.sol#L146

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider using the 'dead shares' technique [used by UniswapV2](https://github.com/Uniswap/v2-core/blob/ee547b17853e71ed4e0101ccfd52e70d5acded58/contracts/UniswapV2Pair.sol#L121). For further desciption refer [OZ's docs here](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/5.x/erc4626) and [mixbytes.io explanation here](https://mixbytes.io/blog/overview-of-the-inflation-attack).


## Assessed type

Other
